articles.title: MSI's Newest QD-OLED Gaming Monitor Is an Absolute Speed Demon With Breathtaking Visuals
articles.summary: The MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 delivers stunning visuals and exceptional speed in a 360Hz ultra-wide monitor package.
articles.body:
MSI is continuing its push into high-quality QD-OLED gaming monitors with the MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36. At $899, it serves as a true successor to one the MSI MPG 341CQPX QD-OLED I tested in late 2024. It comes with some upgrades to the design, extra features, and an updated panel that just gives you more of a great thing while still fitting right into that 34-inch, 3440x1440 ultra-wide curved screen format. With the latest tech and a competitive price, it’s worth a look next to earlier favorites like the Acer Predator X34 OLED or Samsung Odyssey G8 , and it can go head to head with the new Alienware AW3426DW .

MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 – Hands-on Photos

MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 – Design and Features

Like the MSI MPG 341CQPX QD-OLED before it, the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 features a large, 34-inch ultra-wide display with a 3,440x1,440 resolution and a gentle 1800R curve that boosts immersion a touch without looking too funky for regular use. MSI has refined the design a bit, shrinking down the chin below the display and adding a special sensor, but otherwise it’s not so different. The monitor still has a basic RGB-lit segment on the back that adds little to the tame overall design, an easy-to-use five-way joystick for controls, and a power and shortcut button beside the joystick. The latter button annoyingly still defaults to launching MSI Intelligence Center (which tries to install itself automatically over USB or DisplayPort) and can’t be customized to do anything else without the app installed.

One smart change MSI made was in the stand. Rather than the wide-legged base of the earlier model, the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 includes a flat, hexagonal base that doesn’t dominate so much desk space. Though it would seem less supportive at first, the stand is heavy enough in comparison to the monitor that it holds steady even while I make adjustments to the screen position. The stand supports a pretty typical range of movements with a 20-degree vertical tilt range, a 60-degree swivel range and 110mm of height adjustment. It has just a little pivot, but since the monitor is wider than the stand is tall, you can’t plan on pivoting it 90 degrees for a vertical setup. If you don’t like the stand, you can swap to 100x100mm VESA mounting. The stand has a convenient cable-routing hole in the middle to tidy things up, though it’s too small to support every cable if you filled every port on the monitor.

On the underside of the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36, you’ll find two HDMI 2.1 ports and a DisplayPort 2.1a port that all support the full resolution and refresh rate of the monitor. Alongside the DisplayPort and HDMI inputs, the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 has some USB ports that prove highly useful. There are two USB-A ports that can link back to a desktop with a USB-B backhaul or link to a full-featured USB-C port. That USB-C port is a rockstart, supporting the full display resolution and 360Hz refresh rate while also providing up to 98 watts of power delivery. That’s incredibly handy if you ever use the monitor with a laptop. The monitor also includes a 3.5mm jack for audio output, but it doesn’t have any speakers of its own.

Just below the display is a sensor that can enable a handful of extra features. The monitor can automatically turn off the screen to conserve energy and protect the panel when you step away, and it can wake back up when you return (though it takes a few seconds to start back up). It can also automatically adjust the brightness and other settings based on ambient conditions. With all of these enabled, I found the monitor a little tedious to use, with it adjusting the picture too much and the boot-up taking a little too long for my taste, but these can be dialed in to work with the way you use a monitor. One setting could simply dim the display when I wasn’t looking at it seemingly based on eye sensing, and this seemed perfectly practical.

The MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 performs wonderfully in testing. By default, it runs at 70% brightness with Eco settings and an ultra-low power mode, but this still allows it to hit 205.9 nits with 100% coverage of the sRGB color space and 98% coverage of the DCI-P3 color space. The color accuracy is also impressive in this setting, with a dE Max of 2.02. Dialing up the settings to 100 percent brightness sees the display reach 308 nits while maintaining its color gamut and comfortable 6600K white point. Color accuracy dips a little, but the display still hits an average dE1976 of 1.17 and a max dE1976 of 2.21. It may not be perfect for color critical work like photo and video editing, but it won’t be far off the mark either.

As the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 has an OLED panel, it naturally has infinite contrast. It also enjoys very fast pixel response times. When the display is set to 360Hz, I can’t see any ghosting in Blur Busters’ UFO test.

HDR settings give the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 even more means to impress. I measured a peak white point of 366 nits for a full screen window and 603 nits for a 10% window using the True Black 500 HDR setting. With the Peak 1000 setting, the fullscreen and 10% windows didn’t change by more than a few nits, but I measured as high as 1,551 nits for a small highlight comprising less than 4% of the screen area and 900 nits for a window less than 9% of the screen area. Combine these dazzling highlights with the deep black levels, and you get remarkable visuals.

MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 – Gaming and Performance

Gaming on the MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 is a joy. The ultra-wide, 21:9 format gives games an extra level of immersion, by filling that much more of my field of view while the 3440x1440 resolution remains a lot easier for gaming hardware to handle than 4K. That’s important, because the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 runs at up to 360Hz and supports variable refresh rates to help ensure every frame is delivered in full and screen tearing never crops up.

In practice, it delivers on that promise. 007 First Light was all the more cinematic on the wide-screen, and though it took DLSS and multi-frame generation to even come close to scratching that 360Hz ceiling, the game appeared buttery smooth, helping me dash through the higher-octane action sequences of the game with ease.

The rich contrast and bold color really help present the moody, dark scenes and explosive firefights of 007 First Light well. And the 360Hz refresh rate and ultra-fast pixel response time of the OLED panel make snapping to targets much easier as there’s basically no blurring to impede me. All that speed became even more beneficial in fast-paced games like Trepang2, helping me zip through levels and put the moves on enemies that never knew what hit them.

The display can still have some trouble with glare, which spreads out wide thanks to the curve of the monitor, but the panel has a new coating that helps keep reflected light a bit darker than MSI’s prior monitors. As long as you’re not fighting with strong direct lighting or sunlight, it’ll be pretty great looking. In my office, with overhead lighting on and some daylight trickling into the space, the screen treatment was enough to make reflections very hard to see even on a completely black screen.

Another improvement the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 brings is a RGB stripe sub-pixel layout. Early OLED monitors suffer from uncommon subpixel layouts that create issues in fine details, especially text. This presents as color fringing, which can be very distracting. On the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36, that issue is gone. It had already been largely solved in the earlier MSI MPG 341CQPX QD-OLED, but here it’s not even a risk.

Mark Knapp is a contributing freelancer for IGN covering everything electronics and gaming hardware. He has over 10 years of experience in the tech industry with bylines at PCMag, Reviewed, CNET, and more. Find Mark on Twitter @Techn0Mark or BlueSky at @Techn0Mark .

articles.title: Dbrand's Steam Machine Wraps Are Here
articles.body:
Just a few weeks after Dbrand revealed its Companion Cube was a lie (or rather that it didn't get permission to make it), the company is back with some new wraps for Valve's little cube-shaped gaming PC. They include nine fun new skins with matching Steam Controller options, among plenty of other options.

The new skins can make your Steam Machine look like a basketball, black or white dice, a brick wall, a dusty old PC, the planet Earth, and a shabby old shipping package. In addition to those, there are also many familiar skin designs that Dbrand has sold for other products over the years, like its groovy inky color blends and circuitry designs, and even a smattering of pastel, one-color options.

Finally, some proper Steam Machine wraps! When it comes to Steam Machine accessories , the cosmetic kind have been hard to come by so far. You can find all of these new skins over on Dbrand's website . They come in three tiers. The Essential Kit covers just the faceplate and starts at $17.95; the Deluxe Kit is a full wrap and starts at $34.95; and the Everything Kit includes a controller skin and starts at $44.95.

articles.title: Microsoft is bringing original Xbox games to PC
articles.summary: Xbox backward compatibility for PC allows classic Xbox console games to officially run on Windows.
articles.body: Microsoft is expanding its Xbox backward compatibility efforts today by bringing original Xbox games to PC. An early preview release will see four classic Xbox games available on PC today, as part of a bigger effort to bring more Xbox console games to PC in the future. The first four games are Blinx: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge, and Fuzion Frenzy. You’ll be able to purchase and download each of these games on PC, and they’ll also be included with all Xbox Game Pass plans. If you already own a digital copy of these games, you can now play them on PC or handhelds like the Xbox Ally and Xbox Ally X. Microsoft has also added a bunch of PC features to these games to make it easier to customize graphics settings while maintaining the original gameplay. VSync support has been added, alongside up to 4x resolution upscaling, anisotropic filtering, enhanced anti-aliasing, fullscreen and windowed modes, and more. Achievements are also coming to these four classic Xbox games in the coming months, a highly requested addition for both console and PC. All four titles will also include customizable language and audio settings. Most modern PCs will be able to run these Xbox games comfortably, and Microsoft’s minimum system requirements include: * GPU: Nvidia GTX 950 or AMD Radeon RX 550 or Intel UHD 770 or Intel Arc A310 * CPU: Intel Core i3-8100 or AMD Ryzen 3 1200 or AMD Ryzen Z2 A Processor * RAM: 8GB You will also need Windows 11 to run these original Xbox games, and Microsoft recommends a GTX 1070 Ti or equivalent on the GPU side and a six-core CPU like the Intel Core i5-10400 or AMD Ryzen 5 3600 to get the best out of these games. “This marks the beginning of a broader effort to preserve Xbox games from the past and bring them to PC over time,” says Jason Ronald, VP of next generation at Xbox. “Xbox Backward Compatibility on PC is another step toward preserving the games from the past and making it easier for you to enjoy and play more of the games you already own across the devices you use every day.” Ronald first teased that classic Xbox games were coming to PC earlier this year, in a discussion about the next-generation Project Helix Xbox console. Microsoft’s next Xbox will also play PC games, and the company has been working on a disc-to-digital feature that will allow Xbox owners to digitize their existing physical game collections in preparation for future Xbox consoles.

articles.title: Microsoft is testing free, ad-supported cloud gaming for Xbox Insiders
articles.summary: Xbox Insiders can stream certain games from their libraries for free with an ad-supported cloud gaming option Microsoft is testing.
articles.body: Xbox Insiders can stream games from their libraries for free in ad-supported streaming sessions starting today. The free streaming sessions are limited to games you already own, and sessions are capped at one hour. However, ads will only play “before sessions begin.” It’s also optional — you won’t need to watch ads if you have a paid cloud gaming subscription. Microsoft says the ad-supported streaming option will only be available for a limited time during a “test period.” It previously began internally testing an ad-supported version of Xbox Cloud Gaming late last year, with sources telling The Verge at the time that the test included about two minutes of preroll ads before streaming sessions.  Around the same time, Microsoft also increased Game Pass prices, but added unlimited cloud gaming to its lowest-priced Game Pass Essential subscription, which costs $9.99 per month. Previously, you needed a Game Pass Ultimate subscription for Xbox Cloud Gaming. Microsoft says the goal of its current test for ad-supported streaming is to further expand affordable ways to play Xbox games. Ad tiers have become increasingly common on video streaming platforms over recent years — the addition of ads on Xbox’s streaming service could signal a similar shift coming to gaming subscriptions.  Additionally, Microsoft notes that cloud gaming could “help Xbox One owners play newer games built for Xbox Series X/S” without needing to buy a new console. The news comes as Xbox is in a state of upheaval, including mass layoffs, studio closures, and a pivot back toward the fan-favorite Fallout franchise. On top of that, Xbox console prices are set to increase by upwards of $100 starting on August 1st.

articles.title: Samsung S90H OLED Review: Why This 165Hz Gaming TV Is Worth the Premium Price Tag Despite a Few Stubborn Setup Flaws
articles.summary: The Samsung S90H offers an exceptional OLED panel, refined gaming features for PC players, and picture quality that becomes genuinely outstanding the moment you leave Eco and Standard Mode behind. A $1,699 asking price for the 55-inch model is undoubtedly a significant investment, but it's one I think earns it with enticing upgrades and a picture quality that’s hard to beat. If you're willing to forgo Dolby Vision – a compromise that matters even less if you're primarily gaming on a PS5 Pro or Nintendo Switch 2 – you'll be rewarded with one of the most well-rounded OLED TVs you can buy today.
articles.body:
I've been reviewing TVs for the better part of five years now, and few lineups have impressed me as consistently as Samsung's S90-series. Having tested several generations of the OLED, it's become the TV I most often recommend to buyers who want flagship OLED performance and don't mind giving up Dolby Vision. Year after year, Samsung has found ways to squeeze more out of the mid-range panel without reinventing the formula, making the S90 line one of the safest bets in premium TVs, particularly for gamers .

The Samsung S90H OLED TV doesn't stray far from that winning blueprint, but that's hardly a criticism. Building on last year's model with a brighter, more refined panel, a 165Hz refresh rate borrowed from last year’s flagship Samsung S95F OLED TV , and all the gaming features you'd expect from a modern OLED, it's another incredibly capable all-rounder. The biggest hurdle this time is price. At $1,699 for the 55-inch model I tested, the S90H is a significant investment in a time when saving is utterly crucial. Fortunately, after spending several weeks with the set across movies, streaming, and gaming, I came away convinced the improvements are substantial enough to justify the premium.

Samsung’s TV setup was always fairly simple, but it’s been streamlined into a total breeze. The dual feet simply slide into place and lock without the need for a screwdriver or any additional tools, making it one of the easiest TVs I’ve assembled in recent memory. You then simply pop on the pedestal part to the feet and it’s good to stand up on your entertainment system, but I would’ve appreciated a few more built-in cable management touches around the back.

Once powered on, Samsung’s SmartThings app handles most of the heavy lifting. Pairing the TV to Wi-Fi, signing into Samsung services, and connecting compatible devices takes just a few moments all on your smartphone, eliminating much of the usual setup friction. It’s the kind of process that gets you watching content instead of tapping through endless menus. I also love that you can upload and save your home page settings, so if you ever need to upgrade or already live inside the Samsung ecosystem, everything is right there for you on startup.

The 55-inch S90H model I tested is remarkably slim and surprisingly light at around 38 pounds (17.3 kg) with its stand attached, making it easy enough for one person to maneuver during setup. The chassis measures just under 1.6 inches thick at its deepest point, giving it an elegant profile whether it’s sitting on a media console or mounted to a wall.

Around the front, Samsung keeps distractions to a minimum. The bezels aren’t completely invisible, but they’re thin enough to disappear once content starts playing. The overall design feels understated rather than flashy. It lets the panel be the star of the show, which is exactly what an OLED should do, and even more impressive is that anti-glare matte finish that cuts through nasty reflections with ease.

Powering everything is Samsung’s NQ4 AI Gen3 Processor, which handles 4K AI Upscaling Pro, motion processing, and Samsung’s suite of AI picture enhancements. Navigation throughout Tizen feels as snappy as ever, apps launch without hesitation, and switching between HDMI inputs is quick. The Tizen OS has seen several improvements, which makes navigation so much simpler. More importantly, the processor never feels like it’s getting in the way – it keeps the interface responsive while leaving you free to decide how much of Samsung’s image processing you actually want enabled.

Samsung has also quietly improved Tizen over the past few generations. Gone is the older side-panel interface, replaced by a cleaner home screen that keeps apps, inputs, and settings organized across the top of the display. It still takes a little time to learn where everything lives, but once you do, navigation feels faster and far less cluttered than it used to. My only real annoyance is Samsung's optional Daily Board and Ambient features, which can greet you with weather updates and smart home information whenever you walk by the display. It's a clever idea, but one that can feel unnecessary if you're walking through the living room a lot.

I tested the 55-inch Samsung S90H OLED over the course of several days using a mix of movies, games, and calibration software. Alongside everyday viewing, I measured the TV using Datacolor’s SpyderPro in four configurations: Standard Mode (SDR), Filmmaker Mode (SDR), Standard Mode (HDR), and Filmmaker Mode (HDR). Testing focused on brightness, contrast, white point, gamma/EOTF tracking, color gamut coverage, and Delta-E color accuracy to compare Samsung’s default image processing against its creator-focused picture mode.

For real-world performance, I paired the TV with a Panasonic DP-UB820-K 4K Blu-ray player for physical media, a PlayStation 5 Pro, gaming PC, and Nintendo Switch 2, while also evaluating streaming content through Samsung’s built-in Tizen platform. Movies spanning modern HDR releases, classic DVDs, and streamed content helped evaluate everything from HDR presentation and OLED black levels to upscaling and motion handling.

The Samsung S90H OLED is a reminder that impressive hardware doesn't always translate into an impressive out-of-the-box experience. Beneath Samsung's processing sits an outstanding OLED panel capable of exceptional contrast, rich color, and plenty of brightness, but its default Eco and Standard picture modes are the biggest culprits behind the disappointing image quality many first-time buyers may experience.

If you simply unbox the TV and leave everything at its defaults, the S90H delivers the kind of image Samsung has become known for on showroom floors: bright, vivid, and immediately attention-grabbing. During testing, Standard Mode reached 411.8 nits in SDR, proving the S90H isn't shy with its luminance. The problem is that Samsung aggressively manipulates nearly every aspect of the image.

The most obvious example is white balance. As brightness increased, the measured white point climbed from 8,900K at the lowest setting to an icy 11,900K at full brightness. Since films, television, and games are typically mastered around the D65 reference point of roughly 6,500K, that shift introduces an increasingly cool, blue-tinted image – something Samsung users may know all too well. Whites lose their neutrality, skin tones become less lifelike, and scenes that should feel warm instead take on a colder appearance.

That's only part of the story. Standard Mode also alters gamma to brighten shadows and midtones beyond what content creators intended. While that makes dark scenes easier to see in a brightly lit room, it also strips away some of the depth that makes OLED displays such a compelling buy in the first place. Rather than letting perfect black levels create natural contrast, Samsung opts to reveal more of the image, flattening scenes that should feel moodier or more atmospheric. Samsung's motion smoothing, sharpening, and AI enhancements are also enabled by default, and while they're easily disabled, most owners won't venture into those settings on day one.

Those shortcomings became easy to spot once I started watching actual content. Ghost in the Shell on 4K Ultra HD disc looked spectacular regardless of picture mode, but Standard Mode immediately pushed the film's iconic neon-soaked cityscapes further than they needed to go. Blues and cyans became noticeably cooler, while bright signage and reflections carried more intensity than I felt the source intended. It still looked undeniably impressive, but there was a subtle artificiality to the image in Standard Mode that became difficult to ignore once I switched over to Filmmaker. Likewise, Oppenheimer's intimate hearing room scenes exposed the same tendency with skin tones. Faces took on a slightly cooler complexion under Standard Mode, and while the image never looked outright bad, it lacked the natural warmth and nuance Christopher Nolan's cinematography is known for.

Samsung S90H – Performance Charts (Standard Mode)

The calibration results reflected what I was seeing. Standard Mode produced an average Delta-E of 21.95 in SDR, indicating colors regularly deviated well beyond their intended values. HDR was even more aggressive, with an average Delta-E climbing to 24.65. In practical terms, the colors on-screen often become different shades entirely.

Thankfully, switching to Filmmaker Mode changes the conversation. Samsung managed to achieve excellent color accuracy without sacrificing brightness. In fact, Filmmaker Mode measured slightly brighter in SDR during testing, reaching 428.6 nits while simultaneously bringing the white point back to a much healthier 6,200K to 6,900K range. That gives the image a far more natural appearance. Skin tones regain warmth, whites stop looking artificially cool, and the picture no longer feels like it's trying to impress you at every opportunity. Instead, it simply lets the OLED panel and director’s intent speak for themselves.

Samsung S90H – Performance Charts (Filmmaker Mode)

Filmmaker Mode isn't entirely flawless, however. Samsung still trends ever so slightly cooler than the D65 reference, though it's minor enough that most viewers are unlikely to notice. More apparent is the tradeoff introduced by the TV's excellent anti-glare coating. It does an excellent job of diffusing reflections and makes daytime viewing far more comfortable than many glossy OLEDs, but it also introduces a subtle softness to the image. Side-by-side with a glossy panel, the S90H doesn't quite have the same razor-sharp appearance, though it's a compromise I was more than willing to make given how great the TV looks even in my bright living room.

That restraint became especially apparent during Ghost in the Shell's opening flyover of New Port City. Against the OLED's perfectly black night sky, neon advertisements remained vibrant without bleeding into one another, while subtle gradients in the darkness stayed intact instead of being overwhelmed by exaggerated highlights. Even the film's darker sequences, like Major's thermoptic camouflage and the museum confrontation with the Puppet Master, retained remarkable shadow detail without sacrificing the depth OLED displays are famous for. Oppenheimer proved equally revealing in a completely different way. The film's close-up dialogue scenes highlighted just how much more lifelike skin tones became in Filmmaker Mode, while the black-and-white sequences maintained clean grayscale transitions with excellent contrast and no obvious clipping in brighter portions of the frame.

HDR follows a similar pattern. Standard Mode unlocks more of the panel's raw color volume, measuring 93% DCI-P3 coverage compared to Filmmaker Mode's measured 75%. On paper, that sounds like an easy win for Samsung's default preset, but color volume only matters if those colors are being reproduced accurately. Project Hail Mary on Prime Video illustrated that difference particularly well in its vibrant reds and greens against the ink-black backdrop of space. Brilliant stars, spacecraft lighting, and reflective metallic surfaces all carried plenty of impact in both modes, but Filmmaker Mode rendered them with noticeably more restraint, avoiding the exaggerated, almost showroom-like appearance Standard Mode occasionally introduced. The result was a more convincing image, although the limitations of a compressed streaming source were still apparent in some darker gradients. The S90H does an admirable job minimizing those shortcomings, but it can't invent detail that simply isn't there.

Perhaps the biggest surprise, though, was the S90H's upscaling. Watching Ridley Scott's Black Rain on DVD could have easily exposed the weaknesses of a modern 4K display, yet Samsung's processor handled the aging source with confidence. Compression artifacts weren't scrubbed away with heavy-handed noise reduction, film grain remained largely intact, and Osaka's rain-soaked streets retained far more texture than I expected from a standard-definition disc. There were still moments where compression noise and ringing peeked through – as they inevitably will with an older DVD – but Samsung wisely avoids overcorrecting. It's the kind of performance that makes revisiting an older movie collection far more enjoyable on a 55-inch 4K OLED.

Just as importantly, gamma tracking closely followed the BT.1886 reference curve, preserving shadow detail without artificially brightening it. OLED panels don't need help producing convincing contrast, and Filmmaker Mode wisely steps back and lets the hardware's perfect blacks create the depth naturally. Motion handling is equally impressive once Samsung's default smoothing is dialed back. Films retain their intended cinematic cadence without introducing distracting soap opera effects, though extremely slow camera pans can still exhibit the faint stutter that's characteristic of OLED's near-instantaneous response times.

Filmmaker Mode proved that point clearly. HDR color accuracy improved dramatically, with average Delta-E dropping from 24.65 to just 3.75 while the display tracked the HDR ST.2084 EOTF far more closely. The result is an image that looks less exaggerated but significantly more believable, with smoother gradients, more convincing highlights, and colors that appear faithful to the source rather than enhanced for effect.

It's also worth noting that HDR brightness measurements through SpyderPro should be viewed in context. Consumer OLEDs employ automatic brightness limiting, and HDR testing through Windows introduces additional variables that consumer calibration software isn't specifically designed to overcome. While those limitations can affect absolute HDR brightness readings, they don't change the broader takeaway from the testing: Samsung's processing has a much larger impact on picture quality than the panel itself.

That's ultimately what defines the S90H OLED TV. Samsung has once again built an OLED that hides its best qualities behind the wrong default settings. Spend thirty seconds switching into Filmmaker Mode and cutting out some of the AI-assisted features, and you're rewarded with one of the most balanced OLED images in its class, delivering rich HDR, excellent SDR performance, and some of the best out-of-the-box accuracy I've measured from Samsung.

Samsung has spent years building some of the best gaming TVs on the market, and the S90H OLED TV continues that tradition. Equipped with four HDMI 2.1 inputs that feature Variable Refresh Rate (VRR), Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM), and a maximum refresh rate of 165Hz – a beefier number first introduced on last year's flagship Samsung S95F – the S90H feels purpose-built for gamers who want to squeeze every ounce of performance from their hardware. That said, Samsung still hasn’t copied the USB-C video output found on the Hisense U8 Mini-LED TV, a feature I’d love to see on more displays. Plus, there’s still no HDMI 2.2 input, but hopefully TVs will start to pick that up by 2027.

On PlayStation 5 Pro , everything I threw at the S90H looked superb. Grand Theft Auto V showcased deep contrast during nighttime drives through Los Santos, while HDR highlights from headlights, streetlights, and sunsets popped against the OLED's perfect black levels without looking overprocessed. Fallout 4 benefited from the panel's strong shadow detail, preserving environmental textures inside dimly lit vaults and abandoned buildings, while EA Sports FC 26 delivered smooth camera pans and crisp player animations throughout fast-paced matches. Motion remained clean across the board, and I never noticed distracting ghosting or blur during extended play sessions.

PC gaming proved equally impressive, thanks largely to the fact that the S90H is equipped with both AMD FreeSync and Nvidia G-Sync compatibility. Running Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced and Pragmata in 4K highlighted just how striking Samsung's OLED panel can be when paired with modern HDR effects, but it was Armored Core VI that really demonstrated the benefit of the S90H's 165Hz refresh rate. Fast-paced mech combat remained exceptionally responsive, with fluid camera movement and razor-sharp motion that made high frames feel genuinely worthwhile. Whether navigating menus or diving into chaotic battles, the TV always felt quick to respond.

Even the Nintendo Switch 2 looked fantastic in 4K despite its more modest hardware. Pokémon Legends: Z-A benefited from the OLED panel's rich colors, while Mario Kart World looked vibrant without becoming oversaturated. It's a reminder that the S90H can elevate practically every platform you connect to it, even without the quantum dot filter on its more expensive flagship model.

If gaming is your primary focus, I'd have no hesitation recommending the S90H over many of its OLED rivals. Samsung's continued omission of Dolby Vision might sound like a disadvantage on paper, but it's largely irrelevant for PlayStation 5 Pro and Switch 2 owners, as those consoles don’t support Dolby Vision gaming anyway. That means you're getting outstanding HDR performance, a higher refresh rate than many competing OLEDs, excellent gaming features, and one of the most responsive gaming experiences available today without giving up much.

It's funny how a TV's quality is often best judged by people who don't spend their days reviewing them. My daily driver is still a projector, but after a few weeks with the S90H OLED, one of my friends stopped mid-conversation to ask what TV I was using because it “looked incredible." That's the power of Samsung's OLEDs. They don't just disappear into the background, but have a way of making people notice them, even when the screen’s turned off.

If you're shopping for a premium OLED TV and gaming is anywhere near the top of your priority list, the Samsung S90H is an easy recommendation. Its excellent panel, outstanding gaming feature set, and dramatically improved image accuracy in Filmmaker Mode make it one of the most well-rounded TVs Samsung has produced. It isn't a set that demands hours of tweaking or professional calibration to look its finest, simply switching away from the default Eco and Standard picture modes unlocks an image that's bright, cinematic, and impressively faithful to the source.

The biggest consideration is price. At $1,699 for the 55-inch model, the S90H OLED asks for a considerable investment, and that alone may push some buyers toward older models or competing OLEDs that frequently see aggressive discounts, like the LG C-series. At the time of writing, the LG C6 OLED , the S90H’s closest competitor, sits as low as $1,499 on Amazon. While it’s not quite the same, offering just 120Hz and no matte anti-glare coating, it’s always been the best value option for most buyers.

Even so, after living with the S90H TV for several weeks, I came away feeling that Samsung has made meaningful improvements where they matter most. The brighter panel, 165Hz refresh rate, refined processing, and exceptional gaming performance all add up to a TV that's easy to recommend, and one that continues the S90 series' reputation as my go-to OLED for most buyers willing to overlook the lack of Dolby Vision.

articles.title: Tomb Raider: Catalyst pushed to 2028.

Amazon’s games head Jeffrey Gattis confirmed to The Game Business that the title won’t arrive in 2027 as originally expected.

articles.title: Critics of Sony's Decision to Kill Physical Discs Call on Gamers to Boycott PlayStation for a Week Next Month, but Will Anyone Listen?
articles.summary: Backers of physical media have called on gamers to boycott PlayStation for a week in August to send a message to Sony that its decision to kill discs from 2028 is unacceptable.
articles.body:
Backers of physical media have called on gamers to boycott PlayStation for a week in August to send a message to Sony that its decision to kill discs from 2028 is unacceptable.

The Does it play? X / Twitter account , which is a fierce critic of Sony’s plan to do away with PlayStation game discs, issued a call to arms that has been viewed on the social media platform nearly 1 million times.

“Sony wants to abandon fans? Let's give them a small taste of their own medicine!” the Twitter account said. “Together with other creators we call for a 1 week #PSBlackout in August. No logins, no play sessions, no purchases on any of Sony's platforms.”

The 100 Best PlayStation Games of All Time

Sony’s rationale for ditching discs is that it’s simply following consumer trends. “In response to shifting trends in consumer preference, new games will be released on PlayStation Store and at retailers in digital formats only,” Sid Shuman, Senior Director, Sony Interactive Entertainment Content Communications, said in a post on PlayStation Blog .

“As consumer preferences and the broader entertainment industry continue to shift away from physical discs to digital, physical game disc production for all new games releasing on PlayStation consoles will be discontinued starting January 2028. Following this date, new games will be available on PlayStation Store and at retailers in digital formats only. This transition has no impact on games that already released, or will be releasing, prior to January 2028 in disc format.

“This is a natural direction for Sony Interactive Entertainment to adapt to consumer trends as the general preference for digital media significantly outpaces physical discs. This transition will enable us to align more closely with how most of our community prefers to access and play games today."

Reinforcing this trend, Mat Piscatella, Senior Director and Video Game Industry Advisor at Circana, said that just seven PlayStation video games had sold more than 100,000 physical units so far this year in the U.S. . Only two PlayStation video games sold more than 10,000 physical units in the U.S. during the week ending July 11.

However, since the announcement, gamers have called on Sony to U-turn on its decision, signing online petitions and swarming over PlayStation social media posts to express concern about video game preservation and ownership — even overshadowing the release of new games that have nothing to do with what’s going on at Sony.

Complaints have also come from other groups. The UK’s Digital Entertainment and Retail Association (ERA) called Sony’s decision “a triumph of corporate convenience over consumer choice.”

In a statement published online , Kim Bayley, CEO of ERA, said its data shows that 25% of under 25s use discs for gaming, and that discs should remain as a choice on top of digital.

“Every year, millions of gamers still choose to buy physical copies because they value true ownership. A disc can be shared with family, traded in, collected, preserved and, crucially, still played years from now. A download licence often offers none of those freedoms,” Bayley said.

Does it play? and other critics of Sony have remained determined to continue the fight. Here’s the boycott statement in full:

If history has told us anything, it’s that video game boycotts rarely result in the action they desire. It probably doesn’t help that Metal Gear Solid 4 will finally escape PS3 prison via Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 that week. There are of course instances of companies reversing decisions amid a backlash, but, analysts have told IGN , it remains unlikely that Sony will U-turn on this.

Dr. Serkan Toto, CEO of Japanese game industry consultancy firm Kantan Games, suggested that even if half a million people cancelled their PlayStation Plus subscription in protest, it would be just a drop in the ocean for Sony.

"I sympathize with physical media fans, but Sony will not reverse this decision," Toto told IGN. "They of course knew what the online reaction would look like, and they now wait for this storm to pass.

"Sony has over 120 million active PlayStation users," he continued. "Around 50 million people subscribe to PlayStation Plus. As a thought experiment, let's say 500,000 cancel in protest, that would be just 1% of that business gone — of course not enough for Sony to start rethinking. Digital is just too lucrative."

Piers Harding-Rolls, games industry analyst at Ampere, has said a lot has changed over the course of the last two generations. "Console gaming is the last hold-out for physical media in the gaming sector, but physical product has been declining in importance," he said in a post on the Ampere website . "Back in 2013 when the PS4 launched, Ampere data shows that only 13% of total full games unit sales for Sony consoles were digital (including digital-only games). Fast forward to 2025, and this digital share of full game purchases stood at almost 80% of the total.

"Inevitably there will be concerns from PlayStation gamers around various aspects of this announcement including choice, accessing older physical games on new consoles, the ability to collect physical games, and game preservation, however the purchasing trends of gamers are clear."

One analyst said fans of physical media had their chance and blew it, so there’s no going back. “If gamers and preservationists had bought more physical games, Sony wouldn’t have seen the digital sales ratios that justify this decision,” Robin Zhu, a games analyst at Bernstein, told the Financial Times .

For Sony, going all-digital for new game releases will earn it more money from every sale at a time when console sales are expected to plummet due to their rising cost. For a first-party PlayStation game such as The Last of Us, Sony will only keep around 65% of the money from a physical copy, with around 30% going to the retailer and roughly another 5% on manufacturing costs. Meanwhile, for a physical copy of a third-party game such as the Activision-published Call of Duty, Sony will get a licensing fee, likely around 15%.

For downloads, however, the margins are much higher. For a first-party game sold via Sony's own PlayStation Store, the company obviously keeps 100% of the revenue. For third-party games such as Call of Duty, meanwhile, Sony keeps a 30% cut (so, roughly $21 for a $70 game).

Photo by Nikos Pekiaridis/NurPhoto via Getty Images.

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: The New Benchmark for Home Projectors – After Testing the Xgimi Titan Noir Pro, I’m Going to Have a Hard Time Going Back to Regular 4K TVs
articles.summary: Is the $4,999 Xgimi Titan Noir Pro worth it? We test its RGB laser projection, brightness, and gaming capabilities in our in-depth home theater projector review.
articles.body:
In the projector market, Xgimi has been making a name for itself with compelling lifestyle projectors that offer competitive projection alongside stylish designs that better blend in with home decor than the ugly plastic boxes coming from many other brands. With the earlier Titan, Xgimi tested the prosumer waters. Now, the Titan Noir family finds a middle ground, offering something for enthusiasts who want superb projection (and more screen size than a standard 4K TV ) in a living room-friendly package. The Titan Noir family includes the Titan Noir ($3,999), Noir Pro ($4,999) and Noir Max ($5,999) with the key differences between each model being their brightness and contrast ratio. Xgimi sent over the middle sibling for testing, and whether for watching movies or gaming on the big screen, it downrights rocks.

Xgimi Titan Noir Pro – Design and Features

The Xgimi Titan Noir Pro is a looker. Xgimi has shown a knack for fairly elegant-looking lifestyle projectors that step away from the dated designs that look more at home in an office. The Titan Noir Pro follows that trend, combining smooth metal and stylish grilles. It looks less at home on a coffee table than some of Xgimi’s other models, but it’s still somewhat tame for a high-end home theater projector.

It’s also shockingly small and light for a projector delivering as much as it does. I’ve tested models like the Epson LS12000 and Sony Bravia Projector 7, and those things were big units that took up a huge swathe of my mantle and took some care to heft up there. By contrast, the Titan Noir Pro is only 9.1 inches tall, 11.3 inches deep, and 14.9 inches wide, and some of that size comes from the metal legs it stands on. It’s also just 16.75 pounds, and that frankly feels almost too light for a projector aiming to provide so much brightness.

Aside from the legs that the Titan Noir Pro stands on, it’s a tame design. It’s really just a box with various vents for air intake and exhaust, a couple of speakers directly in the front. The lens sits off to one side at the front flanked by a few extra sensors for handling things like autofocus, auto keystone, and an eye-protection tool that dims the output when someone is in front of the laser projection. That last feature is useful, and this model has a special version that tries to only dim the light around where it detects a person’s head, though it doesn’t do a great job compensating when lens shift has been used on the projection.

One major advantage for the Titan Noir Pro is its optical system. The optics of the projector offer zoom and lens shift to a considerable degree (throw ratios range from 0.98:1 to 2.0:1, and the projection can shift 50% horizontally or 130% vertically in either direction). This makes it possible to set the projector in one spot and shrink and move the projection to where it fits quite easily without sacrificing a single pixel. By contrast, many projectors advertise convenient automatic screen alignment but do so digitally, cropping the projection to fit and lowering the resolution you see as a result.

On the back of the Titan Noir Pro are most of the ports you’ll need. There are three HDMI ports. One of them offers eARC for audio, though there’s also a 3.5mm and an optical audio output port. There are two USB-A ports for local media or powering streaming sticks. The projector includes a LAN port and Wi-Fi connectivity, though you might not get much use out of either because the projector lacks Google TV or the like.

Xgimi does include a large styrofoam carrying case that’s helpful for protecting the projector on the go and keeping its remote and power brick all together. That power brick is unfortunately very large and heavy. It would have been convenient to have the power supply integrated into the projector, but I’ve begun to suspect some brands keep them external on premium products like this so they’re easier to replace in the event of failure.

The remote included is also helpful. It provides simple controls for easy navigation of the settings and offers backlighting on a few of the primary buttons. The remote also includes four customizable shortcut buttons that let you quickly access specific settings you’ll use often. The volume buttons are easy enough to feel out in the dark of a home theater, but both the volume and shortcut controls don’t get any backlighting.

Many of Xgimi’s projectors come with a built-in streaming OS like Android TV or Google TV, but not the Titan Noir Pro. It somewhat feels like it has Google TV built-in, because a lot of the menus are similar, but that’s all the operating system handles: settings menus. This means you’ll need to connect video sources (or a USB drive) to get anything out of the projector, but it also makes for a very responsive system that allows for quick changes to settings and faster bootup.

It might have been nice to see a fuller operating system baked in, but in a time when LG monitors are delivering adware and operating systems are plugging large banner ads on startup, I’m starting to think that maybe the better default is actually to not include one. Xgimi could have at least provide a landing screen, perhaps with previews of each HDMI input source, which can be helpful when you – like me – never remember which device is connected to which HDMI port.

One setting I wish the projector supported is the option to skip HDMI 1 as an input source. That port handles eARC audio output, so there’s a good chance it will be used for audio output exclusively in many setups, but the projector still lets you select it was an input source even when it’s handling eARC (sure, some eARC audio devices can also pass through video, but I don’t think most are used in that way), Since HDMI 1 is the first input source the projector boots, too, it won’t be useful at all for folks who just have that connected to their sound system.

Xgimi Titan Noir Pro – Gaming and Performance

The Xgimi Titan Noir Pro is simply brilliant. I’ve been using and testing projectors for a long time, and the Titan Noir Pro may be the most well-rounded and capable model I’ve put my hands on.

To start, its adjustable optics make a perfectly sharp picture easy to get without having to fuss much with where the projector is positioned. Whether low on a coffee table, mid-way up the room on a desk, or perched high on a mantle, I could easily get the projector images squared away on my wall or projection screen using the zoom and lens shift controls. From there, autofocus can sharpen the image quickly and effectively.

Not needing keystone adjustments is huge, as these not only cut into the usable image but also introduce latency, and for gaming, that’s just unacceptable.

That said, the out-of-the-box defaults aren’t exactly the best. I’m always surprised to see high-end projectors like this come running heavy motion interpolation by default, and the Titan Noir Pro is no exception. It introduces unsightly artifacts and awkward motion in a lot of cases. If you’re gaming, the projector will likely automatically switch to game mode that disables this, but with a streaming stick connected, it doesn't.

The projection itself is simply stunning, though. The Titan Noir Pro is fantastically bright. I played through several 007 First Light challenges, including some that took place at night, even while light came in from outside my living room. I was content watching movies and TV without even turning off all the lights, too.

Of course, the Titan Noir Pro looks even better in a dark space. It’s normally too bright to actually use in a dark room (think lights out and blackout curtains in place). But it features a dual-iris system that can clamp down to reduce the overall light output while ramping up contrast. The result is a picture that still can dazzle with highlights while showing off a deep black floor. On a lot of projectors I’ve tested, I can see black letterboxes no matter what’s on-screen, but with the Titan Noir Pro, I could almost never see the letterboxes.

All the brightness and contrast comes by way of an RGB laser light source that simply dazzles when it comes to color output. While a projector may never match an OLED display in terms of contrast, RGB laser light sources offer simply staggering color gamut. The colorful scenery, costumes, and bending effects in the live-action Avatar: The Last Airbender show are stunning to see on the Titan Noir Pro. With support for HDR10+ and Dolby Vision, the Titan Noir Pro has you covered for high-end formats. It’s too bad it’s a little early for Dolby Vision 2 support.

Those visual chops come along for gaming, too. I played through hours of 007 First Light on the Titan Noir Pro, and it kept up brilliantly. The story beats were all rendered with cinematic flair, the projector making it seem all that much more like a movie. Latency was negligible while running at 4K/60Hz, but the projector can also drop down to 1080p/240Hz and enable VRR (AMD FreeSync Premium). In that setting, I smashed through the fast-paced action setpieces of the game with imperceptible input lag, making it easy to dash for cover and snap to enemy targets. I normally game on fast OLED monitors with keyboard and mouse, and gaming on the Titan Noir Pro didn’t feel like it held me back one bit. The Xgimi Horizon 20 Max has some similar capabilities at a lower price and will likely work well if you’re mostly after brightness, but the Titan Noir Pro’s black levels are on another level.

Alongside the great visual performance, the Titan Noir Pro is surprisingly quiet. Though it has a good deal of power to contend with, I never heard its cooling system even from a few feet away.

Impressive though the visuals may be, audio from the projector is nothing to get excited about. The speakers can put out a bit of volume, but they don’t create a sense of space, don’t have deep sub-bass, and are too focused in the mids, creating a harsh sound at high volume. They can do in a pinch, but you’ll absolutely want to pair the projector with speakers to get the most out of it.

Analyzing a projector is a little more difficult than a display, since you can’t simply set up a colorimeter on the lens, and anywhere else the colorimeter will either block the light it’s meant to measure or capture ambient lighting as well. That doesn’t make it impossible to evaluate, but less precise. Still, with my colorimeter set up a foot in front of a 1.1-gain white projector screen, it measured the Titan Noir Pro at 93% coverage of the DCI-P3 color space and 85% of the BT.2020 color space. Having seen my fair share of ultra-colorful displays, I’d say those measurements are on the low side of what I’m actually seeing from the Titan Noir Pro.

Brightness is a little more direct to measure. I displayed a full white screen and averaged the brightness across nine points to find the Titan Noir Pro putting out 4,375 lumens. That was with the Standard picture setting and iris fully open, which thankfully doesn’t lead to a picture that’s overly blue or green as some projectors in their highest brightness modes do.

Contrast is more difficult to measure but not impossible. Switching to a test pattern for measuring contrast with two bright white squares in opposite corners and black everywhere else, I measured an average 4,870 lux for the white areas and just 5 lux for the black space, coming out to a 974:1 contrast ratio. That’s already incredible for a projector, but the Titan Noir Pro still has some moves to bust out.

With its iris shut down as far as possible, its brightness goes down considerably, but its contrast jumps. The same test produced an average 1,238 lux in the corners and 0.77 lux in the center for a 1,608:1 contrast ratio. Here is where we get to the challenge for epic projectors like this: you need to optimize the viewing area as well. A lot of light will bounce off your wall or screen, reflect throughout the room, and land right back on the screen, elevating the black levels. By blocking out most of the projection with a black velvet fabric that absorbed most of the light but had a center hole to allow some of the projected light through, I was able to measure the black center point at an even lower 0.19 lux with all settings otherwise the same as above. This would put the contrast at an exceptional 6,518:1 in a thoroughly light-controlled room.

Mark Knapp is a contributing freelancer for IGN covering everything electronics and gaming hardware. He has over 10 years of experience in the tech industry with bylines at PCMag, Reviewed, CNET, and more. Find Mark on Twitter @Techn0Mark or BlueSky at @Techn0Mark .

articles.title: The Best Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Cases You Can Get Today
articles.body:
Another year, another Galaxy Z Fold phone . The eighth iteration, if you can believe it. And actually, it’s not just one, but two phones this time: the same-as-it-ever-was Z Fold 8 Ultra that looks just like the Z Fold 7 , and the wider, passport-style Z Fold 8.

Before you pick a case for one of these phones, decide how much you want to compromise the look and feel of your phone, versus how much you want to protect it. As someone who sits at a desk all day, I like a slim case if I’m using one at all, despite what the chunky ESR clear case currently on my iPhone 15 Pro says. In my service industry days, I preferred something more protective, especially for something as damage-prone as a foldable.

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Hybrid Shield Magnet Case

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra Case (Official)

Phone makers don’t usually know for certain the precise dimensions and materials of a phone before it’s released, so my general recommendation is go with first-party cases, if you can afford it. Also, since these are brand new phones, keep in mind that this guide – like any others you encounter right as a phone has been released – is based on past experience with phone cases. For me, that’s about 17 years of slapping plastic, rubber and leather on my phones.

Check out the best Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra cases.

How to Pick a Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Case

Your first consideration when picking a case for your phone is to figure out what you want out of it. Are you looking for something slender to protect the phone from scratches? Something purely aesthetic to express yourself? Is it full-blown protection, in-hand comfort be damned?

Next, pick your ideal price range and line up your options. Look first for long-established brands, and if none of those have what you’re looking for, feel free to expand to those that haven’t been around as long. It’s hard to find case reviews these days, but cases have also just generally gotten better over the years, in my experience. Still, foldables remain a relatively young category, so it’s a good idea to find a reviewer whose tendencies jive with your own. I look for commentary about fit and hand-feel: does it want to pop off easily? Is it too hard to remove? Will it slip out of my hand? That sort of thing.

Finally, don’t forget that these are brand new phones and that case makers don’t all get advance information that lets them make a precise fit. Some brands are good about that, and will ship you a replacement as soon as they’re dialed in later. If you’re committed to a third-party option, make sure they at least offer that. Otherwise, if you know you’re clumsy or you just want a guarantee, go with a phone case that’s made, or at least approved, by Samsung itself.

1. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Hybrid Shield Magnet Case

Samsung’s official Galaxy Z Fold 8 case is usually your best bet right out of the gate, and that’ll be especially true in a year when the company has totally overhauled the physical dimensions of its mainstay foldable. Sure, there have been plenty of leaks that have let case makers generate products based on the actual dimensions of the phone, but without the real thing, they can’t truly test them.

The Hybrid Shield Magnet Case features a split-hinge-cover only thing is that first-party cases are pretty much always pricier than third-party options, and that’s true here, too — the Hybrid Shield Magnet Case costs an eye-watering $100.

2. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra Case (Official)

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is the real continuation of the Z Fold 7 design, which could mean better luck with third-party cases. Still, it’s a good idea to go with Samsung’s first-party case if you want the best fit right out of the gate, and of those options, the Hybrid Shield Magnet case again seems like the best option for the most protection.

The main trouble with these cases is the price: it’s $100. Still, that can be worth it for a little peace of mind on day one.

Spigen is one of the longest-running phone case makers, and every case I’ve had from it has been solid. I’d expect no different from this case. It features a generous lip around the outside screen, a smooth, flat-backed design, and a hinge protector with built-in magnets to keep it covering your hinge. That last bit probably won’t mean it never flops off the folding edge of the phone, but it’s almost certainly less likely to break than the spring mechanism found in other Spigen phone cases.

This case is the only one of those Spigen shared with IGN ahead of Samsung’s official reveal that supports ultra-fast wireless charging, meaning it should reach up to 20W charging, or just five watts short of the full 25W offered by proper Qi2 support. And at just $30, I’m not mad at its price point.

Spigen is also my pick for rugged cases for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, thanks to its thick design and its spring-loaded mechanism that keeps the hinge covering the most vulnerable point of the phone. The case takes a dual-layer approach, with raised bezels for the outer screen. According to Spigen, you’ll get ultra-fast wireless charging with the Tough Armor Pro MagFit, which has a magnetic ring on the back for Qi2 charging.

I have my doubts about the longevity of the spring mechanism, but if I’m spending this much money on a phone, I’d like to make sure the hinge is always protected. One thing to keep in mind is that the buttons aren’t covered. That’s one of those divisive things that some will like and others won’t (I’ve always preferred covered buttons, but only when it’s done well, which is rare.) Like the Air Fit Pro above, this case is blessedly cheap at $35.

5. Samsung Clear Magnet Case, Transparent

The Samsung first-party Clear Magnet Case is the obvious choice if you want to be able to see the colorful back panel of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 while it’s in a case, mainly because there’s no doubt it’ll fit your phone. It’s also embedded with a magnetic ring, a necessity if you want to take full advantage of MagSafe-like Qi2 wireless chargers.

At $60, this case also has the benefit of being cheaper than the other Samsung cases I listed above. Unfortunately, it appears to be made of the same soft TPU that has made up most clear cases forever, which means chances are good that in just a few months, it’ll have gained a dingy, yellow hue. Alas.

Dbrand’s Z Fold 8 and 8 Ultra case options are as numerous as they are fun to look at. The company is offering both the expansive patterned cases and a few solid-color options. The Grip Case has a rubbery grip around the outside that should make it easier to keep it in your hand (hence the name), and it will cover the edge of the front display, the hinge, and the back of the Z Fold 8 and 8 Ultra. It’s also got an integrated magnetic ring.

The cases cost up to $60, putting them on the pricey side compared to other third-party options. And Dbrand says they won’t ship until August, but not specifically when, so there’s the chance that it won’t arrive until after Galaxy Z Fold 8 and 8 Ultras start going out on August 7th.

I’ve never used a Benks case, but of the thin case options out there, I like this one for its hinge protection, which is not always a given in this category. Benks uses kevlar for its back case, a pliable TPU frame for the outer screen’s edge, and includes a glass screen protector for the front display. The case also has a magnetic ring embedded in the back edge for Qi2 wireless charging.

One potential issue I see here is that, based on one early video review I spotted online, the hinge protection doesn’t close automatically with the case, so you’ll need to remember to shut it yourself. Also, at $110, it ain’t even close to cheap. If hinge coverage isn’t really a concern, the next best thing could be the Thinborne Ultra Thin Aramid Fiber case, which costs “only” $90, or Samsung’s own $105 Carbon Magnet case.

The Benks ArmorGrid Pro for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is, at $120, just a bit too rich for my blood. Despite its superior-seeming hinge coverage, I’d recommend the Thinborne Aramid Fiber option, instead. It costs just $90.

The major drawback is that it won’t totally cover the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s hinge, but that might not be an issue for this particular phone. After all, Samsung has been making practically the exact same design for many years – plenty of time to make it hold up to punishment.

Wes is a freelance writer (Freelance Wes, they call him) who has covered technology, gaming, and entertainment steadily since 2020 at Gizmodo, Tom's Hardware, Hardcore Gamer, and most recently, The Verge. Inside of him there are two wolves: one that thinks it wouldn't be so bad to start collecting game consoles again, and the other who also thinks this, but more strongly.

articles.title: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra Review: One Thing's for Sure, It's Ultra-Expensive
articles.summary: The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is Samsung's latest flagship foldable, and while it brings the better battery and camera that I've been wanting for years, its $2099 price tag is hard to swallow.
articles.body:
The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is finally here, along with the Fold 8 and the Flip 8. Now, aside from tacking ‘Ultra’ onto the name, the Z Fold 8 Ultra looks and feels a lot like last year’s Z Fold 7 . I’ve even put them next to each other, and apart from last year’s much more vivid colorway, I legitimately can’t tell the difference between them.

However, appearances are only skin deep, and Samsung has made some big improvements over its last-generation foldables, like finally including the same 5000mAh battery you’d find in the Galaxy S26 Ultra that came out earlier this year. That doesn’t necessarily justify adding the Ultra to the name, but I suspect it has something to do with the Fold 8 Ultra’s new $2,099 price tag.

Samsung’s flagship foldables have never exactly been affordable, but crossing that $2,000 threshold, just to start, is a lot to ask for a smartphone . Now that I've spent about a week with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, I'm still not sure it's worth the $2,099 asking price, but Samsung did manage to just create the brilliance of the Z Fold 7, and with a better battery and camera. That's not a lot new for the extra $100, but as much as I loved last year's model, more of the same isn't exactly a terrible thing.

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra – Hands-On Photos

Last year, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 7 was drastically slimmed down compared to the Z Fold 6. Samsung says it’s repeated that success, claiming that the Z Fold 8 Ultra is its thinnest foldable yet, but even when I have the Fold 7 and the Fold 8 Ultra right next to each other, I really can’t tell the difference.

In truth, Samsung shaved just 0.1mm off of the Z Fold 8 Ultra, making it just 4.1mm thick when unfolded and 8.9mm thick when folded. And, all credit to Samsung, that does make it the thinnest foldable the company has made, but by such a small margin that you’d never actually notice. With a phone this thin, especially a folding one, durability is a huge concern, but it seems like Samsung thought about that.

Now, I never had any issue with the Fold 7’s build, and I doubt the Fold 8 would fare any worse with 0.1mm shaved off the chassis, but Samsung added a new titanium alloy film beneath the display, which should help prevent the phone from folding in ways that aren’t indicated by Samsung.

The Fold 8 Ultra’s display is largely the same as the Fold 7’s as well, with a 6.5-inch cover display at 1080x2520, and an unfolded 8-inch display with a resolution of 2504x2256. The main improvement here is that the unfolded display has a slightly higher resolution than the Fold 7.

However, while the crease in the unfolded display is still noticeable when you hold it at a certain angle, it’s the least pronounced it’s ever been. Seriously, looking at the display head-on, it almost seems like I'm looking at an actual tablet, rather than a foldable phone. But, then the display turns off and I look at it slightly from the side, and the crease shows itself again. Either way, though, the crease is smaller than the Fold 7, so I consider that a win.

Around the back is where the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra actually differentiates itself from its predecessor. Last year’s model only had a 12MP ultrawide lens paired with its 200MP main lens, whereas the Fold 8 Ultra bumps the ultrawide lens up to 50MP. More on the cameras down below.

At this point, it's almost a guarantee that Samsung is going to have an absolutely gorgeous display on any of its flagship phones, and the Fold 8 Ultra is certainly no different. The outer display is largely unchanged from last year's Fold 7, which isn't a bad thing, but the inner display has been massively improved.

Samsung has increased the resolution from 2184x1968 on the Fold 7 to 2204x2256. That's a minor difference, but it does mean text and images are sharper than ever before. What's more noticeable is that the display is ever so much brighter than last year's model, with more accurate colors, at least when looking at them side-by-side.

That not only helps the screen stay readable when you're outside, but it helps to hide the screen's crease – not that it really needs the help this time around. I've already mentioned it above, but the crease is hardly noticeable anymore, especially when the screen is actually turned on. You have to do some creative angling to get it to show up, which means its practically not there when you're not actively looking for it.

I spent my first weekend with the Fold 8 Ultra sick in bed, and so I spent a lot of time scrolling through content and playing games. Everything looks incredible, from YouTube Shorts to Netflix.

Speaking of the former, when Samsung revealed the Fold 8 Ultra, it showed off the ability to read comments on the side of the display when you're watching shorts. I thought this was cheesy at first, but a lot can change when you don't have the energy to do anything but scroll in bed. And, because of the size and aspect ratio of the inner display, you can basically watch the reel in the same size it would be on any other phone, while the comments scroll next to it, without intruding on anything. That's not for everyone, but it's now my favorite way to consume vertical video.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 5, just like the Galaxy S26 Ultra that debuted at the beginning of 2026. However, because the chipset in the Fold 8 Ultra has significantly less space to cool itself, it doesn't reach quite the same heights as Samsung's slab.

Due to how thin the Fold 8 Ultra is, the high-end processor heats the chassis up incredibly quickly. Even before I started pushing it in a game or another heavy workload, when all I was doing on it was installing a bunch of apps, I noticed that the phone was very warm to the touch. Now, to be fair, when I’m reviewing a phone I tend to just rapid-fire install everything at once, so the Fold 8 Ultra was doing some work.

When I booted up Arknights: Endfield, I noticed that the phone got even warmer, to the point where it was uncomfortable to hold. You can mitigate this by putting a case on the phone, but even the display can start to feel warm when you’ve been playing games for a while. This was a problem with the Fold 7 as well, and while I got used to it last year, it’s a little disappointing that Samsung hasn’t found a way to dissipate heat a little better. But I guess everything’s in service to having a super thin phone.

Samsung claims that it’s improved the cooling solution with a new graphite cooling structure, which supposedly helps dissipate heat. But, there’s only so much Samsung can do with a phone this thin. Luckily, until you boot up a demanding game, most things you do with a smartphone are bursty enough that you don’t really have to worry about throttling. As soon as you start playing around with CapCut or playing games, though, be prepared for a hot slab of glass in your hand.

I was initially worried that the Fold 8 would throttle quite a bit, like the Fold 7 did. But I was surprised that the phone kept up to 79% of its performance through the Steel Nomad Light stress test. That's better than the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, which only kept 66% of its performance over repeated tests.

The S26 Ultra had higher performance at first, with an initial score of 2,082 points, compared to 1,641 from the Fold 8 Ultra. However, the S26 Ultra dropped down to 1,374 points at its lowest point, compared to 1,296 points from the Fold 8 Ultra. So, the thicker S26 Ultra starts off 24% faster than the Fold, but ends up just 6% faster over a long gaming session.

There's always going to be a tradeoff when you go with a foldable phone like this, and I'd personally take better endurance over faster peak performance, at least with the way I use my phone.

I still wouldn't necessarily recommend the Fold 8 Ultra if all you're looking for is a gaming phone, though. That mostly comes down to how hot the phone gets. After testing the Fold 8 Ultra for a few days, it never got quite as hot as it did on the first day, but the cover display will get quite toasty when you're playing games with the phone open for a while. That meant I had to make quite the annoying choice: either deal with the large camera bump in between two of my fingers when playing games, or hold the phone by the warm cover display. Luckily, putting a decent case on the phone can help the camera bump feel a little less intrusive.

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra – Camera Samples

I'm going to come right out of the gate and say that I don't spend a lot of time shooting photos on my phone, that's what my DSLR is for, after all. However, I've spent a bit of time with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra's camera, particularly at night, and it does seem a bit better than last year's Fold, especially when zooming in on distant objects.

That's mostly because Samsung updated its ultrawide lens with a 50MP sensor, up from the 12MP shooter in last year's Fold 7. It also doesn't hurt that Samsung added an actual optical zoom function to the camera, instead of just relying on AI to fill in the details.

Beyond the physical improvements to the Fold 8 Ultra's actual camera lenses, Samsung is again leaning on AI to do a lot of the heavy lifting. You can avoid that by using a third-party camera app, but the software 'enhancements' aren't super obvious this time around.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra does finally include a better battery, too. For years, Samsung has been shoving slightly smaller batteries into its foldables to save space, but the company has found a way to include a 5000mAh battery in the Fold 8 Ultra, rather than the 4400mAh battery found in the Fold 7. Samsung claims that the phone will last for 27 hours of video playback, and I’ll believe that when I see it, but either way it should last a bit longer than the Fold 7.

With how long phone batteries last these days, I don't really have a way to definitively test how long the battery lasts. However, even after only charging the battery up to 80%-ish each day, there hasn't been a day where the phone hasn't lasted a full day. According to Samsung's battery info meter, the Fold 8 Ultra's battery will last be about one day and 13 hours on a full charge. My Galaxy S26 Ultra, for comparison estimates about two days and four hours on a single charge.

Either way, the Fold 8 Ultra should last a full day, pretty much no matter what you put it through. Obviously, if you use it in tablet mode a lot, you're going to burn through the battery a little faster, but it does help that OLED displays aren't as power-hungry as phone displays used to be.

articles.title: X-Men '97 Season 2 Delivers a very Satisfying, Character-Driven New Chapter as Colossus Finally Enters the Spotlight
articles.summary: X-Men '97 somehow finds room to squeeze in a Colossus and Nightcrawler-focused episode before Season 2's endgame, and we couldn't be happier. Read our review of "Strange Land, Savage Heart."
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains full spoilers for X-Men '97 Season 2, Episode 7!

As strong as the response has been to X-Men '97 so far, I think a lot of X-fans have been pretty impatient for the series to get to Colossus. This is a character who never fully received his due in the original series, and if Nightcrawler can enjoy increased time in the spotlight, why not Piotr Rasputin? Those fans are likely to be thrilled by "Strange Land, Savage Heart," an episode that masterfully explores the compassion that defines both Colossus (Robert Cait) and Nightcrawler (Adrian Hough).

Episode 7 opens by showing us what Colossus and his sister Illyana (Courtenay Taylor) were up to on the day Genosha died. I'll grant that it's pretty disappointing to see a character with as much unexplored potential as Illyana killed off so abruptly, though my hope is that the series can still use her death as an excuse to get into the Limbo of it all eventually. For now, though, her death becomes a logical catalyst for Colossus to do exactly what he did back in the '90s comics - turn his back on Xavier's dream and throw his lot in with the Acolytes.

From there, Episode 7 establishes a new conflict to test the fledgling X-Corp team. Exodus (Bo Poraj) and his Acolytes have kidnapped noted scumbag bigot Graydon Creed (Ben Pronsky), forcing our heroes into action to stop Creed's assassination. The series continues to make the most of the complicated political climate it's established, with this episode really demonstrating the value of having X-Corp operating alongside the more traditional, school-focused X-Men. I only wish Season 2 had a few more episodes, so we could continue seeing the two teams carrying out missions and dealing with this chaotic new reality. But with two chapters left in Season 2, I suspect it's all Apocalypse from here on out.

Episode 7 could have given us a straightforward conflict between X-Corp and the Acolytes, but I'm glad that's not quite the path it chooses. We've already seen the X-Men outnumbered and fighting for their lives in the Savage Land. Instead, this showdown takes a more philosophical and ideological slant, one that befits a storyline with Nightcrawler and Colossus at the helm. This is a war of words more than it is of fists and energy blasts. Though we do still get a little jungle action courtesy of Bishop (Isaac-Robinson Smith) and Polaris (Carolina Ravassa), a duo who are quickly developing into a very entertaining pair.

The trial sequence is handled nicely, with both Exodus and Nightcrawler making a strong case for their respective points of view. The outcome is also well done, with Exodus jumping the gun to execute Creed and viewers only learning later that, no, Nightcrawler did not successfully appeal to Colossus' sense of mercy. The series may have little interest in Illyana right now, but it definitely makes the most of Colossus here. That's why it's so exciting to see the steel-skinned mutant joining up with the Xavier Insititute at the end. I look forward to seeing this series dig into the threeway friendship between Colossus, Nightcrawler, and Wolverine.

Finally, this episode ends with another tease of what's to come in the final two chapters of Season 2, as X-Force encounters the desicated remains of Apocalypse in Greece. That raises some intriguing new questions for the final conflict. Is Gambit a mere Horseman, or has he become the new host for Apocalypse himself? With the next episode being called "The Dead Man's Hand," I doubt we have long to wait before finding out.

articles.title: Xbox outage shouldn’t have affected games on disc, Microsoft confirms
articles.summary: While physical Xbox game discs are subject to licensing inspections, that shouldn’t have prevented them from working during this week’s outage.
articles.body: After the recent Xbox outage even blocked people from playing offline disc-based console games, Microsoft is trying to soothe concerns that you don’t truly own anything under Xbox’s license system. In a statement to The Verge, Xbox technology chief Scott Van Vliet says that while physical game discs are subject to licensing inspections, that shouldn’t have prevented them from working during this week’s outage, or while consoles are offline. “We’re looking into reports that some players were unable to access games using discs as expected during the service interruption. Disc-based entitlement checks should not prevent players from accessing their games and this is by design,” said Van Vliet.  The massive outage started on Sunday night, and lasted for almost a day. It prevented some console owners from playing games — both physical and digital, as confirmed by the Xbox status page — alongside logging in, launching apps, or finding games on the Xbox store. Xbox confirmed the issues had been resolved on Monday evening. In an update on X yesterday, Van Vliet blamed the outage on an external licensing service, but didn’t explain why disc-based games were impacted at the time. Now, Van Vliet tells The Verge that Xbox has identified an issue that prevented some consoles “from correctly using saved entitlements during the outage,” noting that “Offline mode is also designed to rely on those saved entitlements.” A fix to prevent this from happening again will be rolled out in an upcoming update. These “entitlements” are digital rights licenses that indicate what content a user is entitled to access.
