As Tom’s Hardware notes, game discs for Xbox One and Series S/X consoles include encrypted files with the licenses attached, but games with full disc support “should be available for offline use” according to Microsoft’s own documentation. The outage occurred as tensions around the preservation of physical media are already running high. Sony is set to cease all production of physical PlayStation game discs by 2028, and Xbox is currently testing a disc-to-digital feature that will allow console owners to create digital copies of games they physically own. If Microsoft wants to assure people that those discs will still work after being digitized, it needs to make sure they’re playable now in their physical state.

articles.title: Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 feels like the future
articles.summary: The Z Fold 8 looks unusual at first, with its squat outer screen, but you get used to it fast — and the wide inner display makes it all worthwhile.
articles.body: Is this the future of foldable phones?  Samsung clearly thinks so. The company has given its new wide foldable the “Z Fold 8” name, positioning the phone not as a widescreen oddity, but as the new normal, the default design for foldables going forward. Rumor has it that Apple feels the same way, with a similar squat shape widely predicted for the first foldable iPhone, expected to launch in September. Whether you want to give the credit to Apple, Samsung, or even Huawei (which got here first with the Pura X Max), I think they might be onto something. After a week, the Z Fold 8 feels comfortable, natural, and normal, despite being the shortest and widest phone I can remember using. And thanks to the 4:3 inner display — better suited to both reading and watching video — I’m using this as a foldable more than I ever have with previous models.  It isn’t perfect. Not every app plays nicely with the short outer screen, though issues are pretty rare. And the drop from three cameras on last year’s model to two cameras on this year’s feels like a real downgrade for an $1,899 phone. We won’t really know the future of foldables until Apple enters the market. But with the Z Fold 8, Samsung has already made a good case that this design should stick around.  [Product: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 | Until now, foldables have mostly been one of three shapes: flippy, foldy, and more recently (and rarely) trifoldy. Samsung has played a large part in defining those categories. But the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is among the first of a new wave of wider models. The 5.5-inch outer display is both shorter and wider than typical phones, almost the exact same dimensions as a standard passport, with a 10:16 aspect ratio. It looks a little odd when closed, but makes sense when you open the phone up to see its 7.6-inch, 4:3 inner screen — not coincidentally the exact aspect ratio used by most iPads. This feels more like a foldable tablet than any previous Z Fold yet, and perhaps because of that I’ve found myself opening it up more than any foldable I’ve ever reviewed. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: This stretched shape is more natural for watching TV and movies, giving you a wider screen without too much letterboxing. It’s much better suited to this than the Z Fold 8 Ultra, which barely gives you any extra screen space for video when held vertically and has its selfie camera cutout in the way if you rotate it into landscape. The Z Fold 8 is arguably even better for reading, giving a convincing facsimile of the dimensions of a book when you hold it in portrait. The shape takes more getting used to when closed, but less than you might think. Even when I tried the phone for an hour or so at Samsung’s press briefing I was surprised by how natural it felt, and a week with the Z Fold 8 has only cemented that feeling. After a while this doesn’t feel like an especially short or wide device, it just feels like a phone. There are occasional errors that give away that Android wasn’t designed with these dimensions in mind. Once or twice Instagram has failed to fully load, leaving a white bar in the extra space on the right-hand side of the screen; the Withings app once crunched two rows of content together in an effort to fit things in vertically; and even Samsung’s default One UI Quick Settings panel is too long, requiring you to scroll to reach the bottom. [Image: [Image: I’m not saying this squat screen is better than a regular slab phone, because it probably isn’t. You have to scroll a little more often because of the lost vertical space, and it can be a stretch to reach the phone’s far side. But there are advantages too: the extra width makes two-handed typing more comfortable (it’s not been much remarked, but this is a pretty similar size and shape to the classic BlackBerry); and because it’s so short, reaching the top of the phone is easier than ever. Anyone lamenting the death of the small phone may, perhaps paradoxically, find they’re a fan of the Z Fold 8. It helps that all that reduced size keeps the Z Fold 8 light. At 201g, it’s Samsung’s lightest Z Fold yet. It’s slim too. At 9.7mm thick when shut, this is just a little chunkier than last year’s Z Fold 7, or this year’s Ultra, but it’s still far thinner than 2024’s Z Fold 6. Those dimensions put it within reach of a standard smartphone; an iPhone 17 Pro, for instance, is 206g and 8.8mm thick. [Image: [Image: Despite its slimness, the Z Fold 8 actually packs a bigger battery than any Z Fold bar the new Ultra, with a capacity of 4,800mAh. That’s thanks to Samsung finally adopting silicon-carbon batteries, a more energy-dense design that just about every Chinese phone manufacturer has long since adopted.  Samsung has been duly cautious in its approach, emphasizing stability and longevity as it’s incorporated more reactive silicon into the battery anode. Silicon-carbon batteries have a tendency to degrade faster than traditional designs, meaning the battery life gets worse more quickly over time, but Samsung says it’s managed to avoid that risk. It’ll take a year or more to learn just how well Samsung struck that balance, but for now I’m heading to bed with 40 percent of the battery left every night, so the extra capacity is doing its job. Charging is fine, but less impressive. The Z Fold 8 has 45W wired charging and 20W wireless, both of which are good by US standards but sluggish compared to many Android phones available elsewhere. Unlike Google’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold, the Z Fold 8 lacks the built-in magnets required to support Qi2 wireless charging, though it is compatible with Qi2 cases. In fairness, that helps keep the phone itself thinner and lighter, and Samsung is likely betting that you were going to put a case on it anyway. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: That’s a shame, because the phone looks great. It fits right into Samsung’s existing design language, which I’ve long been a fan of for its slick simplicity. I love my lavender model, in a simple, subtle purple, as well as the online-exclusive “pistachio” — though it’s really more of a grayish green than anything resembling the nut. There’s no IP68 rating, which is a shame, with IP48 protection leaving the Z Fold 8 a little more vulnerable to dust and sand than rival foldables from Google, Oppo, and Honor. Samsung says the phone is sturdier overall thanks to new titanium infused layers under the display, which also make the crease on the inner screen subtler. It’s not quite as difficult to see or feel as on Oppo’s impressive Find N6, but the crease really is a complete non-issue now. The cameras might be more of a concern. Samsung has downgraded the Z Fold 8 to just two rear lenses, a main camera and an ultrawide — no telephoto at all. And while the new 50-megapixel ultrawide is a significant improvement on what came before, the main camera uses a smaller sensor, lower resolution, and narrower aperture than the previous generation, making it worse in just about every respect. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The photos it takes are fine. This is a similar main camera to the base Galaxy S26, with similar results, and roughly comparable to an iPhone 17. The low-light processing is better than I expected so long as subjects are mostly still, and colors are vivid but attractive. Like many Samsung cameras it finds fast-moving subjects tricky — almost every photo I’ve attempted of either of my cats has been blurry. The setup is improved by the ultrawide, which matches the main lens on quality in almost every shot, meaning there’s rarely a tradeoff for zooming out. But at this price, a telephoto lens wouldn’t go amiss. Compared to previous generations of Z Fold, Samsung has kept the software updates fairly light. Google’s Gemini Intelligence Task Automation has rolled out to the phone, but isn’t yet available in the UK so I haven’t been able to test it. Then there’s My FanCam, an AI video editing feature which crops in to focus on a specific person. Now Nudge, Samsung’s take on Pixel phones’ Magic Cue, will suggest contextual actions you can carry out in split-screen, like adding an event to your calendar — though since it requires you to use Samsung Keyboard and specific messaging apps, it’s a little limited in practice. [Image: I never expected to like this phone so much. The foldable market is going to change for good in a month or two’s time. Apple’s entry into the space could be the push foldables need to go mainstream, or the final proof that they’ll be forever niche.  Either way, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 makes a good case that this might be the shape their future hopes rest in. It’s compact enough to feel small when folded and wide enough to feel expansive when open. It’s great for watching TV and movies, but just as good for reading, the two things most people might actually want a foldable for, leaving the Ultra for the multitasking productivity obsessives. If I was buying one of Samsung’s new foldables, it would be this one. But while this feels like the future of foldables, it still needs to get substantially cheaper to become the future of phones. Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge --- Agree to Continue: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Galaxy Z Fold 8, you must agree to: * Google Terms of Service * Google Play Terms of Service * Google Privacy Policy (included in ToS) * Install apps and updates: “You agree this device may also automatically download and install updates and apps from Google, your carrier, and your device’s manufacturer, possibly using cellular data.” * Samsung End User Licence Agreement * Samsung Privacy Notice * Samsung Terms and Conditions There’s also a variety of optional agreements, including: * Provide anonymous location data for Google’s services * “Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.” * Send usage and diagnostic data to Google * Google Gemini Apps Privacy Notice if you opt in to using Gemini Assistant * Turn on Samsung offline finding * Samsung news and special offers * Samsung personalized advertising * Bixby personal data intelligence * Samsung customization service Other features, like Google Wallet, may require additional agreements. Final tally: seven mandatory agreements and more than nine optional agreements.

articles.title: The Nothing Ear 3A look great… and sound good enough
articles.summary: At $99, Nothing can get away with some minor flaws, especially when the earbuds look this good.
articles.body: Nothing has had a strong visual identity since the Ear 1 were released in 2021 for $99 and challenged the notion that a highly featured headset requires a high price. The Ear 3A have the same transparent look as Nothing’s previous earbuds, with a clear case and stem design accented by a solid-colored body — this time adding a striking pink alongside yellow, black, and white options. And Nothing continues to improve both ANC and audio performance. But the Ear 3A also share the buggy performance that has plagued Nothing earbuds. While $99 is an attractive price for them, be ready to deal with some minor adaptive ANC and call quality issues. [Product: Nothing Ear 3A earbuds | The Ear 3A have 12mm dynamic drivers and support the high-res LDAC codec, along with SBC and AAC. Their default sound is very heavy on the bass, and while it gives bass lines extra punch, the midrange — which includes vocals and guitars — gets covered by the excessive low end. Bassheads might enjoy it, but it’s far too much for my taste, and I expect that will be the same for most people. Where I might ding some points for this on other earbuds, the Nothing 3A save themselves from that because of the robust EQ in the app. There’s a simple interface with four presets and a custom 3-band EQ, a nice 8-band parametric EQ that gives you more advanced adjustments, and some additional EQ profiles from users curated by Nothing. In less than a minute I was able to adjust the EQ to something far more balanced to my ear (I added a downward slope to the bass below 115Hz, mid boost between 220–540Hz, another slight cut to the shouty frequencies between 2–3.5kHz, and some extra highs above 6.6kHz for a more open sound). It gave Chris Robinson’s voice more presence on “Thorn in My Pride” and his brother Rich and Marc Ford’s guitars nice crunch and bite as the song builds through the solo. And even with the cut to the low end, Johnny Colt’s bass supports the band throughout. [Image: Nothing added a pink color to go along with yellow, white, and black options. ANC performance is improved over previous Nothing earbuds, with solid cancellation particularly in the lower mids and bass range, so low drones like air conditioners or plane cabin noise get filtered out very well. For $99, they also do a decent job with higher frequencies, but if you plan to use them consistently in a coffee shop you’ll still hear orders being called out a bit. And if the high ANC setting is too much for you, there are mid and low settings that let in a bit more of the low end to ground you in reality. There’s also an adaptive ANC setting, but here’s where some of the minor issues I encountered started. While out on walks around the neighborhood, occasionally (maybe two or three times during an hour walk) the ANC intensity would quickly adjust to let in much more ambient noise and then switch back to its previous level. The whole experience lasted maybe two seconds each time and was disorienting. I tried to take note of what might have triggered it, but couldn’t find a consistent situation that would cause it to happen. In general, whenever the adaptive ANC makes a change to the intensity, it’s sudden instead of the more gradual change that my Apple AirPods Pro 3 or Sony WF-1000XM6 do — for hundreds of dollars more. The one issue I was able to figure out, also about volume attenuation, was with my call quality. While talking to a friend I regularly call when testing earbuds, if I was just listening to him, he couldn’t hear anything from my side at all. No traffic, no wind, no breathing, nothing. At one point he wondered aloud if the call had disconnected. When I was talking, I sounded clear and natural to him if I started talking when there wasn’t a lot of ambient noise around me. When the sound around me got louder — such as more cars driving by — a bit of that sound leaked through, although my voice still sounded natural. But if I started talking while there was a lot of noise around me, my voice sounded dark as the earbuds strongly filtered out upper-mid and high frequencies, including doing a great job tamping down the loud ambient sound. [Image: [Image: Both the ANC and call quality issues could be addressed with future firmware updates (my testing was with firmware 1.0.1.59), and if you use one of the static ANC settings instead of adaptive ANC, or don’t plan on making calls in noisy areas, then they’re a nonissue anyway. The Nothing Ear 3A also include 32MB of on-device storage, allowing them to record up to two hours of a call or take an audio snapshot (Nothing’s term) of up to one minute. When you then access the app, you can transfer the recordings onto your device. When beginning a call recording, a message plays to notify everyone. I can easily see the use of recording an important call to make sure you don’t miss any information (although this can also easily be done through your phone), but I have yet to find a reason for the audio snapshot. It only records up to a minute of what you’re listening to, not anything around you using the earbuds’ microphones, at lower fidelity. It’s unique to the Nothing 3A, but also gimmicky. I’m glad the Nothing Ear 3A returned to a price under $100 after the $179 Ear 3. Nothing is at its best when it’s challenging what can be done for less — and I’m more forgiving of its minor flaws. While the sound wasn’t my taste out of the box, the fact you can make meaningful adjustments and tune it to your preferences makes them more versatile than most earbuds at the same price. Photography by John Higgins / The Verge

articles.title: Blacklyte Atlas Lite Standing Desk Review: Solid Features at Half the Price
articles.summary: The problem with a good standing desk is usually its price. Enter Blacklyte and its Atlas Lite Standing Desk. As the "Lite" in the name suggests, it has fewer frills than other standing desks, including the company's own Atlas, but at half the price, you're giving up surprisingly little from a practical standpoint.
articles.body:
We all know by now that even if you have a great chair , sitting for too long brings a myriad of musculoskeletal and metabolic risks. That's why standing desks , which can move to almost anywhere within their range to accommodate the most ergonomic positioning, are such game changers. The problem with a good standing desk, however, is usually its price. Enter Blacklyte and its Atlas Lite Standing Desk . As the "Lite" in the name suggests, it has fewer frills than other standing desks, including the company's own Atlas , but at half the price, you're giving up surprisingly little from a practical standpoint.

Blacklyte Atlas Lite – Options, Assembly, and Setup

The Atlas Lite Standing Desk is available in Obsidian Black, Moonstone White, and Natural Oak colorways. The Obsidian Black is the same color throughout, while the Moonstone White retains the black control panel. The Natural Oak is identical to the Moonstone White, except it features a Natural Oak-colored desktop.

The Obsidian Black is available in Small (47.2 inch width), Medium (55.1 inch width), and Large (63 inch width) sizes. The Moonstone White and Natural Oak are available in Medium, Large, and Extra Large (70.9 inch width) sizes. Small and Medium desktops can handle up to 220 lbs of distributed weight, while Large and Extra Large can handle up to 265 lbs.

All four desktop sizes feature a depth of 31.5 inches, which is on the generous side in comparison to other desks, standing or otherwise. This extra room can easily accommodate large or multiple monitors, allowing you to stand or sit back at a more comfortable distance.

I received the Obsidian Black in Medium, which came in two boxes. The desktop box weighed a beefy 73.6 lbs, with the desktop itself coming in at around 60.2 lbs. The box with the two legs came in at 50 lbs, with the legs themselves roughly 46.3 lbs, thanks to each one having its own motor.

It's not a difficult build, but it definitely requires two people because of all that weight. For the step that involved attaching the feet to the legs, I found that having a third person helped with alignment. In any case, you mostly use the included Allen key to secure the screws, building the legs first, then attaching them to the desktop.

There's a wire cover for the center underside crossbar, which is used to run the cables from the legs to the control panel. The control panel, which can be placed on the far right or far left of the desktop, is attached with different screws using the included Phillips screwdriver. The same screwdriver is then used to attach a cable management box to the rear of the desktop. Finally, the AC adapter is plugged into the control panel and then into the wall.

Blacklyte Atlas Lite – Form and Functionality

The recycled woodfibre desktop material has a nice glossy melamine laminate finish and rounded corners. Save for the flashy Blacklyte logo on the lower left corner of the desktop, it's an elegant design. As expected for a glossy surface, however, it does pick up a lot of fingerprints, so be sure to have a good microfiber cloth on call.

A metal frame runs along the perimeter of the underside of the desktop. This is great for stability, but does create a 2.3 inch thick surface, which can limit what you attach. I found clamp-style accessories work best, but even then, you have to make sure they can open up enough to fit. There's also a centered indent at the back of the desktop that's great for routing cables behind, particularly in conjunction with the cable tray that's directly underneath.

The plastic control panel is a bit flimsy and basic, but it has all of the functionality you need. Besides the up and down buttons, there are four memory presets, which are set at the current position by holding the number down until it beeps. Thanks to the dual motors, you don't have to wait long for the desk to quietly rise or lower. It only takes about 16 seconds to go from its lowest possible height of 27.5 inches to its highest of 46 inches. While more expensive standing desks may go a bit faster and better accommodate individuals taller than 6 feet 2 inches, for most needs, this should be plenty. However, if you're 6 feet 4 inches or taller, definitely look for a standing desk that can go to 48 inches or higher for better ergonomics.

The desk is reasonably solid thanks to the weight and metal frame, although there's some shake when not at a lower, seated height. A stability crossbar between the two legs would have probably helped provide that last bit of extra shake resistance, but its omission does keep the under-desk area far more usable.

Speaking of stability, I have a love/hate relationship with monitor arms. I love the concept, but have rarely found a monitor arm that remains reasonably stable, yet versatile. Fortunately, the optional Atlas Monitor Arm ($149, but like the desk, often on sale) is more in the love category. It's well-built overall and extremely adjustable.

The Atlas Monitor Arm simply clamp mounts in the area behind the desk that has a slight indent. I had no issue attaching it to a 34 inch LG Ultrawide Monitor. One disappointment was that one of the plastic cable clips arrived broken, so that's one thing the company can definitely improve. Otherwise, it's a great first party accessory.

While the Atlas Lite Standing Desk lacks the lighting, magnetic surface, and some of the other features found in the standard Atlas, it's hard to say that most of those are really necessary. Blacklyte made pretty good calls in regards to the essentials when getting the price down to where it is.

articles.title: Tony Tells the Tale of Anthony Bourdain's Teenage Years as the Famed Chef Winds Up on a Journey of Culinary Discovery
articles.summary: Tony review: Matt Johnson zeroes in on a teenage chapter in Anthony Bourdain’s life.
articles.body:
Tony will be released in select theaters on August 7 before expanding nationwide on August 21.

Eschewing the birth-to-death structure of celebrity biopics — as well as estate-mandated aggrandizing — Matt Johnson’s Tony focuses on a few chapters in the life of Anthony Bourdain from his 2000 memoir, Kitchen Confidential: Adventures in the Culinary Underbelly. During a summer spent in Cape Cod in the mid-1970s, teenage Tony learns for the first time that food, travel, and culture might be his forté. However, the late chef is hardly painted with a hagiographic brush; in fact, actor Dominic Sessa ( The Holdovers ) builds on minor details from the book, like Bourdain’s cocky swagger and the ridiculous nunchucks he kept tucked into his belt, to create an insolent, selfish, but ultimately driven version of a man whose name we’d come to know.

The movie is a blast, ensuring that Johnson is two-for-two this year alongside his time travel mockumentary, Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie ; however, the two films could not be more different in scope and style. If anything, Tony — a more measured and intentional work — shares its tonal DNA with Johnson’s BlackBerry , an intense tale of innovators and eventual failures, which grew out of the post- Social Network tech biopic boom. It also wouldn’t be a stretch to call Tony one of the only films to truly understand and recreate what made The Social Network tick: the energy of naïve youth, no matter how destructive.

Part dramatic biography, part coming-of-age comedy, and wholly exciting, Tony begins with a highly fictionalized chapter in Bourdain’s life that sees him fibbing about a writing fellowship at Vassar so he can follow his high school crush, Nancy (Emilia Jones), to Cape Cod. The self-proclaimed author has dreams of grandeur and waxes poetic to anyone who’ll listen (drunkenly, might I add), even if it gets him in hot water. The next thing he knows, he’s working as a dishwasher in a local clam joint to make ends meet while keeping this lowly job a secret from his college peers, and sleeping on the porch hammock of his unnamed Portuguese boss, known only as “Chef” (Antonio Banderas).

The plot follows the growing proximity between Tony and Nancy in the perpetual dusk of Provincetown, but it also sees the young teen learning about the adult world — not only through his boss’ passions and failures, but through the drug-fueled sexual exploits of his coworker, Sal (Leo Woodall). Every male role model in Tony’s life seems to harbor a mysterious melancholy, leading to a fascinating set of performances from the cast. Woodall hides an aggrieved sadness just behind his eyes, while Banderas appears to live with regrets he’s long come to terms with. However, these are mere clues that inform each casual interaction rather than eclipsing the central drama. Ultimately, the mile-a-minute bustle of the cramped kitchen is where the movie lives and breathes, from the uncouth rituals of other supporting players (one particularly verbose cook is played by comedian Stavros Halkias) to the slow transition of Bourdain’s own POV on his new lot in life.

The film adapts only two short initial chapters of Kitchen Confidential, so apart from the broad details of time and place, it may as well be fiction. However, Johnson imbues the story with the spirit of Bourdain himself, capturing not only the tone of his writing (snappy, yet colorful), but the gradual widening of his perspective to consider food as a passion, an art form, and a series of local traditions. Most importantly, it reconnects artistry and artist as broad concepts, refusing to divorce creativity from even the most selfish emotional impulses. If The Social Network reframed Facebook as a romantic wound made manifest in isolation, Tony treats Bourdain’s culinary explorations as stemming from romantic pursuit while surrounded by community.

If the movie drops the ball in one notable way, it’s that Nancy is never quite fleshed out beyond this function in the story, making for some awkward (and at times retrograde) “get the girl” framing. However, Tony also unfolds through the perspective of a hot-blooded teenage boy, and includes all the things a lanky ne’er-do-well like Sessa’s Bourdain might find fascinating or alluring. It moves at the speed of rose-tinted thought, with careful visual compositions that get the point across instantaneously so they can be edited together with controlled chaos. All the while, Sessa makes for a fascinating centerpiece as a young man in search of himself, but with no way to find the right questions, let alone the answers, until he hurts those around him and learns from his mistakes.

It’s a feel-good guy movie in the vein of Richard Linklater’s Everybody Wants Some!! , another college period piece that similarly gazes backward in time while immersing you in its testosterone-drenched escapades, but with enough intellectual distance to excuse its visceral delights as a matter of nostalgic retrospective. It grants permission, in a way, to return to a time when the world seemed so large that anything could be possible, even when the weight of expectations bore down on you with unrelenting force.

It’s perhaps no coincidence that as much as Sessa channels the spirit of Bourdain, he also resembles Johnson himself in look and fast-talking demeanor. This ensures that Tony’s exploration of creative spark as something impure but no less valuable feels deeply personal too, as though the film were about eking out a daring space for filmmaking in the Canadian landscape in the way that Johnson and his cohorts often have. Either way, the result is a biopic laser-focused on the follies of youth and hyper-charged with all its vigor.

articles.title: Final Fantasy 7 Revelation Director Is Pushing for a Physical Edition, But Nothing Has Been Decided
articles.summary: There's a chance that Final Fantasy 7 Revelation may not have a physical edition, but the director of the game is actively pushing to avoid that.
articles.body:
There's a chance that Final Fantasy 7 Revelation may not have a physical edition, but the director of the game is actively pushing to avoid that.

When speaking with GamesRadar , director Naoki Hamaguchi was asked about the state of physical games and whether or not Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will receive a physical disc. Given the game is still almost a year away from release , Hamaguchi was unable to make any guarantees, but admitted that it is something important to him.

“We’re still having internal discussions on what the exact SKU product lineup is going to be for Revelation,” said Hamaguchi, “So, I can’t say anything particularly definitive at this point in time. But I am working to make the arrangements to allow us to have some kind of physical edition.”

Final Fantasy VII Revelation Screenshots

He noted that platforms like Nintendo have certain rules, such as storage limits with things like game cartridges, which can make these decisions challenging. But ultimately, he hopes to have something that satisfies fans to the best of their ability.

"Each platform and first-party have their own specific rules and regulations that we need to take into account, and think about what format is actually going to be best for the game. These are the discussions that we're having at this point in time. I do hope that we'll be able to come up with something that is as close as possible as to what players and fans are going to want, but you'll have to look forward to future announcements for that."

He also joked that fans will "rip him to pieces" if the game doesn't have a physical edition following these comments. As for his personal feelings, Hamaguchi noted he is optimistic that there will always be some kind of physical item, even if it's just a code in the box or game key card, and values the ability to have a physical item commemorating the game that fans can cherish.

“I do feel, as a developer and as a fan, that the general trend is for things to shift away from physical towards downloadable games. But that’s obviously talking about the trend. Personally, here at something like Fan Fest or at community events for games that I’ve worked on, I really think that people bringing up things, asking for autographs. I think that’s lovely. I think it’s a wonderful culture and it would be a shame to lose that. I want that to remain.”

Although PlayStation's digital-only strategy won't begin until January 2028 , almost a year after Final Fantasy 7 Revelation's release, that hasn't stopped some games from going all digital beforehand. Grand Theft Auto 6 will not release on a disc when it launches in November, and reports suggest there are no plans for that to change . While GTA 6 is a unique case and the move is likely being done to avoid leaks ahead of release, it wouldn't be surprising if other companies begin to pull back on physical as PlayStation ramps up its digital future.

Will Final Fantasy 7 Revelation be the next game to go all-digital? Only time will tell.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

articles.title: Xbox revenue drops 10 percent as Microsoft’s cloud and AI business surges
articles.summary: Xbox revenue continues to decline, with Microsoft’s Q4 2026 earnings report revealing a 10 percent dip.
articles.body: Xbox is having yet another tough quarter, as revenue from content and services like its Game Pass subscription dipped 10 percent over the past few months. At the same time, Xbox hardware sales declined 13 percent, according to Microsoft’s fourth-quarter earnings report released on Wednesday. The news comes just weeks after Xbox head Asha Sharma announced a “reset” plan for Xbox that included sweeping layoffs and the spinoff of four games studios, including South of Midnight developer Compulsion Games and Psychonauts creator Double Fine Productions. Sharma has also made some other big changes to Xbox, including lowering Game Pass prices, testing free, ad-supported cloud gaming, and making Gears of War: E-Day and Clockwork Revolution Xbox exclusives. Xbox also plans to raise the prices of its consoles by $100 and more starting August 1st. “When it comes to Xbox, we are making the necessary decisions required across our content portfolio, platform, and operations to reset the business for long-term growth,” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said during an earnings call. He added that Microsoft expects “to return the business to growth in fiscal 2027.” As Microsoft ramps up efforts in AI, its cloud business has pushed the company’s overall revenue to $90 billion. Microsoft Cloud revenue soared 27 percent to $59.3 billion over the past few months, while revenue from its productivity business, which includes services like Microsoft 365 and LinkedIn, spiked 14 percent to $37.8 billion. Microsoft 365 Copilot also reached more than 30 million paid seats and Azure revenue hit more than $100 billion for the first time. But Xbox wasn’t Microsoft’s only segment on the decline. The company’s Windows OEM and devices segment decreased 7 percent “driven by lower PC market demand.” Microsoft took the wraps off a new Surface device with RTX Spark, Nvidia’s new Arm-based processor in June, and is also starting to make quality-of-life changes to Windows 11 as it aims to regain user trust. Update, July 29th: Added a statement from Satya Nadella.

articles.title: Razer’s new keyboards drop the price on powerful gaming features
articles.summary: Hands-on with Razer’s new Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic mechanical gaming keyboards, the brand’s first Hall effect boards. The TKL and Mini 65-percent models bring features like Snap Tap to lower prices.
articles.body: Razer has insisted that optical keyboard switches are the best choice for competitive esports stars and the sweatiest of try-hards, but it’s now relenting slightly by offering cheaper keyboards with magnetic switches and a similar array of gaming features. The $120 Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Mini and $140 Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Tenkeyless, both launching today, are the company’s first keyboards to use Hall effect switches. They’re wired-only boards loaded with gaming-first features, and I’ve had a brief chance to test both and take them for a spin. The new Huntsman boards offer the hallmarks found in many other Hall effect mechanical keyboards, like programmable actuation points, faster key releases with Rapid Trigger, and an 8KHz polling rate. Their linear switches have an average latency of 0.6ms, which is of course very fast but ever-so-slightly slower than the 0.48ms of optical Huntsman boards like the V3 Pro. Razer can stand by its claim that optical analog boards are faster, but we’re really splitting hairs here. [Image: [Image: The new magnetic models offer plenty of speed at significantly lower prices, as the optical Huntsman Pro boards start at $220, and they have Razer’s full arsenal of deeply customizable gaming features. This includes things like Snap Tap, which prioritizes your last movement input on the A or W keys and makes for easier counter-strafing (considered cheating by some and banned by Valve); Snap Flex, for setting up keys to trigger specific actions upon release; and Dual-Keypress Priority, preventing an accidental movement input from interrupting two previously held keys (like diagonal movement). Those last two features are also available on the mid-range optical Huntsman V3 Tenkeyless 8KHz, and coming to the higher-end Huntsman V3 Pros via firmware update. Do these all sound like pretty niche features for specialized use cases? They are. While these cheaper keyboards are designed to appeal to a wider audience, these kinds of features are designed for the most competitive of online shooters — specifically, games with nuances to their movement techniques, like Counter-Strike 2. Razer is primarily competing with Wooting, Asus, and SteelSeries in this space, going feature-for-feature to cater to this hardcore subset of gamers. Wooting’s 80HE and 60HE v2 are some of the most praised gaming keyboards around, but Razer’s new HE boards undercut them by about $60. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: I spent some time testing both the 65-percent and TKL versions of the new HE Huntsman pair, and since my Counter-Strike days are long behind me, these keyboards feel more than fast enough for any speedy inputs my aging fingers can muster. There is obviously not much reason to buy either of these boards unless you primarily care about their deep-in-the-weeds gaming features and making detailed customizations in Razer’s software (especially since entry-level mechanicals have gotten so good). The Razer Synapse app is as burdensome as ever, but you can also use a web version if you don’t need to make frequent changes or just don’t want to deal with it constantly running. Razer’s doubleshot PBT keycaps have a nicely textured feel that’s more coarse than typical keycaps, but boy, do I dislike these shine-through legends. Some lettering and symbols are oddly proportioned and ugly, making an otherwise simple-looking floating keycap design look basic. The plastic base sitting beneath the aluminum top case makes these keyboards pretty light and portable, but the combination feels a bit cheap compared to full-metal keyboards. And there are no added conveniences like a volume knob, included wrist rest, or status screen like on the Huntsman Pro models. [Image: [Image: But the magnetic Huntsman pair both sound much better to my ears than Razer’s pricier models. The new HE keyboards create a nice clacky tone, while the Huntsman V3 Pro is louder and clunkier sounding. (I’ve got a high tolerance for noisy keyboards, but the latter can get on my nerves after typing for a while.) Preferred typing sounds are pretty subjective, but as improved as Razer’s new HE boards are in the sound department, I’ve tested other 8K wired Hall effect keyboards that are much more pleasing to the ears. For the same price of Huntsman V3 HE, you can get more unique looking and nicer sounding keyboards, but if your sole focus is competitive gaming, these new models are a good value compared to other popular (and pricier) boards. Enjoy your speedy keys and all the RGB lighting your heart desires. Just don’t get banned. Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

articles.title: Best Buy is selling an RTX 5080 for more than the RTX 5090’s MSRP
articles.summary: Best Buy has increased the price of an RTX 5080 GPU to $2,099, higher than the MSRP of Nvidia’s RTX 5090 and double the RTX 5080’s MSRP.
articles.body: Best Buy has raised the price of the Asus ROG Astral RTX 5080 OC to $2,099 — the first time a major US retailer is directly selling an RTX 5080 for more than the $1,999 MSRP of the RTX 5090, VideoCardz reports. The ROG Astral RTX 5080 OC now costs 40 percent more than its launch price of $1,499, and over double the $999 MSRP of the RTX 5080 Founders Edition.  As VideoCardz notes, this is currently the only RTX 5080 directly sold by Best Buy that’s priced over the RTX 5090’s MSRP. There are still other RTX 5080 GPUs available for significantly less, including at other retailers — Asus is selling the ROG Astral RTX 5080 OC for $1,899, which is still more than its launch price but a bit lower than Best Buy. However, component shortages and RAM price hikes aren’t showing any sign of slowing down any time soon, so more RTX 5080 GPUs could see similar price hikes.  Best Buy’s price increase also follows reports that Nvidia is planning to increase its GPU prices by 20 to 30 percent, its third such price hike this year. With prices for RAM and other components rising, we’ve even seen the return of GPUs with 4GB of VRAM like the ASRock AMD Radeon RX 9050 Challenger.

articles.title: Xbox CEO lays out priorities in memo after major ‘reset’
articles.summary: In a memo obtained by The Verge, CEO Asha Sharma told staff by the end of June 2027, “we will return XBOX to player and revenue growth.” Sharma’s memo follows a major restructuring.
articles.body: After a massive Xbox “reset” that laid off thousands of employees and spun off four studios, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma wants to get Xbox back to growth. In a memo obtained by The Verge, Sharma told staff by the end of fiscal year 2027 (which runs through next June), “we will return XBOX to player and revenue growth.” Xbox will also “improve profits back in line with industry averages,” Sharma said. “Every function and studio will own part of that outcome.” Since taking over Xbox in February, Sharma has made sweeping changes to attempt to turn things around. Previously, she has cited challenges like a low accountability margin, increasing component costs for hardware, an “over extended” slate of studios, and platform infrastructure that’s “not built for the battle ahead.” In addition to the major structural changes, Xbox made Gears of War: E-Day and Clockwork Revolution Xbox console exclusives and is planning to do more. Sharma has also set an ambitious and nearly impossible goal to make Xbox “one of the few companies that entertains more than a billion people each day.”  In Thursday’s memo, Sharma laid out four Xbox priorities for fiscal year 2027: > CORE: Strengthen our platform, led by console   > CONTENT: Grow great games into global franchises   > CREATION: Make Minecraft the world’s creator platform   > CONNECTION: Extend the worlds that fans love Xbox will measure progress toward its goals in three “stages,” Sharma said. The first is to return to growth by the end of fiscal year 2027. The second is to turn its bets into growth; “In FY28 and FY29, our Four C’s and roadmap must move into businesses producing meaningful player value and revenue acceleration.” The third is to “scale what works,” and by fiscal year 2030, “our ambition is to be halfway to our long-term daily-player goal with sustained double-digit growth in players and engagement and industry leading margins.” Sharma shared some vague numbers about Xbox’s current playerbase. “XBOX is one of the largest stadiums in the world, bringing together more than 100 million people every day, more than 500 million each month, and nearly one billion each year,” she wrote. She also noted that console “generates the majority of XBOX revenue and remains the foundation of our fandom” and that it is still Xbox’s “flagship experience.” Xbox’s OS, Game Pass, Windows, and streaming “become our platform for new players and developers.”  The company is also shifting its studio system from a decentralized model to one that’s “more focused around our strongest franchises and biggest new ideas,” Sharma said — something that’s already become evident with changes like the big new Fallout push. Xbox will build “long-term plans” for its biggest franchises “across film, television, consumer products, sponsorship, live experiences, and form new partnerships globally, including China.” Three Xbox franchises “already generate more than $1 billion annually,” though Sharma doesn’t specify which those are. To grow its share in casual games, Xbox plans to lean on Candy Crush-maker King as well as Microsoft Casual Games, Sharma said. And Xbox is planning to invest in Minecraft “more than ever before.”

articles.title: Xbox Wants to Eventually Reach More Than a Billion People Each Day, Asha Sharma Tells Staff the Target Is to Get Halfway There by 2030
articles.summary: Xbox boss Asha Sharma has told staff that by 2030, Microsoft's gaming business should hit the halfway point of its ambitious target of reaching more than a billion people each day.
articles.body:
Xbox boss Asha Sharma has told staff that by 2030, Microsoft's gaming business should hit the halfway point of its ambitious target of reaching more than a billion people each day.

CNBC reported that Sharma’s memo, which followed hot on the heels of difficult financial results for Microsoft’s gaming business , set out plans for revenue growth in the 2028 and 2029 fiscal years.

Earlier this month, Sharma cut 1,600 Xbox staff , with another 1,600 to go during the rest of this financial year. Four studios are out the door, with another on its way. The restructure will see a doubling down on big Xbox-owned video game franchises, such as Fallout, a significant investment in Minecraft, and a push for a more casual audience via the likes of Candy Crush.

Announcing the restructure, Sharma said she wanted Xbox to be “one of the few companies that entertains more than a billion people each day and gives everyone the opportunity to create and connect.” It was a somewhat improbable target that drew a healthy dose of scepticism from some quarters, but Sharma doubled down:

“I know we can achieve this goal,” she insisted. “Xbox has many of the most beloved franchises in entertainment history, talented studios around the world, and we will return to growth in 2027."

In this latest memo, Sharma went into more detail on this growth plan. In it, she said that her goal is for Xbox to be halfway towards that billion figure by 2030 — so, in four years time, Xbox will have half a billion people engaging with its gaming business each day.

“By FY30, our ambition is to be halfway to our long-term daily-player goal with sustained double-digit growth in players and engagement and industry leading margins,” she said.

To put the challenge into perspective, Sharma said Xbox currently has “more than 100 million people every day.” Xbox revenue declined 10% for the quarter ending June 30. When comparing the entire 2026 fiscal year to the 2025 fiscal year, Xbox revenue decreased by 7%, or around $1.7 billion. Xbox ended the financial year with a 3% internal margin (Sony operates at an around 10% margin, Nintendo 16%).

How will Xbox achieve this accelerated growth? “We will build long-term plans for our biggest franchises across film, television, consumer products, sponsorship, live experiences, and form new partnerships globally, including China,” Sharma wrote.

Xbox has three franchises that generate more than $1 billion annually — they’re thought to be Call of Duty, Minecraft, and Candy Crush. To reach its ambitious growth targets, Microsoft will need all three to grow further, while also growing other franchises, such as Fallout and Halo.

Then there’s the question of the next-generation console, Project Helix. There is talk of it potentially costing north of $1,000 as the RAMpocalypse continues to bite. Will console sales collapse as they become even more premium gaming devices than they already are?

Reacting to Xbox's tough financials in a tweet , Sharma said the company's recovery will take time, but it expects results in the next 12 months.

"In FY26, over 200 million new players came to Xbox and our games, but our business did not grow with our audience," Sharma said. "We need to close that gap by investing in what players value. That will take time, but we expect to return to growth by the end of FY27."

Microsoft boss Satya Nadella also touched on Xbox in a conference call with investors, saying: "When it comes to Xbox, we are making the necessary decisions required across our content portfolio, platform, and operations to reset the business for long term growth.

"We have the best IP in the industry, and talented studios around the world, and believe we can bring these strengths together and expect to return the business to growth in fiscal 2027."

articles.title: HP’s HyperX Omen 15 isn’t quite the budget-friendly gaming laptop its predecessor was
articles.summary: The HyperX Omen 15 gaming laptop offers an Intel Raptor Lake chip and Nvidia RTX 5050 graphics. But while its predecessor cost $800, the Omen is now a $1,200 affair.
articles.body: The HP HyperX Omen 15, which I first saw at CES, replaces the HP Victus 15, a longtime bestselling budget gaming laptop. The Victus cost just $800, or less when on sale, and was a good entry point to decent laptop gaming. The Omen 15 has nice little upgrades over the Victus. Its RTX 5050 Laptop GPU can play 2026’s latest games, albeit on low-ish settings. But it’s also got a brighter 16:10 aspect ratio display with higher refresh rate, and a 1080p webcam to make it a little better for non-gaming stuff.  I’d call it a working-class gaming laptop, but thanks to RAMageddon, the Omen 15 starts at $1,200 — a far cry from the $800 that made its predecessor so appealing. But laptop prices are way up across the board, and if you want current-gen gaming hardware, this is about as cheap as you’re going to find it. [Product: HyperX Omen 15 (Intel Core 5 210H, RTX 5050) | --- Component report card * Screen: C * Webcam: C * Keyboard: C * Trackpad: D * Port selection: C * Speakers: C * Number of ugly stickers to remove: 3 --- Our HyperX Omen 15 review unit is a $1,199 configuration sold through Walmart with an eight-core Intel Core 5 210H “Raptor Lake” chip, RTX 5050 discreet GPU, 16GB of DDR5 RAM, and 512GB SSD. There are pricier Omen 15 configs out there with RTX 5070 GPUs and OLED screens, but that’s like spending Acura money on a Honda Civic. On the lower end, HP still has a Victus 15 config with the RTX 5050 for $900, but it has 8GB of RAM — that’s not really tenable, especially for playing the latest games. The good news is that the Omen 15 with an RTX 5050 is pretty serviceable for playing games at its 1920 x 1200 native resolution. Last-gen games like Control can get a smooth 70 to 80fps on High preset while using DLSS. Cyberpunk 2077 can run on the Ultra preset (no ray tracing) with DLSS set to Quality and get 60 to 70fps— sometimes dipping down to 40 while driving with lots of stuff onscreen. Standard frame generation boosts it to 95 to 105fps, and 70s to low 80s in a car. Multi Frame Gen, which you don’t get on last-gen GPUs, can push that ever further if you don’t mind more “fake frames.”  Newer games are a more Medium to Low affair. For example, Helldivers 2 runs comfortably at just above 60fps on its Medium preset with DLSS set to Quality — though it dips into the 40s when the bug guts hit the fan. But Battlefield 6 was lower, down in the 50fps range while running Medium preset with DLSS cranked to Performance. I also tested Halo: Campaign Evolved, which defaulted to its Very Low preset, where it looked like a potato. On Low settings, with DLSS set to Medium, it mustered between 50 to 60fps, but with frequent drops into the 40s with lots of enemies onscreen.  [Image: [Image: [Image: While playing all these games, the fans kicked up to a decent volume, but they weren’t obnoxiously loud, and the chassis stayed reasonably cool. The hottest point, a small spot under the chassis, rose to 113 degrees Fahrenheit / 45 Celsius. But the main areas that normally make contact with your hands or lap didn’t get too warm — pretty good thermals for a somewhat compact gaming laptop. So the RTX 5050 GPU and its 8GB of VRAM can get by with the latest graphically intense games, so long as you’re not expecting a visual powerhouse. But what about living with the rest of the laptop?  Much of the Omen 15’s price has gone to its specs. That means there are some rough edges showing in the usual areas. The trackpad has a responsive mechanical click, but if you pick up the laptop by either of its front corners the chassis flexes and causes an accidental click. This is common in mostly plastic laptops, but still annoying. The keyboard has decent enough tactility when typing. But even though I know gamers love a number pad, it makes this 15-inch laptop feel cramped. I don’t enjoy typing on it like I have other HP laptops. The speakers? A little muddy-sounding — especially for music. And the ports? It has HDMI 2.1 and gigabit ethernet, which is great, but only one USB-C to go with its two USB-A ports. And all of them are a modest 10Gbps — not particularly speedy compared to USB4 or Thunderbolt 4. Gaming laptops are supposed to have ports aplenty, but this is just ports apassable. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Aside from its gaming performance, the Omen 15’s other strength is its screen. The 1920 x 1200 IPS panel isn’t particularly special, but at 400 nits it’s decently bright and it has nice contrast and colors. It’s good for games, and fine for productivity work and light content creation. I did a bit of Lightroom Classic editing on the Omen 15, and my 50-megapixel RAW files were workable at a modest clip. (It helped that I was editing a batch of under 50 images, and not, like, 2,000.) The bigger problem with trying to do creative things was the Omen’s paltry 512GB of storage. It fills up quickly when games like Battlefield 6 take up 142GB. There’s a second M.2 slot for another drive, just as there’s a second RAM slot, which is great for future upgrades — but boy will that cost you right now. You can hold out for RAM and SSD prices to come back down to Earth, but if that takes as long as it’s expected to, the Omen 15 might feel pretty outdated by then. The Omen was also fine for my everyday work: Chrome tabs, four virtual desktops, Signal, Slack, music streaming, etc. While the 1080p webcam is a little grainy and slightly low in saturation, it looks fine on video calls. The main barrier to getting work done on the Omen 15 is that its battery never lasted me more than five and a half hours. That’s far from the worst for gaming laptops, but keep that chunky power adapter with its barrel plug nearby. [Image: That HyperX lid logo still doesn’t look great to me, but I’m getting used to ignoring it. The HyperX Omen 15 is a decent gaming laptop. It’s just not the value the Victus 15 used to be. But neither is anything else. Absent a really good sale, you’re going to pay over $1,000 for anything with the RTX 5050, and usually a lot more. But buying into even the bottom rung of the 50-series gets you all of Nvidia’s latest features, like Multi Frame Gen and whatever DLSS 5 eventually shapes up to be. Last-gen 40-series or AMD GPUs aren’t bad options, but Multi Frame Gen can help keep frame rates playable for longer. It’s still worth looking for those sales, though. HP, Best Buy, and Walmart often have deals on most of HP’s product line. Even now, there’s an Omen 16 with an RTX 5060 GPU and slightly larger (but dimmer) screen for just $100 more than the Omen 15.  RAMageddon makes buying a new gaming laptop daunting. If you need to buy now and you don’t want to go open-box or secondhand, you just have to come to terms with the fact that you’re going to be paying higher prices than equivalent models from a year or two ago — even in the “entry level.” Considering the circumstances, the Omen 15 is an okay value at $1,200 for getting into laptop gaming. --- HyperX Omen 15 specs (as reviewed) * Display: 15.3-inch 1920 x 1200 165Hz IPS, 400 nits, anti-glare * CPU: Intel Core 5 210H (Raptor Lake, 8 cores) * GPU: Nvidia GeForce RTX 5050 * RAM: 16GB DDR5 (two SODIMM slots, user-accessible) * Storage: 512GB NVMe M.2 (two slots, user-accessible) * Webcam: 1080p * Connectivity: Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.3 * Ports: 2x USB-A 10Gbps, 1x USB-C 10Gbps, AC power (barrel plug), HDMI 2.1, RJ-45 gigabit ethernet, 3.5mm combo audio jack * Biometrics: none (lockscreen password only) * Weight: 5 pounds / 2.27kg * Dimensions: 13.5 x 9.96 x 0.89 - 0.93 inches / 342.9 x 252.98 x 22.61 - 23.62mm * Battery: 70Wh * Price: $1,199 --- Photography by Antonio G. articles.title: Xbox prices are increasing by up to €200 or £170
articles.summary: Microsoft’s struggling Xbox console continues to see unprecedented price bumps in the face of RAM and storage shortages.
articles.body: When Microsoft announced its latest round of Xbox price bumps in June, it only gave US pricing. Now we know the pricing increases for the EU and UK, and they’re dramatic. Depending on the model, Xbox prices are increasing by up to €200 or £170. The 1TB Xbox Series X with a disc drive is going up by over 30 percent from £499.99 / €599.99 to £669.99 / €799.99. The 512GB Xbox Series S is getting a price increase of over 43 percent, jumping from £299.99 / €349.99 to £429.99 / €499.99. While other consoles have received price bumps as RAM and storage prices skyrocket due to demand from the AI industry, none have been quite as dramatic as Microsoft’s. This is the third round of price increases since May of 2025, with the highest-end model now costing $300 more than its launch price of $499.99 in 2020. The 2TB model is also being retired in the face of the storage crunch. Here’s the full list of price changes: > 512GB Xbox Series S was €349.99 / £299.99, now €499.99 / £429.99 > 1TB Xbox Series S was €399.99 / £349.99, now €599.99 / £519.99 > 1TB Xbox Series X Digital was €549.99 / £449.99, now €749.99 / £619.99 > 1TB Xbox Series X Disc was €599.99 / £499.99, now €799.99 / £669.99

articles.title: The Targaryens Remind Us Why Their Civil War Is Called the Dance of Dragons in This Week's Lizard-Rich Episode of House of the Dragon
articles.summary: House of the Dragon Season 3, Episode 7 Recap and Review: The Targaryens remind us why their civil war is called the Dance of Dragons in a lizard-rich episode.
articles.body:
Full spoilers follow for House of the Dragon Season 3, Episode 7.

There’s a great fundamental issue at the heart of House Targaryen that has too often gone unexamined and underexplained in House of the Dragon, despite its name, and that’s how the dragons work. This show has followed its predecessor’s example in leaning into the human drama of Westeros and away from its more fantastical aspects, but there’s a limit to how well that works, and in this engaging and generally fun episode (unless you’re Emma D’Arcy’s Rhaenyra), they finally get their teeth, and claws, into it.

The question is what, exactly, is the relationship between rider and dragon for House Targaryen and their allies? What are the obligations between rider and beast, if any? How (or how much) do they communicate? Do their feelings affect one another? There have been suggestions, occasionally, that having a dragon may affect one’s temperament (or that one’s temperament may affect one’s chance of bonding with a dragon); there’s a clear implication that losing your dragon is a form of emasculation for Tom Glynn-Carney’s Aegon II and the late Viserys (Paddy Considine). But it’s never been clear if it matters, and how much, beyond prestige in the internal Targaryen pecking order.

This time, however, we get some key hints that there’s more of a link than perhaps we were shown before. The scenes of dragon conflict, as when Rhaenyra finally discovers that her husband Daemon (Matt Smith) has been lying to her to protect his daughter Rhaena (Phoebe Campbell) and flies to confront both along with Addam (Clinton Liberty), suggest an emotional closeness. As the humans shout at one another, their dragons roar and bellow and, occasionally, threaten to flame, and it’s absolutely clear that they’re reflecting something human and vice versa. Later in the episode we see Aegon screaming in sync with his steed Sunfyre, both disfigured and defiant and apparently on the verge of madness, and the impression is confirmed.

The episode also begins with a dream of Helaena (Phia Saban) and in fact heavily features her dreams - or perhaps Dreams, of the prophetic kind. So what does it mean that she sees herself on her dragon, Dreamfyre, shouting “Dracarys!” as an angry mob rushes at them in the Dragonpit? What does it mean that she imagines a quiet life on the farm with her children (it looks like both Jaehaera and a younger boy, presumably the one she’s currently expecting) when an eclipse occurs? Rhaenyra is putting her younger half-sister under pressure to share her Dreams, desperate for reassurance that she is on the right path, but it’s not clear that Helaena has any such comfort to offer.

Of course, that’s far from the most screwed-up dream this episode. That prize goes to Aemond (Ewan Mitchell), who sees his mother Alicent (Olivia Cooke) arriving at Harrenhal and the two of them tumbling into bed together before realising it was all a dream. And then he wakes up and she has indeed arrived. Awkward! This may not be the dictionary definition of “headfuck” but it should be. Alicent babbles, Aemond is more taciturn, Alys (Gayle Rankin) is rightly suspicious of the newcomer. Aemond shares her wariness to a degree, enough to murder Alicent’s travelling companion (who, to be fair, is there to help assassinate him), but not enough to refuse the poisoned nightcap she offers after the world’s most awkward meet-the-mother-in-law dinner. Alicent creeps out of the castle and into the wind, figuring that the job is done and stricken by it, but Aemond stumbles to Alys at the first stomach pangs so he’ll probably recover.

Meanwhile Rhaenyra is still pulled in every direction and failing to deal with any of her problems, and it creates a vacuum at the seat of her power. Torrhen Manderly (Dan Fogler) is furious that he’s been left to hold the bag for everyone’s money woes – something that is literally his job -- and Mysaria (Sonoya Mizuno) is trying to make herself a conduit to the people and being rejected on all sides. She manages to, ahem, reconnect with Rhaenyra herself by the end of the episode (is that what the kids are calling it these days?), but she’s still caught in-between a regal rock and a common hard place, and that’s a tough situation to be in.

Daemon, too, is looking more woebegone than we have seen him before. He has belatedly realised that his daughter may desperately need him, which by Westeros standards makes him father of the year against almost zero competition, but in trying to protect her he has broken his wife’s heart. And also, he’s almost entirely failed to protect her; he’s just separated her from her dragon and gone home. He’s also increasingly floundering in council, suffering the same myopia as Rhaenyra and failing to look past his personal passions to the big picture.

It’s a mess. The only person laughing – and laughing a lot this time -- is Ormund (James Norton), who’s riding high despite the imminent arrival of the Rivermen outside his hastily built walls and the fact that he’s probably in last place in that aforementioned father of the year competition. He holds Corlys Velaryon (Steve Toussaint) captive, and cuts off his finger as proof of life to attempt to keep the Velaryon men from plugging the policing gap in King’s Landing (an efficient and speedy postal system still appears to be operating between Tumbleton and King’s Landing). He’s also keeping his ward Daeron (Benjamin Evan Ainsworth) and cousin Gwayne (Freddie Fox) in the dark about his plans, to their increasing frustration. And, in the episode’s final big reveal, he’s courting the dragon rider Ulf (Tom Bennett), trying to turn him from Rhaenyra’s service with the promise that he’ll become Lord of (Corlys’) Driftmark fortress, and also that he’ll be free to drink whenever he wants. It’s not clear which is the bigger inducement to the big ol’ lush but it could spell big trouble for Rhaenyra if he turns.

So the tally was six dragons for Rhaenyra (Syrax, Caraxes, Vermithor, Silverwing, Moondancer, Seasmoke) plus one unreliable wannabe ally (Sheepstealer). Then there was one MIA for the Greens (Vhagar) and one out of combat (Dreamfyre). Now there are five for Rhaenyra, two of them perhaps injured; two for the Greens (it looks like Ulf’s Silverwing and the resurgent Sunfyre) and potentially two MIA dragons (Sheepstealer and Vhagar, still) to potentially change that calculus further. It’s all at play going into the Season 3 finale, and it’s still not clear how far these flames could spread.

articles.title: 'Final Nail in the Coffin': Xbox Price Rises Revealed, Leaving Fans Stunned as Series X/S Spike By More Than a Third in Europe
articles.summary: Microsoft has increased the price of its consoles by more than a third in Europe, leaving fans stunned at how much an Xbox Series X/S now costs.
articles.body:
Microsoft has increased the price of its consoles by more than a third in Europe, leaving fans stunned at how much an Xbox Series X/S now costs.

While these price rises are not a surprise — Microsoft announced they were coming back in June — the exact pricing for Xbox Series X and S in mainland Europe and the UK remained under wraps until now.

In the U.S., Microsoft previously stated that the 512GB Series S would rise by $100, while 1TB Series models would rise by $150 — increases that equate to around £74 and £111. The 2TB model will be discontinued completely, meanwhile — presumably because it would have become too expensive to be worthwhile making.

But in the UK and mainland Europe, the actual price rises in pounds and euros are much steeper. The 512GB Series S has jumped from £299 to £429, an increase of £130, while its 1TB model has increased from £349 to £519, a leap of £170.

Worse still are the increases for Series X models, with the 1TB Digital up from £449 to £619 (£170), but the 1TB Disc model up from £449 to £669 — whopping 48% increase, and £220 difference.

Fans have slammed the huge changes, which are far higher than expected. "Final nail in the coffin," wrote one user on the video game forum ResetEra . "Great strategy, that'll definitely lead to more sales," said another. "There is no way in 2026 I would be paying nearly £700 for a Series X with a disc drive," wrote a third.

"Still trying to process how a console that was sold for €499 almost six years ago is now €799," noted another fan. "The Series S 1TB is now €100 more expensive than the Series X at launch. This is just mindblowing."

Xbox Series S (512GB) – $499.99 (was $399.99)

Xbox Series S (1TB) – $599.99 (was $449.99)

Xbox Series X (1TB, Digital) – $749.99 (was $599.99)

Xbox Series X (1TB, Disc) – $799.99 (was $649.99)

Xbox Series S (512GB) – £429.99 (was £299.99)

Xbox Series S (1TB) – £519.99 (was £349.99)

Xbox Series X (1TB, Digital) – £619.99 (was £449.99)

Xbox Series X (1TB, Disc) – £669.99 (was £499.99)

Xbox Series S (512GB) – €499.99 (was €349.99)

Xbox Series S (1TB) – €599.99 (was €399.99)

Xbox Series X (1TB, Digital) – €749.99 (was €549.99)

Xbox Series X (1TB, Disc) – €799.99 (was €599.99)

Back in June, Microsoft blamed this latest set of price rises as the result of console storage and memory prices having "increased by more than 2.5x," with another "doubling by the fall of 2027" expected.

"The entire consumer electronics industry is struggling with the current components crisis, but the effects are particularly hard on consoles," Microsoft wrote. Unlike phones, computers, speakers, and other consumer devices, consoles are typically not sold at a profit, but instead for less than they cost to make."

The anouncement of the Xbox console price rises comes ahead of the release of GTA 6 in November, which is expected to increase demand for PS5 and Xbox Series X and S significantly. However, there are concerns that neither Sony nor Microsoft will be able to meet the demand caused by the release of GTA 6, with the AI boom making it particularly hard for hardware manufacturers not only to source components, but to release products at affordable prices.

Earlier this year, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma said the spiralling cost of new and existing consoles would require "radically different business models" over the coming generation. She added that the industry had "reached a point where it will be hard to imagine" mass audiences still being able to afford "thousands of dollars" for a new console generation.

The current PS5 and Xbox Series X and S generation of consoles have seen price increases rather than cost savings. Sony itself raised the price of PS5 consoles back in March , blaming "continued pressures in the global economic landscape." Nintendo has also not been immune, and recently acknowledged it would up the price of Switch 2, just over a year after its arrival. And Valve has bemoaned its struggle to release Steam Machine at the price it had initially hoped , instead having to go for an eye-watering $1,049.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social
