articles.title: Microsoft is bringing Xbox 360 games to PC
articles.summary: Microsoft is also planning to let developers bring their Xbox 360 games to PC, according to a leaked document. The company is also planning a disc to digital program.
articles.body: Building on its recently announced plans to bring original Xbox games to PC, Microsoft is also planning to let developers bring their Xbox 360 games to PC as well, according to a leaked document, seen by The Verge, that was sent to developers recently. Xbox 360 games will be able to run on the next-gen Project Helix console, “Xbox PCs,” and handheld devices, the document says. Microsoft has already said that Helix will play PC games, so making these older Xbox titles available on PC helps build a broader Xbox library that can travel between devices, similar to what’s already possible with Steam. Creating all these digital licenses also helps set up for a future of consoles without disc drives; Sony has already declared game discs dead, and Microsoft may follow. With 360 games, developers can opt into making them backward compatible, and they will have control over things like a game’s price and if it’s available on Game Pass. The feature is expected to have a “gradual” rollout between 2027 and 2028 “across next-gen devices.” The “full launch” of original Xbox games on PC is also set for October 2026; the initial program announced in July included just four games. The document also includes details about a way for players to get a digital version of a game that they already own on a physical disc, which The Verge’s Tom Warren reported on in July. The document says that if a player puts an Xbox One or Series game on disc into an Xbox One or Series X console with a disc drive, they’ll be granted a digital license that’s bound to “that disc and the player’s account.” The license will stay with a player across Xbox devices, but if the disc “changes hands,” the license will transfer to the new person. That should mean that gamers can still trade and sell discs; once the original owner of a disc does so, they can’t play the digital version they got from that disc anymore. According to the document, a public beta for the disc-to-digital program was set for July with general availability set for August. We understand Microsoft had originally planned to test its disc-to-digital program with Xbox Insiders in July, but the beta was delayed. It’s unclear if the timeline of August general availability is still accurate. The planned changes follow Microsoft’s major Xbox “reset” announced in July, which included thousands of layoffs and the company selling off four studios.

articles.title: The next Xbox could play every Xbox game ever made
articles.summary: Microsoft’s Project Helix is set to run games from every Xbox generation, but it’ll need publishers to buy in.
articles.body: The next Xbox, Project Helix, could theoretically have the largest library of any home console. Not only will it play PC games, but we now know, courtesy of a leaked memo obtained by The Verge’s Tom Warren, that it will run games from every generation of Xbox: the original 2001 Xbox, the 2005 Xbox 360, the 2013 Xbox One, and the 2020 Xbox Series, as well as any new Helix titles. We already knew that Microsoft was bringing a limited sample of original Xbox games to PC, and we already knew it was prepping a way to digitize your Xbox One and Xbox Series discs. The leak fills in the missing puzzle pieces. Microsoft is bringing Xbox 360 games to PC, too, and explicitly states that those games will run on Helix in addition to “Xbox PCs.” The document also clearly states that your digitized Xbox One and Xbox Series discs can follow you to “any Xbox device,” so Helix will get those too. Five generations of Xbox games under one roof. [Image: “You keep rights, pricing, and brand control.” But before you get too excited about “backwards compatibility,” you should know this isn’t the same as sticking a PS4 disc in your PS5 (or a Switch cartridge in your Switch 2) and pressing play. First, Helix may not have a disc drive at all. Last we heard, Microsoft is still deciding that. Second, it appears that these forms of backwards compatibility are at the mercy of game publishers. The leaked memo is Microsoft trying to convince those publishers by dangling profit in front of their eyes. The memo is literally addressed to publishers, and it’s transparently a sales pitch. One section is titled “Why publishers win.” Spoiler: Publishers primarily win because they can sell old games like they’re new again. [Image: “Dormant SKUs become live, purchasable products again.” Even with the disc-to-digital where publishers presumably don’t get a new sale, Microsoft offers a carrot: “Turn physical disc owners into digital customers” is the company’s sales pitch there. Maybe Johnny won’t buy a new copy of Mass Effect from you, EA, but perhaps he’ll buy five future games digitally! Don’t get me wrong, it’s good that Microsoft has carrots to dangle here. Because it sounds like the Xbox maker can’t even convert Xbox discs to digital without that publisher buy-in. In terms of engineering, Microsoft says publishers don’t need to lift a finger to make disc-to-digital work — “Publisher action: none required,” it writes. But Microsoft says early on that both of its new game preservation programs require opt-in. [Image: “You, the Publisher, keeps full control over rights, pricing, and brand.“ With original Xbox and Xbox 360 games, Microsoft is even more explicit: Publishers will have to give their permission for each and every title, decide how much they should cost, and decide whether those games should be included in an Xbox Game Pass subscription or be only available for standalone purchase. It’s not surprising that Microsoft would need permission. When Nvidia’s GeForce Now cloud gaming service tried to let you stream even your own already purchased PC games without permission, it got in trouble with lots of publishers and eventually went opt-in. [Image: “Turn physical disc owners into digital customers.” But GeForce Now also shows how you can’t rely on those opt-in permissions to stick. Some will disappear when publishers later revoke that permission or other rights issues creep up, and some publishers won’t opt-in certain games to begin with. At least Microsoft is a giant game publisher itself, even if it has fewer studios after its big Xbox “reset” that’s putting thousands of employees out of work. But even Microsoft may only have so much appetite to make old games run like new when it has to do all the work itself. Microsoft made roughly a quarter of the Xbox 360 library and around 6 percent of the original Xbox library play on Xbox One and Xbox Series consoles between 2015 and 2021, but that’s as far as it got. [Image: Also, Microsoft ownership is no guarantee a digital copy will remain available for purchase: Multiple Forza Horizon games have been delisted, including the backwards compatibility version of the original game, because their developer only secured temporary licenses to content inside — licensed cars and licensed music rights can expire. I hope it works, because it sounds very cool — Xbox 360 games with cloud saves, starting as soon as 2027! — and because the Xbox and PlayStation will badly need to justify their price tags in the age of RAMageddon and in the post-disc era. What would make a next-gen console great? With Sony, I think the answer is handheld. With Microsoft, maybe we’ll get one Xbox to play them all, but only if the publishers can be convinced.

articles.title: 'It Would Be a Real Shame for That Culture to Disappear': Final Fantasy 7 Revelation Director Says Physical Game Releases Must Continue
articles.summary: Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy director Naoki Hamaguchi has said that the end of physical games risked part of our culture disappearing, in the wake of Sony's controversial decision to kill PlayStation 5 discs.
articles.body:
Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy director Naoki Hamaguchi has said that the end of physical games risked part of our culture disappearing, in the wake of Sony's controversial decision to kill PlayStation 5 discs.

Last month, Sony made headlines when it announced and end to new games shipping on disc from January 2028 onwards, triggering a huge backlash from many fans. Now, at the recent FF14 Fan Fest, Ashif’s Release Notes asked Hamaguchi for his personal thoughts on the matter.

"In terms of my thoughts on physical editions, as a gamer myself, I love them," Hamaguchi replied, adding that, as a game creator, it made him happy when fans asked him to sign their physical copies.

"It would be a real shame for that culture to disappear," Hamaguchi continued. "I think physical games will still be sold in some form in the future, for example as a download code in a box. Moreover, I want physical games to continue — both as a creator and a game fan."

Final Fantasy VII Revelation Screenshots

This isn't the first time that Hamaguchi has addressed the end of physical games. At the same event, the director said he was pushing for a physical release for Final Fantasy 7 Revelation , though admitted that the matter had not yet been decided.

The long-awaited final part of FF7's remake trilogy, Revelation is currently slated for a spring 2027 release, when it will also launch across multiple platforms simultaneously. Asked again about a physical launch for the title, Hamaguchi reiterated that he would "like to have some kind of physical edition available," though could not yet make any promises. "We are looking into what the best options are, but I hope we will be able to live up to your expectations," he added.

"As it's nearing completion, I can personally pick it up and say, 'this feels good, this feels satisfying'," Hamaguchi said of the game in general, "so I’m quite confident about it. Of course, the final judgement will be down to the players but I feel confident, I can see the end, and I can finally feel the pressure lifting."

Final Fantasy 7 Remake and Rebirth started out as PlayStation exclusives before being released on other platforms, including Nintendo Switch 2. However, FF7 Revelation is due to ship on PC, PS5, Switch 2 and Xbox Series X/S simultaneously — a first for the remake trilogy.

"For me, it is quite meaningful to be able to bring it back to Nintendo platforms," Hamaguchi said of Revelation's multi-platform launch. A self-confessed FF6 fan , Hamaguchi recalled witnessing Final Fantasy's move from Nintendo to PlayStation as a child, and remembers playing the original FF7 on PS1, when the series moved from SNES cartridges to the greater possibilities offered by Sony’s compact disc format.

Other Japanese game creators have also given their opinions on physical games and the all-digital future we seem to be heading towards. Disgaea creator and former Nippon Ichi Software CEO Sohei Niikawa addressed Sony’s decision directly , saying that although it made sense from a business perspective Sony “may never have considered what physical editions mean to the people who value them." Hideo Kojima said of Sony’s decision that "I grew up with physical media, so I find it really sad." Nier creator Yoko Taro also echoed these sentiments in an X post where he encouraged people to buy physical game releases while they still can.

Verity Townsend is a Japan-based freelance writer who previously served as editor, contributor and translator for the game news site Automaton West. She has also written about Japanese culture and movies for various publications.

articles.title: Is the Ultra-Thin Motorola Razr Fold Worth Its $1,899 Price Tag? We Put Its Gaming Performance, Cameras, and Battery to the Test to Find Out.
articles.summary: Motorola packs it all in for this foldable, providing great screens, cameras, performance and features, even if it does end up a bit expensive.
articles.body:
The Motorola Razr Fold takes the Razr family to a new dimension. While earlier foldables from Motorola followed in the footsteps of the original Razr, offering a flip-phone style footprint, the Razr Fold opts for a hotdog fold, akin to what Samsung has offered from its Galaxy Z Fold lineup. Motorola hasn’t taken generations of iterations on this design to get to a very solid point, though. The Razr Fold is impressively thin and looks like all the experience gained from the earlier Razr foldables is paying off big. At $1,899, it’s not a cheap option, but it may still have what it takes to earn your money or at least due consideration.

Motorola Razr Fold – Design and Features

As mentioned, the Razr Fold opens like a book rather than an old school flip phone. Where Samsung’s early folders were normal-size while open and double the thickness of a typical smartphone while closed, the Razr Fold has jumped straight to ultra-thin dimensions.

Closed up, it looks almost like any other smartphone, and it’s a pretty one with a textured, rubberized back. It’s a little thicker than most, and the camera bump adds quite a bit of depth (that’ll prove worthwhile), but it doesn’t feel unusually large. Unfolded, it becomes impressively thin at 0.19 inches to edge out even the Samsung Galaxy S25 Edge or iPhone Air – camera bumps aside. The hints that it’s a foldable are the asymmetry and the seem running around the perimeter of the phone. It is a bit on the heavy side at 8.6 ounces, but that’s not so crazy next to the 8 ounce iPhone 16 Pro Max .

Folded shut, the 21:9 exterior display is a large 6.6-inch, 1080x2520 panel, and it opens up to reveal an even larger, nearly square 8.1-inch, 2232x2484 internal display. Both screens are sharp and bright LTPO pOLED displays with the internal reaching 120Hz and the external hitting 165Hz. For ultra-wide cinema, the external display will probably be the one to go with, and then it won’t really stand out from the crowd of bigger flagship phone displays. But for the wealth of 16:9 content out there (or even squarer formats like 4:3 or The Snyder Cut ), the internal display can provide a larger surface for viewing than the competition. That inner seam where the phone folds remains a minor nuisance. It shows glare readily, and it’s all the more apparent when displaying dark content or viewed at an off angle. You can also easily feel it when swiping across. That said, when the screen is lit up and you face it head-on, the seam mostly vanishes.

Either way, both screens can look gorgeous in the right conditions, and even though they love to show finger oils and glare on the interior folding seam is apparent, they push out enough brightness to easily get past that glare. You won’t want to treat the two displays the same, though. The exterior has Gorilla Glass Ceramic 3 that should withstand drops and scrapes a lot better than the internal display’s Ultra Thin Glass.

While you’ll want to be gentle with the phone, it’s still tougher than early foldables. It has an IP49 rating to keep a good deal of dust and debris out (just don’t fold it closed with a bunch of crud inside. It can also withstand submersion in freshwater and water jets.

It’s truly a shame we as a body of consumers let smartphone makers get away with killing the microSD card slot, because the Razr Fold likely could have had one. The SIM try in the phone is extra long, with easily enough space to accommodate two SIMs or a SIM and a microSD card, yet it only holds one SIM card. I might have accepted space constraints as an excuse if the SIM tray didn’t just have dead space built in.

Motorola includes facial recognition for sign-in. It also has a fingerprint scanner built into the power button, which makes it conveniently accessible whether using the phone folded open or closed.

Motorola has a bonus for creatives and handwriting enthusiasts. The Razr Fold supports a pressure-sensitive active stylus, and it worked quite well in my brief testing with it. I’d be careful about pushing too hard on the internal display, though. It’s also an optional accessory (i.e., even more money out of your pocket), and it doesn’t attach to the phone or charge from it either. It has its own separate charging sleeve that it inserts into for storage and recharging.

The speakers on the Razr Fold are decent, offering loud stereo sound that’s a decent match for the display.

Motorola has fitted a 5Gbps USB-C port with DisplayPort 1.2 output, letting the Razr Fold connect to an external display and work as something of a portable computer.

The Razr Fold is pricey, so it’s good to see that Motorola isn’t holding back on long-term support. The company is promising seven years of Android OS and security updates, which helps keep it competitive with Samsung and Google on those fronts.

The software itself is a tame implementation of Android. The phone came running Android 16, and it’s not heavy handed about AI features or bloated with unwanted software, though there is a button dedicated to recording notes, making images and quickly tapping into other AI features. The OS is fairly flexible with customization as well. I found the default quick setting buttons a little large, but the OS let me shrink some of them down. I could also go from a 4x6 home screen app grid to a 5x7 to get more apps just a tap away.

Motorola Razr Fold – Gaming and Performance

The Razr Fold doesn’t feature Qualcomm’s top-of-the-line chip, but it comes close with the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5, which gets 16GB of memory and 512GB of storage. This is a chip I saw in the OnePlus 15R , which mustered solid performance, and though the Razr Fold is wielding this chip in a much thinner chassis, it nearly keeps up. It’s not quite up to iPhone 17 or OnePlus 15 speeds, but it’s no slouch. The sustain is also impressive.

The phone performed surprisingly well for how thin it is. I played over a half hour of Neverness to Everness with the graphics settings at their max cinematic level, and though there was the occasional stutter, the game generally ran smoothly at 60FPS. At the end of my session, the phone wasn't even noticeably warm. It even managed 70% consistency in 3DMark’s Steel Nomad Light stress test.

The Razr Fold’s performance is enough to rival the Galaxy Z Fold 7 and even the new Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra despite the latter’s more advanced Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip. In my colleague Jackie’s review, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra could struggle under sustained loads. It started the Steel Nomad Light stress test with a high score of 1641 and sank down to 1,296 by the end of the 20-run gauntlet. That may have been more stable technically, but the Razr Fold started out higher at 2289 and finished with a low of 1600 points. It had also settled into a groove after 5 runs, so it seemed unlikely to ever sink as low as Samsung’s fold in the test.

The fact that Jackie found the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra uncomfortably warm to the touch after gaming while the Razr Fold was chilling puts the Razr in a great position to be the better gaming device.

The phone has a sizable 6,000mAh battery despite its thinness, and it’s even willing to take some pretty fast charging. It can juice back up at 80W from a wired connection of 50W from a wireless one. Sadly, even with some magnetism going on at the back of the phone, it doesn’t support Qi2. While battery life can vary dramatically from person to person, I was easily able to get through the day even while squeezing in some time gaming on the big screen.

Motorola didn’t skimp on the cameras included in the Razr Fold. It decked out the rear with a triple-sensor setup to rival Samsung, OnePlus, and Google, and it even has a couple of sharp selfie shooters. Here’s a quick rundown of what’s on deck:

50MP wide, f/1.6, 2.44-micron, 1/1.28”, OIS

50MP ultrawide, f/2.0, 1.28-micron, 1/2.76”

50MP telephoto, 3x optical zoom, f/2.4, 1.6-micron, 1/1.95, OIS

20MP exterior selfie, f/2.4, 1.22-micron, 90-degree FOV

32MP interior selfie, f/2.4, 1.28-micron, 88.5-degree FOV

I can’t say that the camera system is faultless, as it occasionally exhibits some oversharpening on the telephoto sensor, and it can get a bit soft and noisy in dimmer settings, but beyond those fairly common faults, it is excellent.

The cameras blend together well, matching one another’s color and dynamic range for a great consistency between shots. The sensors capture vivid color, bringing life to nature shots and street scenes alike. The cameras also snap sharp photos for loads of detail even when zooming in on them a bit. It’s just a bonus that the internal display’s squarer aspect ratio is all the better for previewing and reviewing the 3:2 photos that cameras will take.

The zoom is actually exceedingly strong. Though it has just a 3x optical, the 50MP sensor is happy to keep cropping in a bit further, and it has some impressive results. I could snap photos of details well beyond what I could see with my own eyes.

The sensors also do a great job handling macro shots, letting me get much closer to small subjects than I’m used to. The selfie sensors are no slouches either, snapping crisp photos with natural exposure. All of this combines to make the Razr Fold a rather excellent all around shooter for big and small subjects near and far.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra may have added in some higher-end cameras for this generation, but it will likely have its work cut out for it beating the Razr Fold. Motorola included a bigger, higher-res telephoto sensor than the Z Fold 8 Ultra’s 10 megapixels, and the main sensor here may be lower resolution, but it’s offering a slightly wider aperture, bigger sensor, and bigger pixels.

articles.title: Naoki Hamaguchi Doubles Down on Connecting All Final Fantasy VII Spin-Offs Into Revelation’s Ending
articles.summary: Final Fantasy VII Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi opened up on the game’s connection to the Advent Children film, saying that more than one of FF7’s spin-offs are going to tie into the game’s ending.
articles.body:
Final Fantasy VII Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi opened up on the game’s connection to the Advent Children film, saying that more than one of FF7’s spin-offs are going to tie into the game’s ending.

In an interview with YouTuber Ashif’s Release Notes at Final Fantasy XIV Fan Festival Berlin 2026, Naoki revealed that he’s well aware of the fan theories surrounding the next game in the Remake trilogy, particularly where ties to other properties in the FF7 universe are concerned.

He assured Ashif that he’s carefully considering all of these titles, specifically mentioning Dirge of Cerberus , Crisis Core, and of course, the Advent Children movie.

Final Fantasy VII Revelation Screenshots

"I see a great deal of that discussion. I've seen a lot of people discussing and speculating off the back of interviews with myself and with Kitase-san, 'Is the ending of this going to connect to Advent Children?'” he began.

“But it's not a question. I don't want to sit here and say it connects to this, it connects to that. But obviously, there are a lot of other titles within the VII universe. So, we're talking about Advent Children, we're talking about Dirge of Cerberus, Crisis Core . And we want to bring all of those in and make sure we're not leaving those out.

“And then on top of that, once we have all of those in place, we're looking towards the ending. And then the question is, what kind of ending are we going to head for in Revelation that still has those ties? And I think that's something that I really hope players will look forward to finding out."

While Hamaguchi was careful not to say anything that would outright spoil things, his answer has certainly fueled an animated debate within the community, especially following similar comments previously made by other devs working on the Remake trilogy.

Hamaguchi made similar remarks in an August 1 interview with Automaton , confirming that the Remake series is a “new, overarching universe that encompasses the lore of the many various spin-offs” in the FF7 universe — “not just Advent Children, but also Dirge of Cerberus and Crisis Core.”

“We’re not denying the possibility of the ending tying into FFVII AC, but rather, we’re saying that FFVII AC has just been incorporated into the overarching FFVII remake series, including the ending. However, I won’t comment on whether the ending is positioned to lead into it,” he told the outlet.

And in 2023, producer Yoshinori Kitase told Eurogamer very definitely that this is the case: "We are finally going to link up with Advent Children, that is going to be part of canon," he said. "The overall storyline, the developments, will not go wildly out in a way that will not add up to Advent Children in the end. I don't think anyone wanted that, that's not what we're looking to create here.

"[But] to make sure it doesn't become stale and people know exactly where it's going, [that it] doesn't just follow the original word for word, we add in extra elements which add that little bit of doubt. Getting the right balance of that is so key. Ultimately, we're not trying to change the Final Fantasy 7 story into something really different. The overall balance wouldn't really allow for that anyway."

Hamaguchi’s latest comments have created stirred up a heated conversation within the fanbase, with some lamenting the trilogy’s shift away from the original game’s storyline in favor of a metaverse-style combo of all FF7 properties, while others remain cautiously optimistic about what this entails for the fates of Cloud, Tifa, Barret, and co.

In June, Hamaguchi spoke further about Revelation’s ending, saying that while players will be able to shape the story in some way, everyone will ultimately come to a "singular ending."

"The idea is to kind of change the approach and the depth of these story moments for these characters in this final chapter," he said. "We hope players look forward to that moment in the game."

Final Fantasy VII Revelation releases in spring 2027 on Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S, and PC via Steam and Epic Games Store.

articles.title: Ted Lasso Sets the Stage for a Soft Reboot With a Kansas City-Set Season 4 Premiere
articles.summary: Ted Lasso Season 4 premiere review: Ted returns with an engaging Kansas City-set season premiere that catches us up with a few key characters, setting the stage for the show’s new soft reboot approach following a three-year absence.
articles.body:
Ted Lasso Season 4 debuts August 5 on Apple TV .

Three years after a Season 3 finale that sure did feel like a series finale at the time, Ted Lasso is back for a fourth season after all. In the modern streaming world, it’s become far too typical for a three-year gap between seasons to become something of a norm. At least Ted Lasso is accounting for this prolonged break in a bigger way, with a semi-reboot approach that feels more akin to a show being revived 10-15 years later rather than one we last saw the same year Oppenheimer was in movie theaters.

The third season ended with Ted (Jason Sudeikis) returning home to America and realizing it was time to stop being the semi-deadbeat dad he’d become, given his young son was back in Kansas City while Ted had been overseas coaching AFC Richmond. Season 4’s premiere is notable, because it’s actually entirely set in Kansas City. Ted is surprised when Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham), Leslie (Jeremy Swift), and Keeley (Juno Temple) show up on his doorstep, hoping to recruit him to return to London to coach the new AFC Richmond women’s division team.

The premiere was shot on location in Kansas City, giving it a markedly different visual landscape than your typical Ted Lasso episode, and it makes the most of it. And there’s plenty of comic mileage drawn from making Rebecca, Leslie, and Keeley the fish out of water for once, as they take in these new sights and sounds. The cast all slip very comfortably back into their characters, whether it be the sweet and funny sisterly connection Waddingham and Temple exude, or the lovably dorky demeanor of Swift’s Leslie.

As for the title character, series co-creator and EP Sudeikis still wears the smile and stache of Ted like he was born for it. Ted’s gotten through the mental health issues that plagued him early on, but we find him at a restless point of his life, working as an assistant manager at a supermarket. He’s still maintaining his usual sunny disposition, but clearly without a true sense of fulfillment. Of course, there’s not a lot of dramatic tension as to whether he’ll accept the offer to coach again — there’s a whole season’s worth of episodes to fill, and we’ve seen the trailers — but the premiere does a solid job of showing how Ted gets to the point where he can admit that’s what he wants to do.

Pushing things on the credibility side though is how the premiere deals with the fact that Ted not only wouldn’t want to leave his son Henry (now played by Grant Feely) again, but wouldn’t want to ask to separate Henry from his mother, Ted’s ex-wife Michelle (Andrea Anders). The solution feels far too easy and convenient, awkwardly handwaving what would likely be a very difficult conversation in real life.

Given the nature of the premiere and how focused it is — no other series regulars appear beyond the four mentioned above, and we never actually see London — it’s hard to be sure how much it will reflect the remainder of the season. But the approach it takes is promising as far as its willingness to lock in on just a few characters and interconnected situations.

While Ted Lasso never lost its kindhearted center, Season 3 was notably overindulgent and often felt lacking in form after EP/co-creator Bill Lawrence stepped back as showrunner. This was demonstrated by its incredibly overlong episode runtimes, which frequently hit a full hour or more in the midst of a show that began with half-hour installments. The amount of subplots and side stories got out of control to the point that we somehow were following the inner workings of two different restaurants at one point on a series that was meant to be about a soccer team.

As we prep to meet AFC Richmond's women's team, it’s definitely going to be odd adjusting to saying goodbye to the entire team we’ve spent the last three seasons invested in, and I do worry that it will feel even more difficult to move on thanks to the show still being set in the same location as before with most of the same support staff in place. It likely would have been an easier transition to send Ted and a few key players to an all new part of the world for a cleaner break from what came before, but even as we prep for these big changes, the premiere does give hope that Sudeikis and new co-showrunner Jack Burditt have learned that less can be more. Ted Lasso needed to feel more reined in again… albeit with a 47-minute runtime. Hey, that’s still short by Season 3’s standards! And while we have yet to meet the new team, the prospect of returning to the Season 1 feel of Ted and his team getting to know each other and once more starting from a true underdog perspective is a welcome one.

articles.title: X-Men '97 Season 2's Penultimate Episode Features a Reunion We've Been Waiting For, But the Results Are Strangely Underwhelming
articles.summary: X-Men '97 Season 2, Episode 8 features a return fans have been waiting for, so why does it leave us feeling so cold? Read our full review of "Dead Man's Hand."
articles.body:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for X-Men '97 Season 2, Episode 8!

I have to wonder if it was the smartest idea for the X-Men '97 crew to telegraph the resurrection of Gambit (A.J. LoCascio). At the time, that stinger scene was a great way to cap off Season 1 and tease what was to come. But now that we've finally arrived at Season 2, is having that knowledge working against the show as it actually brings Gambit back into play? All I can say for sure is that something is missing in Episode 8. Gambit's resurrection doesn't pack quite the emotional punch his death did back in 2024.

Maybe part of the problem is that we don't get a great sense of what Apocalypse's (Ross Marquand) larger goals are here. The obvious assumption was that he was assembling his latest and greatest team of Horsemen with which to dominate the world, and Gambit was his Death. But there's no indication that En Sabah Nur has been gathering other minions. He simply revived Gambit and then turned into a desiccated monkey corpse for some reason. I suppose we're meant to assume his spirit now resides within Gambit? Whatever the case, now back among the living, that simply leaves Gambit to assemble his old posse of thieves and assassins and do... whatever it is Apocalypse wanted him to do.

Part of that seems to involve punishing Candra, the X-Ternal to whom the two guilds have been paying their tithes for all these years. In what is easily the most disappointing element of Episode 8, we learn that Apocalypse and Candra were former lovers, and the latter stole a piece of his power before forsaking him. That all of this backstory is conveyed through a brief, matter-of-fact flashback sequence does this episode no favors at all. The Apocalypse/Candra dynamic needed to be a lot more fleshed out than it is, particularly with the previous foreshadowing in Episode 4.

Not to mention that, if the series really wants to dig into the concept of Apocalypse having a long-lost lover, the character Genesis holds far more storytelling potential. We can only hope this show sticks around long enough to tackle a proper House of X/Krakoa adaptation.

None of this is to say that Episode 8 doesn't sink its emotional hooks at times. While the long-awaited reunion between Rogue (Lenore Zann) and Gambit isn't quite what I hoped for, the two characters do have some strong scenes together. Rogue's opening nightmare is a strong start to the episode, and her entrance into Gambit and Xavier's (Marquand) psychic battle also stands out as one of the better moments of the episode. But again, too often throughout "Dead Man's Hand," I was left with the feeling that something is missing.

It's telling that I wound up finding more weight in the Summers family drama than Gambit's return. Episode 8 makes the most of the fleeting alliance between the X-Men and Cable's (Chris Potter) team, along with all the awkwardness that comes from father and mother being reunited with their now much older son. That plays right into Cable's more ruthless nature and his struggle to still be the man his parents (briefly) raised him to be. The Summers family tree is so stupid and so convoluted, but somehow this series makes us care about all of it.

It's also fun seeing the X-Men fully reunited after spending nearly all the season split into different camps. There's a small part of my fanboy brain that dislikes seeing the team simultaneously decked out in a mixture of classic '80s costumes and more modern New X-Men suits, but I'll allow it. In what is definitely the highlight of Episode 8, we see the combined might of the X-Men and X-Force take on Gambit's forces, only to get absolutely wrecked by Nightcrawler (Adrian Hough). It's a blast seeing what happens when this normally benevolent hero finally cuts loose.

"Dead Man's Hand" certainly has its moments, but this episode doesn't come together as well as I would've liked. And that's a little worrisome now that we only have one chapter left in Season 2. The show has an awful lot of ground to cover in terms of reestablishing Apocalypse in the present and orchestrating this final showdown between rival mutant teams. As strong as Season 2 has generally been, it would be a huge shame for it to collapse at the finish line.

articles.title: Burnt Out in Disney Star Wars? Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi Might Be Just What You're Looking For
articles.summary: Despite some early growing pains, Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi is a terrific and excitingly unique take on the iconic franchise.
articles.body:
This is a spoiler-free review of all eight episodes of Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi. The entire series is live now on Disney+ and Hulu.

The Star Wars franchise is definitely in a bit of a slump lately. The Sequel Trilogy ended poorly, and Lucasfilm is still in the process of figuring out how to move forward in that era. Meanwhile, the mediocre performance of The Mandalorian and Grogu shows that even that once dependable pillar of the franchise is hemorrhaging support. But one thing fans can generally count on is that Star Wars will always deliver when it comes to new animated projects. Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi does nothing to change that fact.

As the title implies, The Ninth Jedi is a spinoff of the two short films included in Seasons 1 and 3 of the Star Wars: Visions anthology series. As such, it's best to watch those first and get a feel for this futuristic setting and cast of characters before diving into the new series. Building on those shorts, this new series follows up-and-coming Jedi Lah Kara (Chinatsu Akasaki/Kimiko Glenn) and her allies as they search for Kara's father, Lah Zhima (Shin-ichiro Miki/Simu Liu), and battle the tyrannical Nawaam (Nao Omori/Young Mazino).

The core appeal of The Ninth Jedi is and always has been the blank canvas it offers. Many argue the best thing Lucasfilm can do for the franchise in its currently troubled state is to carve out a new storytelling era completely free of the baggage that is the Skywalker Saga. Well, that's precisely what you get with The Ninth Jedi. The series is set centuries after the films, establishing a completely new blank canvas on which to paint.

Mind you, the picture it paints isn't always that dramatically different from what's come before. Despite the massive time jump, this is a series that deals in a lot of familiar elements. You have the wide-eyed neophyte Jedi coming of age under the watchful eyes of a grizzled Jedi Master. You have a galaxy plagued by war after the Jedi have been all but wiped out. You have an evil empire that trades in planet-destroying super-weapons and is ruled by a foreboding, lightsaber-wielding villain in black armor.

The Ninth Jedi walks a fine line between celebrating the tropes of the franchise and becoming bogged down by them. Early on, the series tends to fall on the wrong side of that divide. It gets off to a fairly sluggish start in the early episodes, which tend to highlight just how little has really changed in this galaxy after all this time. If you took umbrage with the Sequels and the idea that the ending of Return of the Jedi wasn't a permanent victory over evil but merely a temporary reprieve in a neverending conflict, you may have a similarly hard time swallowing what this series has to offer.

But, eventually, The Ninth Jedi does find its groove, and with it, opportunities to take advantage of this wide-open new era. The show builds steam as it pivots away from simply focusing on the ragtag rebels fighting the evil empire and more into the motivations of figures like Zhima and Nawaam. With time, they become more than simply recycled archetypes, but fascinating characters with their own, unique views on the Force and the dichotomy between Light and Dark. Kara herself develops into a compelling protagonist whose journey doesn't simply mirror that of Luke and Rey Skywalker. One caveat, though - definitely watch the show in subtitled Japanese language form, as the English dubbed voices are mostly flat and bland by comparison.

Technically, The Ninth Jedi is a non-canon series (not that this distinction matters much when the setting is so far removed from the rest of the franchise). Regardless, it manages to hit on and develop some of the same ideas and themes that have been slowly percolating in other contemporary Star Wars projects. There's the notion of democratizing the Force . Here, being a Jedi is less a question of innate ability than courage and a willingness to fight in defense of others. There's also the concept of lightsaber blades changing colors and serving as a window into the wielder's psychology and moral compass.

Most interestingly, The Ninth Jedi dabbles with the concept of Gray Jedi in a more direct way than we've seen anywhere else in the Disney Star Wars era. In that sense, the lack of canonicity may actually be a boon, because it gives the writers and animators room to dig into an idea that the Lucasfilm Story Group still seems hesitant to embrace. This series is very interested in exploring that struggle to achieve a state of enlightenment beyond good or evil. There's power in embracing both the Light Side and Dark Side together. But is that the true endgame for a Force user? Is pure detachment a desirable state, or must it be tempered with compassion? All of these questions are explored over the course of the season. For a show that initially starts out on such familiar turf, it's satisfying to discover that The Ninth Jedi has so much on its mind.

Every Upcoming Star Wars Movie and TV Show

And even when the show is at its most predictable, it does have the benefit of not looking like any of Lucasfilm's more traditional Star Wars projects. The Ninth Jedi is once again animated by Production I.G, and they bring a very distinct look and feel to the franchise. The ships and droids are very different. The general vibe is more purely fantasy-oriented. Heck, there's an entire group of characters that are basically Tolkien-style dwarf space miners. Compare this to something like the MMORPG Star Wars: The Old Republic, where many of the character and ship designs feel right out of the movies despite the game being set thousands of years beforehand. This fresh take is greatly appreciated.

It's also worth pointing out how much the score adds to the whole endeavor. Composers Nobuko Toda & Kazuma Jinnouchi manage to capture the majesty and scope of the classic John Williams music without actually recycling any of Williams' leitmotifs. The music is both fresh and unique and deeply Star Wars-y, which is ultimately a solid metaphor for the show as a whole.

articles.title: Xbox Console Updates Adding New Capture and Achievement Features
articles.summary: Xbox has announced another set of new console features, which will begin rolling out to some users from today.
articles.body:
Xbox has announced another set of new console features, which will begin rolling out to some users from today.

As ever, these new features will begin being tested by Xbox Insiders in the Alpha Skip-Ahead ring, before slowing becoming available to all Xbox owners over the coming weeks.

The biggest addition here looks to be the ability to include party chat audio within gameplay captures, so you can fully remember a particular gaming moment and the reactions that came along with it. This feature has been designed so that individual party members can choose whether their audio can be captured, and only will be after players manually opt in.

Achievement hunters will likely celebrate to see an expanded set of options for tracking your progress, with your cheevo list now sortable by Last Played, Completion Percentage, Gamerscore Earned, Number of Achievements Unlocked, and more. And yes, you can sort these categories in ascending or descending order, allowing you to highlight where you're close to the full 1000G, or ready to start unlocking a new game's achievements from the off.

Next up, cloud saves. Players will be able to view and restore previous cloud save versions in supported games, starting with Forza Horizon 6, allowing you to recover an older progress point if necessary. If you ever experience a corrupted save (or want to go back and replay part of a game differently), this option should help you out.

And finally, Xbox is expanding your game wishlist — allowing you to add up to 1,000 titles. That should be enough, surely?

Today's updates come just days after Microsoft's latest set of Xbox console price rises have kicked in , raising the cost of some Xbox Series X and S models by up to $150 in the U.S., and up to an additional £220 in the U.K.

articles.title: This Unique 'Solo Journaling RPG' Has a Kickstarter Campaign that's Ending Soon
articles.summary: This unique 'solo journaling RPG' comes in the form of an advent calendar, and the Kickstarter campaign is ending soon.
articles.body:
Here's a unique take on a single-player tabletop game : Advent of Adventure is a solo journaling RPG that comes in the form of an advent calendar. The game is live now on Kickstarter . The campaign ends in just a few days, in fact, so now is the time to pledge if you're interested in this unique creative endeavor.

In Advent of Adventure, a greedy dragon has descended onto the North Pole and taken a stack of gifts for its hoard of treasure. Naturally, it’s up to you to save Christmas. You’ll set the scene for the unfolding adventure by imagining your character, and then each day a new door will reveal a fresh prompt for you to continue writing their story, leading up to a conclusion of your own devising.

This new, fantasy-themed calendar is following up from the independent UK-based publisher’s previous offering Advent of Abomination , which was conceptually similar but told a darker tale of Yuletide horror. Each day had a scare rating to guide you on how sinister it should be, and some entries offered a decision on additional prompts to vary things up.

If you want to get a sense of how a journaling game can pan out, you can read one gamer’s story on their blog , although obviously it’s full of spoilers if you’re planning to play yourself.

That first game proved a popular and unique offering, healthier and more imaginative than chocolate and rather more affordable for gamers than luxury dice or miniature figure calendars. Both are now being reprinted and you can back now for a November delivery, ensuring you get your game in time for the holiday season.

Each physical calendar is £15, or £5 for a digital PDF version (currently about $20/$6.50) and delivery is approximated at £6.50/$11-14 depending on your location. There are some fun extras to add if you’re interested, such as stickers, and coloring sheets or prints of the cover art.

articles.title: Xbox Is Planning Its Own Version of the Platinum Trophy
articles.summary: Xbox achievement hunters have something to look forward to this year, as the platform is planning its own take on the platinum trophy.
articles.body:
Xbox achievement hunters have something to look forward to this year, as the platform is planning its own take on the platinum trophy.

When the Xbox 360 launched in 2005, it came with a new feature known as achievements. If you do something cool in the game or make progress in the story, you'll be rewarded with points and an achievement to display on your profile. It was a really smart way to keep players engaged, push them to do things they might otherwise avoid, and increase competition. While Xbox wasn't the first company in gaming to utilize a feature like this, it absolutely popularized it, and it led to competitors like PlayStation mimicking the idea with trophies.

The trophy model is nearly identical to achievements, but the only difference is that you get a special reward when you get all the trophies in a PlayStation game: the lucrative platinum trophy. It's the end-all, be-all for completionists and now, Xbox is trying to emulate that. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has confirmed that, along with other updates to achievements , the team is looking to implement some kind of platinum trophy equivalent on Xbox later this year.

No details were provided on what that will look like, but it is exciting nevertheless. Typically, the average game's achievements cap out at 1,000 gamerscore, unless it's a collection of games or there's DLC. It's unclear if this new completionist achievement will add more gamerscore or be standalone as a recognition for your efforts.

This is something the Xbox community has wanted for a while, so it's great to see Microsoft implementing this level of feedback. It would be one of the biggest changes and additions to the Xbox achievement system since its introduction 21 years ago. It's unclear if this will retroactively apply to other games or if it will only be possible in new games, but it should be really cool regardless.
