articles.title: Nintendo beats earnings thanks to US tariff refunds it won’t share with gamers
articles.summary: Nintendo has smashed its first-quarter earnings estimates for the fiscal year, bolstered by strong games sales and US tariff refunds it won’t share with gamers.
articles.body: Nintendo has smashed its first-quarter earnings estimates for the fiscal year, bolstered by strong games sales and US tariff refunds, though its customers likely won’t receive anything from the latter. In its latest financial results, Nintendo reports that operating profits soared to 142.5 billion yen (about $902 million) between April 1st and June 30th, compared to 56.9 billion yen (about $360 million) for the same quarter last year — an increase of 150.5 percent. This spike is partially attributed to a boom in game sales, with Switch 2 software sales increasing by 9.2 percent compared to the previous year, and software for the original Switch console increasing by 38.6 percent. Sales for the Switch 2 console itself fell from 5.82 million units to 3.82 million units over the same period, though that current figure is higher than the 2.49 million units Nintendo sold last quarter. A sizable chunk of the boosted profit comes from refunds for US tariffs, with Nintendo saying it recorded “approximately $300 million as a reduction of cost of sales” for this quarter. While the company has increased the price of both Switch consoles over the last year, Nintendo says it bore the brunt of costs associated with tariffs instead of passing them over to consumers through increased product prices. That means it believes anyone who paid a higher price for their Switch console isn’t entitled to part of that tariff refund. Nintendo is currently defending this argument in court, in a bid to dismiss a lawsuit alleging that it’s retaining tariff refunds despite passing those costs to its customers. Other gaming companies have faced a similar legal battle — Sony was also sued by customers in May, who alleged it saw a “double recovery windfall” by collecting tariff refunds after increasing PlayStation console prices.

articles.title: Viture’s cheapest AR glasses have the sharpest image clarity I’ve seen yet
articles.summary: Its $299.99 Pro 2 cost the same as Xreal’s A01 Plus, but diopter dials make a big difference.
articles.body: I enjoy using display-mirroring glasses as a way to play Steam Deck games on a big screen, and I’m always on the hunt for the best pair. There’s still not one perfect model I can recommend to everyone, but Viture’s new $299.99 Pro 2 have sharper-looking screens than models that cost hundreds more. It’s mostly thanks to the simple but effective diopter-adjusting dials that sit above each eye. The dials move the lenses, helping more people get the clarity they are hoping for out of the box. These have been in some past models that sold for around $400 or more, but now they’re in glasses that cost a lot less. Most models have few, or no, built-in methods to improve clarity. The only recourse for blurry screens is to pay $50 for prescription lens inserts. That, or just return the glasses. (The Pro 2 glasses support lenses, too, in case the dials alone don’t help.) [Image: Each side has one of these dials that move the optics. Another perk here is the consistent sharpness across the Pro 2’s 50-degree field of view. I didn’t struggle to find a sweet spot; their entire FOV is easy to parse, be it text or other small details, like minimaps in games or menus. Sure, their FOV is smaller than some competitors, but I’ll take smaller and sharper over bigger and blurrier. Screen sharpness aside, the Pro 2 are basic screen-mirroring glasses without extra features that let you augment how big the screens are or where you can put them virtually. Their micro OLED screens can mirror or extend another device’s screen via a tethered USB-C connection at up to 1080p with a 120Hz refresh rate — standard stuff. They have buttons to adjust volume, brightness, and the screens’ color temperature. They’re even simpler than Xreal’s A01 Plus, which includes a stabilization feature to keep the screens still when you make small head movements, though it’s not a good substitute for three degrees of freedom, a feature found in pricier glasses that both of these lack. [Image: The Xreal A01 Plus (left) next to the Viture Pro 2 (right). In lieu of fancier features, Viture aimed to make these comfortable enough to wear for hours, and it mostly succeeded. The Pro 2 glasses weigh 63 grams (just a gram more than the A01 Plus), and both have a subtle clamping force that floats on top of my ears, touching the back of my head instead of painfully pressing on my cartilage. Their comfort let me play XCOM 2 and Red Dead Redemption 2 in 90-minute spurts — longer than I usually sit down to play games. I could do that with the A01 Plus, too, but I needed $50 prescription lenses to get similar clarity to what the Pro 2 offers out of the box. Even then, Xreal’s screens weren’t as consistently crisp. [Product: Viture Pro 2 glasses | One of the biggest differences between Viture and Xreal’s cheapest AR glasses and their pricier models is flimsier build quality. The Pro 2 and A01 Plus aren’t poorly designed, but the temple arms have more flex, and I noticed some heat on the Pro 2’s right temple arms during extended testing, which wasn’t pleasant to feel during these warm months.   It’s delightful not just to have more options in the budget-friendly AR glasses space, but to have good options, too. If you’re considering your next or first pair, the Pro 2 are excellent for the price. What they’re lacking in features they make up for with very good image clarity. Photography by Cameron Faulkner / The Verge

articles.title: Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' Episode This Week Unfortunately Proves That Humor Is Indeed a Difficult Concept
articles.summary: In Episode 3 of Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, we are remined that humor is indeed a difficult concept.
articles.body:
Spoilers follow for Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, Episode 3, “Human Best Friend.”

Ortegas and Scotty (Melissa Navia and Martin Quinn, respectively) get the spotlight this week, as their long-simmering (well, two-episode long) dislike for one another comes to a head in an attempt at a comedy episode that’s not necessarily funny , but is at least kind of fun at times thanks to game performances from some of the cast.

With the crew burning the warp core intermix chamber at both ends lately, and a key peace negotiation pending, Captain Pike (Anson Mount) and First Officer Una Chin-Riley (Rebecca Romijn) decide Alpha Shift needs a vacation. So a quick trip is planned to a resort planet where the unique atmosphere causes a type of inebriation for all who land there… and, of course, a lot of silliness too.

Look, Star Trek has been doing comedy episodes practically since the very beginning, and sometimes quite well, but there’s a trick to it. You can’t really make fun of your characters or break the logic of how they fit into the Star Trek world, and I’m afraid that “Human Best Friend” skirts dangerously close to both of those no-nos on occasion.

Again, it’s a fine line. When a sober Ortegas and not-so-sober Scotty visit an apparently wasted Spock (Ethan Peck) , he’s still very Spock-like. “I apologize for the mess,” he says as he adjusts a chess piece’s placement on the board by about one centimeter. It’s subtle and one of the funniest moments in all of “Human Best Friend,” but later, when the pair visit Pike as he’s getting a tattoo, it feels like the entire Strange New Worlds universe is cracking around us thanks to Mount’s over-the-top take on an inebriated Pike. It’s like seeing your boss drunk at the office holiday party, or even worse… your dad at a family gathering! Get it together, man.

Yes, I understand that Christopher Pike is capable of getting drunk (or whatever we’re calling this state), and yes, I also understand that he deserves some R&R like anyone else does. I also recognize that Mount is doing a swell job with the performance. But for the captain of the Enterprise to allow himself to be seen in such a state by his crew… I’m sorry. Maybe I’ve just spent too much time with Captain Picard in my life, but that sort of cheap gag breaks the show.

So each character gets their own bit to play: Workaholic Uhura (Celia Rose Gooding), so unwilling to relax, becomes the ultimate relaxer and relaxation host; Una sings Klingon karaoke power ballads; Dr. M’Benga (Babs Olusanmokun) does his best Cocktail impression; La’an (Christina Chong) is in commando mode (again); Chapel (Jess Bush) becomes a win-or-die Bingo player; and so on. Some of these bits are cute, some are a bit eye-rolley, but none really pop.

If the episode works at all, it’s because of Navia and Quinn, who have good chemistry and whose characters actually get to grow a bit through these shenanigans, as they’re forced to work together first to deliver a letter to the captain (“A piece of paper!?” says an amazed Scotty) and then to find their missing shuttle. That the two realize they’ve likely been butting heads because they’re, as Scotty puts it, “not so different after all,” is a nice enough thread for “Human Best Friend,” and sweetly played.

But again, the logic of the episode is flawed. By the time Pike and the crew are trying to fake their way through the negotiations back on the ship while still drunk – negotiations involving a civil war, mind you – it’s pretty clear that Alpha Shift really shoulda called in Beta Shift not just for the negotiations, but for the episode itself.

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

Dave Foley is mostly wasted as one of those annoying Star Trek alien salesmen types, but he does get a line or two that are worth a chuckle.

“It’s green.” Now we know where Scotty picked that one up !

I guess Ortegas keeps the gaffer tape handy.

Why waste a mugato costume when you’ve got one laying around?

We don’t usually hear about duty shifts (Alpha, etc.) on Starfleet ships. No doubt Captain Jellico would be pleased by all the mentions here (while simultaneously disappointed that it’s only a three-shift rotation).

The animated sequence in the planet’s advertisement is cute, but did you notice the woman wearing the same outfit that Andrea has on in TOS’ “What Are Little Girls Made of?”

So now we know that Scotty has six brothers. And this doesn’t include the at least one sister he has, who will one day have a son – the ill-fated Peter Preston from Wrath of Khan.

articles.title: Big Walk Is Unlike Any Other Co-op Game Around, Pushing You to Solve Clever Puzzles With Your Friends by Truly Working Together
articles.summary: A clever co-op puzzle adventure that uses communication like no other.
articles.body:
To know something's name is to understand it — at least just a little, be it the thing itself, or the world around it. In Big Walk, there are lots of things yet unnamed. You will certainly recognize trees, mountains, that dang cowbell. But there are plenty of things you won’t: the red, peanut-shaped objects my group calls a bean, which makes the structures they must be delivered to the bean towers. To us, the underground tunnel system is the backrooms, and the glowing medicine balls that light paths throughout the world are simply orbs – but not to be confused with the Big Orb, a mysterious and ominous structure looming in the distance. Big Walk is a co-op-only puzzle adventure that relies heavily on shared experience, shared language. Its genius lies in how it pushes you to decipher the logic behind the clever puzzles spread around its open world in a way that only you and your companions will understand. With all the twists and limitations it imposes, it’s unlike any other multiplayer game out there.

Big Walk is a puzzle game, and the puzzle is communication. Everyone is initially dropped into a playground of sorts with some colorful, blocklike structures to climb on, light switches to flip, and your controls pinned up as posters. I call this place home. Crucially, you are given no objective. We fiddle about with the buttons, obnoxiously clang the cowbell. We test out our movement options – mostly arm gestures – by looking at our shadows. Eventually, we head out into a lifelike world with lush foliage and waves breaking on the beach; it's a direct contrast to our charming, goofy characters, who are, essentially, a stack of three colored balls with googly eyes, stick arms, and twig legs (and a nose that moves like a mouth as we speak in-game).

When someone asked what we're supposed to do, what the objective of this game was, I couldn’t really answer that. And so we walked. But here's what I knew at this point: Big Walk has walking and puzzles. That, and outside of arm flailing or typing out written messages, we can only communicate through proximity-based voice chat. This means your voice is muffled when you're behind a wall, and echoes when you're in a vast tunnel. If someone wanders too far off, I can no longer hear them, and as a game that can only be played with others, it’s “cooperative” in the very sense of the term. There's no way to play Big Walk alone, and it supports up to 12 players with different settings for different sized groups: two, three, or four-plus, which adjusts puzzles slightly to suit the number of people in a session. Big Walk cleverly takes advantage of the essential limitation of proximity chat, and it wouldn't be the same without it.

Venturing out, my group of three walks together along desert terrain and up a cliffside until we find a button on a platform. We originally think nothing happens when it's pushed, but someone notices a faint red light flashing in the distance. It illuminates each time it's pressed, so we send someone in its direction to see what’s out there. There's a red bean in a box, which opens when the button is pushed. He grabs it and rushes back. No one knows what to do with it but it seems important, so we hold onto it (or try our best until someone drops it while falling off a cliff). Through that simple opening task, we start to get it: This puzzle, this bean, they’re teaching us something about the world and what we need to do within it. We're starting to create our own language.

Each piece of this map is cleverly designed to nudge your group to build something together, forms of communication that feel like only you understand. We keep walking, keep exploring and finding puzzles that require real teamwork, and continue to build our language. My group played in several sessions across a few days: a core group of three, with some stragglers jumping in here and there. We spent nearly 20 delightful hours romping around. It's easy for people to jump in and out of the session, popping in to adventure for a bit. There is a kink in this system, though. The save file is tied to the player who originally hosted the game. For my group, that was me. If my companions wanted to play when I wasn't there, they'd have to start a new save file—and a new big walk. This may very well be by design; developer House House wants a group to stick together. But I felt bad when someone wanted to play, but I couldn't.

Big Walk's world runs on a day-night cycle, with sun-soaked days and pitch-dark nights. And in the latter, a different kind of communication is built. Early on, my friend Riley dropped our only flashlight off a cliff, immediately after I accidentally kicked our walkie-talkie down the same one. We spent a not-insignificant amount of time looking for our tools because, without them, we could easily lose each other in the dead of night. (Even more so when looking for Riley, who got stuck in a hole while searching for our gear). Perhaps in another game, losing your tools or falling in a ditch would be frustrating. Not so here. While movement can be finicky at times, and you will briefly get stuck in spots, Big Walk often felt even more impactful when things were going very, very wrong.

We spent plenty of time doing Big Walk's actual puzzles, which are scattered around the map and usually embedded in big, brightly colored structures: a green horror movie house, an orange colosseum, a blue sound stage. Some of them are relatively easy, like throwing an orb into a basketball hoop multiple times, or playing a game of telephone to identify a specific sequence of shapes or buttons to push. But there are mechanical challenges as well, ones that require platforming and precise movement or throws. There's an entertaining puzzle that requires one person to put on a blindfold (which is actually a big, weird gold head that blocks their view) and navigate through an obstacle course. The others then have to yell instructions at them about where to go and what to do; the scariest part of this was figuring out how to time a jump over a gap. These challenges don't necessarily get progressively harder, because you're free to do whichever puzzle in whatever order you discover them. Some are certainly difficult, but never cruelly so. Big Walk always gives you the tools you need to solve them, so there's no danger of a dramatic learning curve.

One particularly inventive puzzle had my friend Chris locked in a soundproof room trying to relay little musical jingles to us so we could match that to stereos playing the corresponding melodies. Another forced us to split up onto three platforms that were pretty far away from each other and correctly time a synchronized button push. There are a couple puzzles with similar ideas, and the problem was often that we only had two walkie-talkies amongst us. So, we used our laser pointer to signify a countdown or our arms to send a silent message. Little by little, we created a sort of body language cipher to help solve matching puzzles and timing-based challenges alike, and it was a thrill to naturally develop our own system of visual cues.

Each of these puzzles rewards us with another red bean we have to take care of as we bring it back to a bean tower for deposit. Once you've found enough beans for a given tower, you get a special key to unlock something new and helpful: stuff you otherwise couldn't figure out how to operate, like a stalled train or an island-spanning chair lift. And in this progression, Big Walk further embeds the ethos that these discoveries are yours to make.

Big Walk's puzzles are always sharp, and always fun. The use of proximity chat makes the process of solving them feel special in a way I haven’t experienced in a game for a long time. Despite the recent wave of co-op games with an emphasis on hanging out with your friends, it feels so new to play in this particular way, as if we were all physically in this virtual space together. Video games often make us feel like superheroes, like the world revolves around our individual characters. In Big Walk, relationships and language are that superpower. The world doesn't revolve around me, but us .

So much of Big Walk's fun is found in the spaces between the puzzles, too. One of my favorite moments was this time Riley and I wandered away from Chris to go gallivanting in nature without care. This would not have been a big deal… if Riley and I did not have both walkie-talkies. Notoriously bad at navigating, we got wildly lost, even more so after we tumbled down the mountains once again. We were lost for nearly an hour, maybe longer. We went to the train to honk its horn. We tried to follow the coastline, then the train line itself, to make our way back to the place where we first realized we'd lost Chris. Then, a flare shot up in the distance. We walked toward the sound and eventually the direction of the green hue the blast gave off. That's where we found him, at a bean puzzle, firing off flares. Eventually, we sent Chris off to follow the curve of the flare and the bean was waiting at the end of it, like a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow. Riley and I certainly couldn't have been trusted to go find it.

I spent a lot of time playing Big Walk over the last week, but I also spent a lot of time thinking about it, and talking about it with the folks I played with. I'm thinking a lot about names, and the power they hold. In the book Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge, and the Teachings of Plants , author and scientist Robin Wall Kimmerer writes that names are how we, as humans, build relationships with each other and "the living world." She muses on what it might be like to not know the names of things around you. Kimmerer writes, "I think it would be a little scary and disorienting – like being lost in a foreign city where you can’t read the street signs." Big Walk's opening feels a little bit like that. Its island is not yet a place with which we've built a relationship, or developed a language. The moment you understand this, Big Walk changes. And what a special thing it is to name this world with friends.

articles.title: The Asus ROG XReal R1 XR Glasses Would Be Great If You Didn't Also Have to Buy the Mediocre Dock
articles.body:
Sometimes it feels like XR glasses are the next frontier when it comes to gaming accessories. And it makes sense, with the rise of handheld gaming PCs – at least before RAM prices started making them nigh unaffordable – these glasses are a great way to get something like the Steam Deck a bigger screen while you’re away from home.

So, it makes sense that Asus would team up with XReal to make a bespoke pair of gaming glasses, especially off the back of the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X . And when the glasses are plugged straight into a handheld, the ROG XReal R1 is awesome, with a clear picture and some nice RGB lighting. But, these glasses cost $849, and at least part of that goes to the dock, which allows you to connect multiple devices through HDMI and DisplayPort. That’s a cool concept, but it ends up being the worst part of the entire package.

Out of all the XR gaming glasses I’ve tried so far, none of them look especially good . Just due to the fact that there needs to be displays, mirrors and whatever else built into the glasses themselves, the format lends itself to bulky, garish designs. The ROG XReal R1s are no different.

The little hood that houses the displays measures about an inch thick, which naturally makes the glasses protrude a bit from your face. The outward-facing lenses, then, have this angular design that does look a bit more attractive than something like the Viture Beast , but not by much.

The ROG XReal R1 does hide the little camera that powers head tracking a bit better than most of its contemporaries, though. The entire front of the glasses is one piece of dark plastic, with a small section kind of boxed off in the center. The 3DoF sensor lies in that little boxed off section, and if I didn’t know that these kinds of glasses need a camera sensor to function, I wouldn’t have even guessed that it was there.

There are plenty of these kinds of glasses out there that try to at least maintain an air of professionalism. The Viture Beast, for example, prides itself as being great for productivity. But the temples of the ROG XReal R1 are about as ROG as you can get. In the middle of each temple are nine RGB lighting zones, arranged in little diagonal lines. By default they have the standard cycling rainbow effect we’ve all seen a million times, but you can change the lighting by messing with the settings.

Most of the time, you’ll do that through the buttons found on the left temple. On the bottom, you have a button that either centers the screen in your field of view, or opens the settings if you double tap it. Behind that button is what you’d expect to just be a volume rocker, but instead pressing it in either direction will bring up a little menu with which you can adjust things like tint, screen size, and, well, the volume.

The speakers are also in the temples, and they’re fine. They’re loud enough that you’ll be able to clearly hear the game you’re playing, but they’re not great at drowning out everything around. That’ll be fine for most people, but if you really want to get immersed in your game, or you just don’t want people around you to hear what you’re playing or watching, you should probably use some headphones.

I don’t think I’ve ever used a pair of XR glasses where the menu setup was intuitive, and the ROG XReal R1 follows that trend. After fiddling around with it for a couple of hours, everything did kind of click – but there’s a definite learning curve.

Everything changes once you plug the glasses into the dock though. The dock itself looks even more like a generic ROG accessory than the glasses do. It’s essentially a gemstone-shaped hunk of plastic with angular lines engraved into it. Shockingly, though, despite the need for dedicated power in the back of it, there is no RGB. The only lighting to speak of are indicator lights that tell you whether or not connected devices are on.

Above those lights are two triangular buttons and a little control stick. The button on the left is the power, and the triangle on the right turns on fps boost. This essentially lowers the resolution and ups the refresh rate from 120Hz to 240Hz. That sounds cool, but in practice it ended up with a glitchy picture where looking at text instantly gave me a headache.

The little control stick is how you’ll usually mess with the settings. There are shortcuts, where pushing to the right, for example, will switch the glasses between Anchor mode – where the display is held in one space – and Follow mode, where, you guessed it, the display follows you wherever you look. Most of these controls work fine, even though it is easier to use the buttons on the glasses. After all, when you’re using the glasses your vision is going to be a bit obscured, so it’s a bit awkward to try and look at what you’re doing down on your desk.

On the back of the dock, you’ll find two USB-C ports, one of which supplies power, along with two HDMI ports and a DisplayPort. Then, on the front is another USB-C port, which is meant for the glasses themselves.

However, the biggest problem with the dock was that when you push the stick upwards, it’s supposed to toggle between different visual profiles. That’s pretty standard for monitors these days, but for some reason, it simply didn’t work on the unit I reviewed. Even after updating the firmware and trying several different devices, the ROG XReal R1 was stuck on “Racing” mode the entire time I was reviewing it.

That mode didn’t necessarily look bad but, it’s always a bit of a red flag when a button just doesn’t do what it’s supposed to.

The dock being mediocre would be one thing if it was just an added accessory, but you can’t buy these glasses without it. And given that XReal and Asus are asking $849, when the XReal 1S is just $449 for a pretty similar experience, it does make you wonder how much extra you’re paying for the dock.

By itself, the Asus ROG XReal R1 is a 1080p display with a 120Hz refresh rate that sits on your face. Asus and XReal talk a big game about the actual display too, claiming brightness of up to 700 nits, and that it's 106% of the sRGB color gamut. I can’t actually test that, because the display is too small for a colorimeter. However, at its best, the display is quite colorful, though it is a little washed out and dim most of the time – but that might be the visual profile that the glasses were stuck on.

When the glasses are plugged into something like the Xbox Ally X, they’re pretty solid. Games look great, and XReal has done a lot of work to make text less of a pain to read. However, it’s important to keep in mind that this is still a 1080p display. You can stretch the display out to the equivalent of a 171-inch display, but when you do, the image can start to look a little pixel-y. The sweet spot, then, is having a smaller display in follow mode. That way, you can see the entire display without moving your head, and it’s not so blown up that you start to see the imperfections of the 1080p image.

I spent quite a bit of time laying in bed and replaying Final Fantasy XIII on the Lenovo Legion Go 2 with these glasses, and the game looked great – if a little dated. But one of the cool features on these glasses is an instant 3D mode. For some reason, that just wouldn’t work when plugged into the dock, but when plugged straight into the handheld it used the X1 chip built into the glasses to transform FFXIII into a 3D game.

That wasn’t perfect, obviously, but it kind of made it look like I was playing the game on a very large 3DS. But, because it was strapped to my face, rather than held awkwardly in front of me, the 3D effect didn’t immediately give me a headache as soon as I moved my head a little bit. I don’t know if I’d use the ‘Instant 3D’ mode all the time, but it is a cool little effect that adds, well, another dimension to whichever game you’re playing.

The big selling point of this ROG and XReal crossover, though, is plugging in a gaming PC or console and playing via the dock. After fighting with a firmware update, this worked fine enough. The display doesn’t change all that much when it's plugged into the dock, so it was still a good 1080p image, just with the same weird text shimmer that all XR glasses have right now.

But as soon as I enabled the 240Hz mode, everything went downhill. Motion is smoother with this mode turned on, there’s no doubt about that, but pixels that aren’t supposed to be moving start wiggling around a little bit. There’s this strange shimmer to the glasses when the 240Hz mode is turned on that makes subtitles actually painful to read and makes the rest of the image look downright strange, like static elements of the scene are moving somehow.

This problem goes away as soon as you push the little triangle button to swap the refresh rate back to 120Hz. I’m not sure what’s causing the problem, or even if I’m just particularly sensitive to it, but I’ve used plenty of regular 240Hz monitors without seeing that weird behavior.

It’s just another point against the dock, though. Really, the benefit of the dock is just the ability to easily plug in a gaming PC or a PS5. That’s a neat feature, to be sure, and I loved playing a bit of Beast of Reincarnation on these glasses through my gaming PC. But that’s not worth twice the added cost over the $449 XReal 1S or the $549 Viture Beast.

Jackie Thomas is the Hardware and Buying Guides Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: House of the Dragon's Season 3 Finale Had Little Sense of an Ending... But a Spectacular Battle That Leaves Everything in Play for the Last Season
articles.summary: House of the Dragon Season 3 Finale Recap and Review: There’s little sense of an ending here, but this spectacular battle left everything to play for in the final season.
articles.body:
Full spoilers follow for House of the Dragon Season 3, Episode 8, “The Traitors of Tumbleton.”

Back in the day, Game of Thrones typically delivered its big action beats in a season’s penultimate episode and spent the finale wrapping up loose ends and setting the stakes for the following year . House of the Dragon is a different beast: this season began and ended with all-out war, and if anything, this finale leaves too many loose ends dangling. If it’s less punch-the-air satisfying than the season opener, it may have more consequential revelations for what’s to come.

In King’s Landing, Rhaenyra (Emma D’Arcy) continues to make one unforced error after another. Driven to near hysteria by the news that Aegon (Tom Glynn-Carney) has survived, she exiles one of her more clear-eyed advisers, Mysaria (Sonoya Mizuno) and baffles her subjects, speaking to them about prophecies – occasionally in High Valyrian – when they’re worried about putting food on the table.

More troublingly, she makes a classic Henry II of England error and has the head of her church assassinated in his cathedral. That didn’t go well for Henry, who sparked widespread unrest and had to make significant concessions to the Pope to settle things down, and doesn’t seem likely to go well for Rhaenyra either. Perhaps significantly, Rhaenyra has the generally likeable Alyn (Abubakar Salim) strike the fatal blow. His brother Addam (Clinton Liberty) accused him of being overly ambitious and under Rhaenyra’s thumb; he may have had a point. Rhaenyra is no longer as hesitant as she once was, but fear has also made her vicious. The woman who hisses commands to Alyn in the Sept is not the same one who wrung her hands over violence last season. Something has broken in her; she may no longer be one of the Targaryens capable of greatness.

We also bade farewell this week to Queen Helaena (Phia Saban) , who has given one of the most quietly and consistently compelling performances this season as a woman who knows how tragically it’s all going to play out. The manner of her death – she threw herself out a window – was the same as the book, but there are some differences: her youngest son, Maelor, was born before her death on the page, and met his own tragic end. This is less horrible than the murder of an infant might have been, but it’s plenty disturbing. Her final scenes with Rhaenyra are also superbly done: watch how Viserys’ older daughter, when she tries to force Helaena to eat, impatiently puts aside the very tapestry that might have given her the answers she so desperately sought.

At Harrenhal, Aegon arrives on Sunfyre and resolves to work together with his wayward brother Aemond (Ewan Mitchell) for maybe the first time in their lives – albeit not before slapping him around a bit and threatening to kill him for, in fairness, his attempt on Aegon’s life. But Aemond’s obvious guilt and true repentance saves him; the pair set off to find the still-missing Vhagar and take the fight to Rhaenyra. We also learn, by the way, that Alys Rivers (Gayle Rankin) is the former Lady of Harrenhal. She was the wife of Black Harren, its builder, and was cursed to remain in the limits of its lands and never die when she sought dark powers in the forest to save the life of her badly-burned son. Alys’ background was never established fully in the book, so this is a new and potentially pretty potent wrinkle. In fact, Aegon and Aemond’s reconciliation is also new territory, and it’s going to be interesting to see how much trouble that terrible twosome get into as a united front.

The majority of the episode, however, concerns the attack on Tumbleton. Despite the efforts of the late Ser Criston Cole (Fabien Frankel) , the Rivermen have arrived en masse and Daemon Targaryen (Matt Smith) has flown down on Caraxes to take command and, oh yes, flame anyone who needs flamed. Ser Gwayne Hightower (Freddie Fox), one of the most likeable characters on the board and therefore probably doomed, tries to make peace by offering the return of the imprisoned Corlys Velaryon (Steve Toussaint), but no dice. He and Daeron (Benjamin Evan Ainsworth) are left trying to survive in the besieged city; it’s not clear by the end of the episode that Daeron is OK.

Meanwhile, Ormund is searching desperately for his ace in the hole, the dragonrider Ulf (Tom Bennett), who is so excited about his heel turn that he’s drunk himself into a stupor. Here, Ormund makes an ultimately fatal mistake. He’s so overcome by the stink of the privy where he finally discovers Ulf that he entirely loses his temper and whales on the other man. Ulf still does his bidding long enough to flame half the army of Rivermen – but he then turns his fury, and Silverwing, on Tumbleton itself and Ormund in particular. So long, you prissy little manbaby bully.

Ulf is not the only dragonrider who’s in trouble this week: Hugh (Kieran Bew) also left his post in King’s Landing to look for his wife in Tumbleton, running in with the ground forces, while Baela (Bethany Antonia) is grounded in the Keep after daring to criticise Rhaenyra. As for the episode’s title, there are any number of candidates. Ulf obviously, but Hugh also disobeys orders to go to Tumbleton. Daeron and Gwayne both betray Ormund in attempting to sue for peace; Ormund has arguably betrayed Aegon in elevating Daeron. And Daemon accuses Corlys of treachery when he argues for peace. There’s a lot of it going around.

The end result is shellshocked troops stumbling around a charred battlefield, trying to collect corpses, while Caraxes and Hugh’s Vermithor chase off Ulf’s Silverwing. The Battle of Tumbleton is – at best – a draw for the Blacks, and if it’s a victory for the Greens it might prove to be a Pyrrhic one, what with the loss of Ormund, their best strategist, and the uncertain fate of Ulf and Silverwing afterwards.

House of the Dragon: Season 3 Official Images

At this point it’s a positive disadvantage to have read the books; some of us have been waiting for one face-off for nearly half a decade now, since that could plausibly have happened at the end of Season 1 or the start of Season 2. Now we will have to wait two more years if it’s even going to happen as written. The overall shape of the show is also becoming more evident, and something that I wrote about last season seems to be taking shape ( read that here if you’re not scared of major spoilers ). Whether showrunner Ryan Condal and his team can stick the landing for the finale better than Game of Thrones did remains to be seen, but they have made a great foundation for it this year.

articles.title: Final Fantasy Fans Convinced Dirge of Cerberus Remake on the Way After Gackt Posts Photo in Genesis Cosplay
articles.summary: Final Fantasy fans are convinced a Dirge of Cerberus remake could be on the horizon after one Japan’s most famous rockstars, Gackt, posted a photo of himself cosplaying as Crisis Core's Genesis.
articles.body:
Final Fantasy fans are convinced a Dirge of Cerberus remake could be on the horizon after one Japan’s most famous rockstars, Gackt, posted a photo of himself cosplaying as Crisis Core's Genesis.

Gackt famously voiced Genesis Rhapsodos in the Japanese dubs of both Crisis Core and the not-so-secret secret ending in Dirge of Cerberus . It’s fairly well-known that he helped inspire and even design the character, who’s been a fan-favorite since his first appearance nearly twenty years ago.

While Gackt reprised his role for the Crisis Core remake in 2022, not much has been seen of Genesis since then — until now.

Crisis Core –Final Fantasy 7– Reunion Steam Screenshots

On August 6, 2026, Gackt posted an Instagram reel showing himself decked out in a Genesis cosplay (though, can it truly be called a cosplay if Gackt is literally him?) with his song Redemption playing in the background. Eagle-eyed fans will have clocked that Redemption was written and performed by Gackt as the official theme song for Dirge of Cerberus, and it’s causing a frenzy as fans speculate about news of a possible remake of the Vincent Valentine-focused game.

It’s one of the few remaining Final Fantasy VII spinoff titles left that hasn’t received an official remake, and it’s one that could certainly do with a refresh. While it's status as a beloved entry in the FF7 universe is unquestionable, its control scheme and overall gameplay looks a bit rough in the rear-view , making the idea of a remake pretty appealing.

One fan noticed a similar pattern in Gackt’s Instagram posts that lined up with his previous social media activity leading up to the Crisis Core remake. As told by ‘ nibelbound ’ on X, Gackt posted about returning to a studio he hadn’t visited in “over ten years” to perform some voice recordings just four days before the Crisis Core remake was announced at Summer Game Fest 2022.

Of course, a Dirge of Cerberus remake isn’t the only idea sparking a furor among Final Fantasy Fans; others speculate that this means Genesis could make an appearance in Final Fantasy VII Revelation , which is set to be shown off at Gamescom 2026.

It wouldn’t be a complete reach to think so, either; Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi recently doubled down on connecting all the Final Fantasy VII spinoffs into the game’s ending, making special mention of Crisis Core and Dirge of Cerberus.

"There are a lot of other titles within the VII universe. So, we're talking about Advent Children, we're talking about Dirge of Cerberus, Crisis Core. And we want to bring all of those in and make sure we're not leaving those out,” he said in an interview with YouTuber Ashif’s Release Notes at Final Fantasy XIV Fan Festival Berlin 2026.

“And then on top of that, once we have all of those in place, we're looking towards the ending. And then the question is, what kind of ending are we going to head for in Revelation that still has those ties? And I think that's something that I really hope players will look forward to finding out."

With Dirge of Cerberus's storyline getting some time to shine in Ever Crisis , along with subtle nods to the game in Final Fantasy 7 Remake Intergrade, it's looking more likely than ever that DoC, as well as Genesis, could be getting a long-awaited 'Reunion' with their fans, if you will. (I'm here all week, folks.)

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze .

articles.title: The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Nintendo Switch 2 Console Images Reportedly Leak
articles.summary: Leaked images of a The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Nintendo Switch 2 console and Pro Controller appear to be circulating online.
articles.body:
Leaked images of a The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Nintendo Switch 2 console and Pro Controller appear to be circulating online.

Photos of the unannounced Nintendo hardware were posted to X/Twitter today by Necro Felipe, the owner of well-known Brazilian gaming site Universo Nintendo, who stated that, per his sources, the designs were legitimate. IGN has contacted Nintendo for comment.

The images show a Switch 2 dock with golden Triforce design printed on one side, and a Switch 2 console with black/teal Joy-Con controllers, each also adorned with Triforce patterns.

VAZA encarte do Nintendo Switch 2 temático de Zelda (40 Anos) pic.twitter.com/4cmTceyxeb — 'Necro' Felipe #UnivNintendo (@necrolipe) August 11, 2026

VAZA encarte do Nintendo Switch 2 temático de Zelda (40 Anos) pic.twitter.com/4cmTceyxeb

A matching Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller: The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition mirrors the black/teal coloring for its base, with a golden central Triforce design and gold shoulder buttons and triggers.

Mais ângulos (e encartes) do encarte para o Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller - The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition pic.twitter.com/RiCOSEiZto — 'Necro' Felipe #UnivNintendo (@necrolipe) August 11, 2026

Mais ângulos (e encartes) do encarte para o Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller - The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition pic.twitter.com/RiCOSEiZto

An unrevealed Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary logo can be seen on packaging for both items, featuring a small NES-era Link icon. It'll be interesting to see where else this logo pops up, and how Nintendo markets its big Zelda anniversary.

To date, Nintendo has not marked Zelda's 40th anniversary year — and the actual date that the first Zelda game launched on NES has now come and gone. But there are still several months of 2026 left, and the company has now confirmed it will release its The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Switch 2 remake before the year ends.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Trailer June 2026 Nintendo Direct - Screenshots

Nintendo fans expect a big Zelda 40th anniversary push soon, with more details of that Ocarina remake, the official reveal of this hardware, and a first trailer for the franchise's live-action movie that's set to debut on April 30, 2027. Perhaps we'll see all of this revealed in an upcoming Nintendo Direct?

Last week, various pieces of casting information also leaked , adding to the sense that leaks are happening now as Nintendo begins readying a big reveal. The late, great Sam Neil was reported to be part of the film's cast, alongside the previously leaked Dichen Lachen (Succession) as Impa, Uli Latukefu as Ganondorf, plus Yvonne Strahovski and Lydia Peckham in unknown roles.

Benjamin Evan Ainsworth, the young House of the Dragon star set to play Link, has recently offered his first thoughts on playing the Nintendo legend , meanwhile.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls Ticks Nearly Every Box, With Gorgeous Art and Excellent Action That Can Appeal to Players of Any Skill Level
articles.summary: A gorgeous and innovative fighting game that can appeal to all skill levels.
articles.body:
It’s a very rare feat when a fighting game manages to tick virtually every box across the board: Excellent fighting mechanics, fantastic teaching tools, great netcode, and both hardcore extras like Replay Takeover alongside more casual treats like a worthwhile story and ancillary modes. Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls is about as close as a game has gotten to checking all of those boxes since Street Fighter 6. This is a gorgeous and innovative fighting game that can appeal to players of all skill levels, with characters that are easy and satisfying to just mash some buttons with, but equally fun to dive deep into and tinker with in the lab. The albatross that used to hang around its neck was the poor performance of the PC version at launch, but thanks to a recent patch that seems to have fixed most of those issues, Tokon is now a recommendation I can make wholeheartedly without any caveats.

Let’s start with the fundamentals: Tokon is a 4v4 tag fighter with a bunch of unique rules that attempt to control the inherent chaos of having eight swappable characters in a single match. For example, all characters on a team share the same lifebar, removing one of the core elements of traditional tag fighting games, which typically let you swap in a fresh fighter so the damaged one can restore health while they sit on the sidelines. It’s a smart adjustment that allows for a much cleaner UI, avoids the pitfall of 4v4 matches that would otherwise run too long, and removes one of the big barriers of entry to any traditional tag fighter: the need to learn multiple characters in order to have a competitive team.

But what’s especially cool is that while you can be very strong by knowing how to play just one character, there’s still a ton of value in crafting a well-synergized team. For instance, if you know that your main struggles in a particular match up, like maybe your opponent plays Magneto and you would have trouble against his strong zoning, you could have a better option waiting in the wings. Or maybe you have a character that you really like but have trouble opening opponents up with, like in my case, Blade – you could lead with a more mix-up-heavy character, and once you land the hit, swap to continue the combo and deal more damage than the mix-up character might have been able to get on their own.

What I really love about this system is that you can add new elements to your gameplan piece-by-piece rather than feeling like you need to have everything on lock right from the start. When I first started playing, all I needed to do was get competent with Spider-Man. I learned some high/low mix-up options, some bread and butter combos, got a basic understanding of how to use his web-zip to maneuver around the screen, and I felt ready to start playing against other people online. When I started to feel like I hit the ceiling of what I could do with just Spider-Man, I went back into training mode to learn more about Blade, and was able to add new layers to my gameplan. After that, I added in Magneto as an assist to help me convert more damage off of the low part of my high/low mix-up. Now I’m experimenting with the fourth position to try to find someone else with an assist that adds extra value to my team. This process of being able to start with a small foundation and build upon it is the ideal way to learn a fighting game, and Tokon feels designed specifically for it.

Those assists are where things start to get a little strange. You see, Tokon doesn’t begin as a 4v4 fighter. Instead, every match starts with just two of the characters on each team available, with the remaining fighters needing to be unlocked by either landing a light auto-combo, hitting the opponent with a move near the corner that causes a stage transition or wallsplat, or losing a round. Unlocking these characters is important, because each one increases your overall health and adds another bar to your Assemble meter, which governs the ability to call assists during specific moments.

Tokon has a lot of hyper specific rules surrounding its assists, which leads to a system that can be fairly overwhelming for newcomers – it was certainly a lot to take in for me, even as someone who’s played many tag fighters like Marvel vs Capcom, Dragon Ball FighterZ , 2XKO , and more. Before a match begins, you place your four characters into various positions: Leader, Shooter, Vertical, and Assault. These placements determine what kind of assist is used when you call them out in neutral (meaning when you’re just standing still or walking without pressing a button or blocking). Leader is whoever the current point character is, Shooters will use a projectile, Verticals predictably cover a vertical hit box, and the Assault spot is generally reserved for each character’s most powerful assist.

These neutral assists don’t cost any meter, but if you try to call an assist after landing an attack to pick up a combo or to cover your recovery after a blocked move, you’ll instead get a universal dash-attack assist that costs one bar of the Assemble meter. What’s finicky about this system is that you have to be very precise with your assist call, because if it happens too early (or too late) the assist won’t come out. This extends to the active tag system, which allows you to switch control to your assist character for a brief period while they’re on the screen. It’s very similar to 2XKO, but here it feels much more restrained. In 2XKO, you can basically swap to your assist character at any point, enabling some really tricky mix-up opportunities. Tokon, on the other hand, seems to be much more hesitant to allow these kinds of unrestrained mix-ups. That isn’t to say that you can’t do gnarly things with the active tag system once you lock your opponent down in blockstun, just that the rules that govern the system are a little more rigid than what I’m used to.

And you know what, that’s probably for a good reason – given how cluttered the screen can get with four characters throwing nonsense out all at once, I think the amount of chaos that Tokon allows is already more than enough. Especially when you’ve got characters like Peni Parker, who takes up a huge portion of the screen and can send out a bunch of random drones; Magneto, who can fill the screen with literal garbage that can enhance his attacks; Magik, who can summon fire pillars that cover a fourth of the field. It can be very easy to lose track of what’s going on.

There are some cool nuances to the tag system as well: The raw tag outs have a bit of delay to them, so you can do cool stuff like tag, perform a move during the delay, and when you take control of the incoming character, the previous character’s move will cover your approach without needing to spend a bar of the assemble meter. It’s touches like these that really add that extra layer of depth that makes learning Tokon on a deeper level so much fun.

The characters themselves are Tokon’s greatest strength. We’re no stranger to seeing a lot of these faces in fighting games before, but ArcSystem Works has gone above and beyond in terms of making them feel authentic to their comic book counterparts, while also ensuring they are each a blast to play in their own particular way. Spidey is able to zip all across the stage, baiting anti-airs by hanging and then jumping off his webs; Storm can manipulate the weather to push and pull objects and enemies (or even snatch her opponent in a command grab from half-a-screen away with a gust of wind that pushes her forward); Deadpool is a walking love letter to the FGC with a kit that is almost entirely comprised of memes and special moves from Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat, King of Fighters, Tekken, Guilty Gear, and much, much more.

It’s an impressive roster of 21, and while there are certainly some notable omissions (especially on the X-Men front) and curious inclusions ( *cough Danger cough* ), the characters who did make the cut do a good job of justifying their spot with very unique playstyles that add something special to the roster. I can’t imagine Green Goblin being at the top of anyone’s list of characters to include in a Marvel fighting game, but he has ended up being one of the most interesting thanks to his unique ability to fight both on and off his glider.

The most delightful surprise about Tokon is that its story mode is actually pretty dang good! It’s broken up into five episodes, with each episode essentially being its own graphic novel centered around one of the five canonical teams of four: The Fighting Avengers, The Unbreakable X-Men, The Amazing Guardians, Samurai Outriders, and Knights of Doom.

The set up for all of this in-fighting between Marvel heroes and anti-heroes (and a few straight up villains) is the same throughout each of the episodes: an otherworldly being known as The Champion has challenged five of the Earth’s mightiest warriors to compete in a tournament, with the winners getting the opportunity to do battle with him – and, should they win, he will grant them any wish they desire. So it’s basically a Marvel version of Mortal Kombat meets Twisted Metal, and while that concept doesn’t win any points for creativity, it does for execution.

The episodes themselves are presented like motion comics, each illustrated by a different famous manga or comic book artist. This gives each story its own distinct art style, and I loved seeing all the different takes on these iconic characters. It’s especially cool as a big anime fan to see famous mangaka like Hiro Mashima of Fairy Tail fame and Betten Court, the creator of My Hero Academia: Vigilantes, each apply their very distinctive art styles to classic Marvel characters like Captain America and Spider-Man.

It’s not just the art though, the writing is strong as well. Kieron Gillen, the writer of all five mini-stories, does a great job of tailoring each one to the strengths of the characters involved. The Amazing Guardians focuses on Peter Parker struggling with the need to be a leader and reluctant mentor to Ms. Marvel, while also trying to rein in the added chaos of having a wildcard like Peter Quill on his team. Meanwhile, the Unbreakable X-Men episode deals with the familiar conflict of Storm, Magik, and Wolverine being heroes to a population that reviles them purely because they’re mutants. There’s not a lot of time to explore these themes beyond anything but a surface level, but the fact that there’s at least something to chew on at all is a step in the right direction for fighting game stories.

These episodes aren’t the end of Tokon’s ancillary modes either. There’s a survival mode that challenges you to take on 100 fights against steadily more difficult foes, giving you a variety of stat boosts to choose from as you increase your power level every five rounds. Your progress is saved at those five-round milestones as well, so it isn’t a true survival mode, since you get to restart without losing much progress, but it’s still a nice diversion for people who want another challenge to conquer before taking the fight online.

And then there’s Arcadia Rumble, which is entirely its own beast. It’s almost structured like a fighting game version of the City Trial mode from Kirby Air Riders , in that it’s split up into two phases that alternate for a total of five rounds, with the first phase being all about powering up your characters, and the second phase being about taking your powered up characters and competing against other juiced up fighters. Up to eight players and their customizable avatars roam around Tokon’s gigantic lobby with the goal of collecting stars. Stars can be obtained by beating up other players and knocking them out, participating in limited time events that pop up around the map, or defeating other players in the second phase, which are the traditional 4v4 battles. It’s actually pretty fun, and while I don’t see myself personally spending a ton of time with it beyond what I’ve played for this review, I can definitely see its value as a mode where players of all skill levels can play together and still have a chance to win.

This whole package is rounded out with some of the best teaching tools I’ve seen in a fighting game: General mechanics breakdown with playable lessons, character guides that explain the basics of each kit, practical combo explainers that cover things like how to convert a combo off of a unique skill, and my favorite feature, free-form combo challenges that simply give you a move you need to include in the combo and a damage threshold you need to hit.

I love this so much, because it really encourages people to actually experiment and learn the characters rather than just memorize a string of buttons. The prompts you’re given are often very practical as well, teaching me how I should combo off of Spider-Man’s overhead, or what I should do when I land a hit but don’t have any assemble meter, or what my big cashout combo is when I land a hit and have full resources. Not to mention the excellent training mode, replay searching, replay takeovers, training presets, and so on. It’s everything I could ask for when it comes to learning tools, and Tokon has it all right out of the gate.

I’d be remiss not to mention the PC performance woes that many people have had since launch, and even in the beta before it. Personally, I didn’t actually have any notable issues on my rig, but I say that as someone running a GeForce RTX 5090 and AMD Ryzen 9 16-Core processor with 32 GBs of RAM, so I would certainly hope that’s the case.

That said, on several occasions while I was playing online this past weekend, I’d be in a match where everything moved at a fraction of the normal speed. These games always were against other PC players who had green network connections when I accepted the match, and they felt very different from the standard experience of playing someone on a poor connection. My guess is that these opponents were having performance issues, and that those problems were affecting my game even if I wasn’t personally experiencing them.

But wait! Good news arrived just as I was finishing up this review: A patch dropped only a few days after release that has seemingly fixed many of the PC issues that were being reported. True enough, since then I haven’t seen any matches like what I just described. I haven’t done a ton of testing myself yet, so I’ll continue to play on PC and will update this review should any issues arise, but it seems like the Tokon team may have managed to narrowly avert disaster.

However, the one minor complaint I do still have regarding online play is the fact that matchmaking has been quite slow considering how many players Tokon has. The speed of getting in and out of matches is the one place Tokon pales in comparison to other modern fighters, which is a bit of a bummer. But since you can mess around in training mode during a queue, it’s at least more time that I get to spend working on my combos, and I certainly need the practice.
